It had all been for him, and now he was gone. The very reason for her existence had died, leaving her lost. Again. And utterly alone.

Without realizing it, her grip tightened, crushing the aluminum in her hands. With a sharp grunt of frustration, Rio hurled the can away, listening to it clatter loudly against the bedroom wall.

“Rio?”

The voice was faint, barely a whisper, but it made her jolt as if she’d been struck by a current. “Are you okay?”

Five short, rhythmic knocks followed the question — a familiar wooden pattern she hadn’t heard in ages. Rio let out a weary sigh, sinking deeper into the mattress.

“Yeah, I’m fine,” she grumbled reluctantly, her voice a raspy growl before she buried her face in the pillow. Of course the universe wouldn’t grant her a single minute of peace.

“Are you sure? Can I come in?” The persistence from the hallway made her groan again. Rio rolled her eyes in the dark, closing them tightly a second later. “It’s me.”

“I know it’s you, pendejo,” she muttered.

When she finally opened her eyes, her brother was already peering through the crack of the door, his brow furrowed with worry. She exhaled, exhausted to her core.

Benito offered a hesitant, uncertain smile and shrugged. Rio remained silent, simply watching him walk in. It wasn’t that they hadn’t seen each other in years; his last visit was relatively recent. Still, it was jarring to look at the man he had become — tall, strong, and carrying the same magnetic presence as their father. Yet, the moment their eyes met, he looked like a little boy again. Her boy, her pendejo.

It was like looking at a stranger who, by some inexplicable magic, held her heart in the palm of his hand. As he paced the room in short steps, taking in details that no longer felt familiar to him, she couldn’t tear her eyes away. He was a distorted mirror: everything that had made her bitter had made Benito sweet. And yes, she was angry, but it was love and longing that made her eyes well up — a sudden emotional overflow that she tried to hide behind a mask of resentment, tightening her lips and forcing shallow breaths.

She resented him deeply — so much that her chest physically ached — but god, she loved him. Watching him now — wary, frowning, analyzing the corners of the room — Rio wondered how she could have ever forgotten the sheer weight of that affection. Damn pendejo, he always knew exactly how to disarm her. She let out a faint, self-contemptuous huff; even when she admitted her love for him, she found a way to make it sound bitter. Broken. Just like she was.

When he looked back toward her, Rio sharply averted her gaze and lowered her head, sniffing. She silently begged her body not to betray her; she couldn’t let her brother see her cry.

“I like the new color… It looks nice,” he murmured, his steps hesitant and guarded as he approached.

She gave a vague nod, her eyes scanning the olive-green walls.

“It’s not new. It’s been over five years,” she countered quietly.

Benito merely grunted, a self-conscious mix of surprise and awkwardness. Rio shook her head, more to herself than to him.

Without another word, Benito sat beside her on the bed. His face creased into a frown as he stared at his clenched fists, clearly lost in thought. Rio felt her defenses soften slightly. In the body of a giant man, he still looked like a little child; she clenched her own fists against her sides, fighting the overwhelming urge to reach out and stroke his wavy hair. Instead, she stayed perfectly still, maintaining a blank expression while a whirlwind of emotions turned her inside out.

“What?” she asked, her voice a tense blend of impatience and nervousness as she slowly arched her eyebrows.

Her brother turned to face her fully. With a worried expression, his large, gentle brown eyes locked onto hers, silently pleading for something. Something she knew that, deep down, she was begging for too.

Looking into his eyes, Rio felt swallowed by her own reflection. She saw the exact same pain there, the same resentment, the same profound love. They were different pieces of the very same whole. And what hurt more than she cared to admit was the simple fact that, despite everything, he was still a part of her, just as she was a part of him.

“I really am sorry. For everything,” he said.

The moment the words left his mouth, the knot in Rio’s throat tightened, and she instantly looked away.

“I know. You already said so; we talked today,” she replied, shifting uncomfortably on the bed to hide her distress.

Benito only let out a tired, heavy sigh.

“Rio, I lost him too. I lost my father, too.”

The sudden crack in her brother’s voice sent a physical ache through the tight know in her throat. Breaking down, she nodded silently as tears finally began to stream down her face.

“I know,” she whispered through gritted teeth. Looking at his face, at his brow furrowed in shared pain, she let out a shaky breath. Benito was just as unmoored as she was, and seeing his utter helplessness only amplified her own grief. “And I really am sorry, Benny. I’m so sorry, because I know you lost him. That hurts, too. We both lost him.”

When Benito buried his face in his hand and began to weep, Rio closed her eyes tightly, cursing herself as her own tears flowed uncontrollably. Shaking her head at her own hesitation, she finally reached out and pulled him close, wrapping an arm around his shoulders. Her body tensed automatically, but she felt him instantly relax against her, resting his heavy head on her shoulder. All she could do was lean her head against his.

“You’re bigger than I remembered,” she murmured after a quiet moment, catching the wet sniffle that followed his low, sudden laugh.

He pulled back to look at her, a fragile smile touching his lips. Rio couldn’t help but smile back, though she rolled her eyes a second later.

“Seriously?” he asked, laughing softly through his disbelief.

She shrugged, giving a small shake of head. “I’m trying, Benny,” she admitted, her voice faint, almost defeated.

He nodded gently, leaning to press a brief kiss to her shoulder. Rio stiffened slightly at the physical affection but held her tongue, unwilling to ruin the fragile peace between them.

“I know you are,” he murmured, his tone so thick with genuine understanding that it made her jaw clench.

Almost instantly, the comfort evaporated. A familiar awkwardness rushed back over to her, prompting her to shift on the mattress and pull away. Rio deliberately looked down, pretending not to hear the heavy sigh that escaped him as she created distance.

“How was your race today?” Benito offered, a desperate note of hope in his voice.

She shrugged again, her gaze drifting toward the wall. “Just another race,” she muttered indifferently, though his nod prompted her to add, “I won.”

“Of course you did,” he said, a faint smile returning to his face.

Rio arched her eyebrows in her usual conceited fashion, but looking into his eyes — still brimming with that intense, expectant affection — she sighed and shook her head.

“And how was the family lunch?” she asked, making an effort of her own.

Her body relaxed a fraction as she watched him smile weakly. She really was trying.

“It would have been better if you were there,” he replied, giving a slight shake of his head that made Rio let out a low grunt.

“Yeah, I’m sure,” she muttered dryly, her eyes scanning the bedroom floor, which was cluttered with empty beer cans.

Benito followed her gaze, his expression falling into deep regret. “Rio, you’ve been down this read before. You know exactly where this ends,” he said, his brow creasing with worry.

In a heartbeat, the lingering warmth of affection vanished, replaced by a sharp, familiar spike of adrenaline. Rio gritted her teeth.

“I really don’t understand why you’re doing this to yourself again,” he added.

Rio let out a sharp, mocking laugh, throwing the blankets off as she stood up and shook her head. Of course he didn’t understand. Nobody ever did, which was precisely why she couldn’t stop spiraling. They were right back to square one. Sometimes, no matter how badly she wanted to make amends, moments like this made her wonder why she even bothered.

“I don’t need a lecture from my little brother,” she growled, spinning around to point a finger at him. “Especially when you weren’t even here when I needed you.”

Benito just shook his head, letting out a weary breath. “What about you, Rio? Were you ever there for me when I needed you?”

“And when the hell did you ever need me?” she snapped, her voice rising as she began to pace the room. She threw her hands on her hips, letting out a bitter, sarcastic laugh. “Did you need me while you were off at your playboy college? While you were surfing on the coast? Racking up achievements as far away from this place — and from me — as you could get?”

“You put that distance between us!” he shouted, snapping to his feet and pointing right back at her. “I wanted you by my side for every single bit of it. I wanted to tell you everything!” His arms dropped to his sides in sheer exasperation as she shook her head in refusal. “Of course I needed you! I wanted you there because you were the one who inspired me to build a life for myself in the first place! You were the one who told me I could be whoever I wanted, that I had to find my own path”

“Oh, I inspired you?” she mocked, her voice dripping with venom. She watched him roll his eyes with a stubborn petulance that perfectly mirrored her own. “I can only imagine how truly inspiring it was to grow up with me, especially during those six years!”

Benito opened his mouth to cut in, but Rio forged ahead, drowning him out. “When I told you to find your path, I didn’t mean it literally! I didn’t want you to run to fucking California! I wanted you to find your path here. To make a place for yourself here!”

“Just because this ranch is your entire world doesn’t mean it has to be everyone else’s!” he shouted back. The raw resentment in his voice was so loud it made her nearly flinch, her eyes widening as the words hit her. “I never fit in here, Rio, and you damn well know it!”

“Oh, so now you fit in? Because you said you wanted to stay.” She fixed him with a sharp, accusatory glaze. “Suddenly you’ve magically found yourself here, how convenient! Are you sure it’s not just your guilt talking?”

“People change, Rio. They grow up,” he shot back, his authoritative tone cutting right though her humorless laugh. “I could never have found my place here if I hadn’t figured out who I was first, or what I was actually good at.” Rio parted her lips to speak, but he cut her off instantly. “I’m truly glad this ranch is your home, but you can’t force everyone else to want the exact same life you do. It’s not about you. Not everything revolves around you.”

“It’s never about me, is it?” she muttered with deep derision.

Benito let out a sour, bitter laugh of his own. “Everything has always been about you,” he said, narrowing his eyes as Rio gave an incredulous huff and shook her head. “Your grief, your resentment, your habit of pushing people away just because they don’t live exactly like you do. It’s incredibly ungrateful of you to weaponize those six years and claim nothing is about you, when everyone was exhausting themselves trying to help you heal and find yourself.”

“I never asked for anyone’s help,” she snarled. “Least of all yours.”

“Are you sure about that?” he asked, his voice dripping with sarcasm. “Because from where I’m standing, that’s exactly why you’re so furious with me.”

“You don’t understand a single thing, do you?” She laughed weakly, shaking her head.

“Because you don’t let anyone in!” he yelled in pure frustration. “You built a wall between us, Rio. What did you expect me to do?”

“I wanted you here!” she screamed, the force of her voice making her entire body tremble with raw vulnerability as tears flowed completely out of her control.

Benito’s anger dissolved into a frustrated, quiet shake of his head. “Then you should have just said so,” he murmured. “If I had known you wanted me around, I would have driven down every single week. I wanted to be here, but you pushed me away, and you know it. Yes, I moved to another state, but it’s a few hours’ drive, Rio. Hours! Leaving didn’t mean I didn’t want to be with you — that’s all I ever wanted. But I have my own life to build, and that doesn’t change how much I love you. My decision to leave had nothing to do with you. I don’t get why you can’t see that, especially when everyone respected your choice to stay here. You did whatever you wanted with your life, so why doesn’t anyone else get that same right?”

“You think I actually wanted my life to turn out like this?” she shot back, gesturing wildly to the state of herself.

“Not this,” he replied, pointing directly at the empty beer cans littered across the floor. “But everything else, everything you built over all these years. This mess” — he gesture to the room around them — “isn’t who you are, and you know it. You’ve found your path before, Rio, and you damn well know this isn’t it.”

Taking slow, deliberate steps, Rio closed the distance between them until she was looking straight into his eyes.

“You’re proud of your journey, aren’t you? Good for you,” she said, her voice dropping to a harsh whisper as she pressed her index finger firmly against his chest. “But you aren’t the one walking in my shoes. You live your life, I live mine, and I take care of my own path.”

Benito nodded in silent surrender, the sorrow evident in his eyes. He turned away and walked toward the door, but stopped abruptly with his hand resting on the doorknob. He turned back to face her one last time.

“I hope you head to the right direction,” he murmured.

Rio furrowed her brow, watching him with deep suspicion as he pulled his wallet from his pocket. He tossed something toward her, and before she could even process what it was, he walked out, slamming the door behind him.

When Rio looked down at the bed, her breath caught. Tears flooded her eyes all over again as her brow creased in recognition. Resting on the blanket was one of the very first alcoholics anonymous chips — a token from thirteen years ago, marking the day she had achieved three months of sobriety.

She picked up the small metal chip, turning it over between her trembling fingers, and let her body collapse onto the mattress. Burying her face in her hands, she finally let the sobs take over.

***

Thirteen Years Ago

Rio was still adjusting to the new rhythm of her days. She kept reminding herself to take things one step at a time, but knowing the mantra didn’t make practicing it any easier. For years, she had convinced herself she was in complete control, when the reality was she had been entirely consumed by a whirlwind of her own making. The more she refused to see it, the deeper she sank. Now, despite the daily struggle, a profound sense of relief washed over her just from being able to breathe again.

She couldn’t pinpoint exactly when she had lost her grip — whether it was triggered by deep-seated frustration, grief, denial, or a broken heart. Yet, as painful as it was to admit defeat to her own demons, she was finally reaching out to the people around her to pull herself back to the surface. Slowly but surely, it was working.

It wasn’t easy by any means, but she no longer had to face it alone. Every week, Natasha drove her to support meetings out of town. Though opening up felt incredibly unnatural to Rio, there was a quiet comfort in realizing she wasn’t the only one fighting this battle. She rarely spoke during the sessions, finding it impossible to lay her vulnerabilities bare in front of the group. Instead, she saved those unspoken thoughts for her father, who would sit up with her late into the night, listening to everything she couldn’t bring herself to tell anyone else.

She still missed the protective numbness of alcohol. The sobriety was fresh, and even though her days were packed with managing the ranch and launching new vineyard projects, silencing the inner anguish remained a constant battle. A heavy storm cloud still lingered in her chest. But she was truly committed, anchoring herself to the promise of one step at a time.

Despite the intense cravings for those brief moments of unconsciousness — where she could simply forget who she was and what she felt — viewing the world through a clear lens felt remarkably good. Not every day was a victory, but she could finally feel a newfound vigor taking root. She was learning to taste the present moment, to appreciate the small, everyday triumphs. It felt grounding to spend her days working alongside her father, sharing blueprints, checking on the stables, and making deliberate, purposeful decisions. It felt good to smile at the little things, to speak without an edge of anger, and to actively show up for the people she loved. Best of all was watching her brother grow, greeted by his wide smile every time she pulled into the driveway.

And god, he was shooting up fast. Benito was practically a man now, fiercely proud of the sparse peach fuzz he called a beard. It made her laugh every single day when he would dramatically ask if she had noticed it growing. She couldn’t be prouder of him; he was the top student in his class, and while he didn’t possess much of a natural knack for the physical ranch work, he was thriving on his own terms. He had taken up soccer, instantly drawing the attention of scouts from all across the country. She was certain he already had a spot locked down at the University of Montana. Even if he wasn’t cut out for hard manual labor, he had a sharp mind for business, and both she and their father knew a bright future was waiting for him.

It had been a highly chaotic year — a brutal roller coaster with far more heartbreaking lows than highs — but Rio forced herself not to dwell on the wreckage that had brought her here. She anchored her focus on what truly mattered: moving forward. She refused to simply drag her existence along anymore; she wanted to actually live, just as she had always dreamed she would. Now, in the final days of the year, she felt the first real certainty she was charting the right path. The recent past still pressed heavily against her chest, but taking in one step at a time, she knew she had to keep moving forward.

“Mi cielo, you’re home early!” her father called out the moment she crossed the threshold, hurrying down the stairs to sweep her into a hug. Rio laughed, letting herself be completely enveloped by his burly arms. “I thought you wouldn’t be back until tonight. How was the meeting?”

“I left before it ended,” she replied with a quick shrug. Before he could question her, she pressed on, “Lilia called me, so I rushed back. What happened to him?”

Her father rolled his eyes, giving a dismissive shake of his head. “You didn’t need to worry; Lilia loves to make a mountain out of a molehill,” he said, waving it off as if it were nothing. “I’m home, he’s perfectly fine, and you really should have stayed. Today is a massive milestone for you!”

“Dad, it’s just another day.” She shrugged, pointedly ignoring the look of clear disagreement on his face. “There are plenty more ahead, I promise.”

“I know, but even so, I am incredibly proud of you,” he said softly, flashing warm smile as he squeezed her shoulder. The affectionate gesture brought a faint, genuine smile to her lips. “Three months… I know how brutal it is, but you are showing such incredible strength. You are strong, Rio, and that is why I am so proud of you.”

Rio felt a sudden warmth flush her cheeks. She had never been good at handling compliments, and the praise made her shift uncomfortably. Yet, beneath the awkwardness, his words brought a deep, profound comfort — because she knew he meant every word.

“Dad…” It was her turn to roll her eyes, a bashful smile breaking across her father’s boisterous laughter echoed through the room. “It’s just another day, okay? One day at a time. Now, tell me what happened.”

Javier shook his head, letting out a heavy sigh. “He decided to go for a ride and fell right off the horse— I have no idea what went through his head,” he murmured.

“What was he doing riding in the first place?” she asked, genuinely astonished. “He can barely saddle a horse!”

“That’s exactly what I told him!” her father agreed, a spark of lingering frustration in his voice. He exhaled sharply. “But he’ll survive. It’s just a broken leg.”

“He broke his leg?!” Rio nearly shouted, her eyes widening in disbelief. “How can you brush that off like it’s nothing? Dad!”

“How many times did you break your arm growing up, Riandra? Accidents happen, he’ll be fine.” She opened her mouth to argue, her worry morphing into exasperation, but her father cut her off, placing both hands firmly on her shoulders. “We fall, we get a scrape here, a scratch there. Bones break and they heal, it just means we’re actually out there living. He’s fine. Two weeks in a cast and he’ll be good as new. It’s a learning experience, it’s just part of life.”

“But what about the game? It’s this week!” she countered, growing more frantic.

Her father simply shook his head. “It happens, mi cielo.”

“He must be absolutely devastated!”

“Well, he’s certainly not throwing a party.”

“And here you are, completely making light of it,” she pointed out, thoroughly indignant. Turning away, she began storming up the stairs.

“You spoil him too much,” her father teased after her, prompting Rio to roll her eyes yet again.

“Look who’s talking!” she muttered, throwing the words over her shoulder as she strode down the hallway, her father’s rich laughter still trailing behind her.

Rio didn’t even bother to knock. Pushing the door open, she found Benito sulking on his bed, aggressively clicking through TV channels with a massive cast encasing his left leg.

“A horse? Seriously?” she murmured, a smirk tugging at the corner of her mouth as she leaned against the doorframe, arms crossed.

The moment her brother looked up, he rolled his eyes and let out a miserable grunt.

“What were you thinking, pendejo?”

“I don’t know…” he muttered defensively, looking away.

Rio smiled, shaking her head. Walking over to the bed, she sat down beside him and lopped an arm around his shoulders, planting a kiss on his wavy hair while laughing softly

“How do you do it?” he asked suddenly. He pulled back just enough to look her in the eye. His brow was knit so tightly with raw frustration that it made Rio furrow her own in concern.

“Do what?”

“Everything.” He shrugged, letting out a defeated sigh. “The ranch, the horses, the racing…” His voice trailed off, his gaze drifting to a distant corner of the room while she watched him tenderly. “It feels like you were just born for this life. Meanwhile, I can’t do a single thing right.”

“What are you even talking about?” she asked, a gentle smile lifting her face as she took him by the shoulders, forcing him to meet her gaze. “Benny, you’re brilliant! I barely scraped through high school, and you’re the top of your class, you literally won a math olympiad! You accomplish so much more than I ever did.”

“Yeah, but what good is any of that out here? There isn’t a single problem on this ranch I can solve with an equation,” he muttered with a touch of self-scorn.

Rio laughed softly. “Not right now, maybe. But you know half of running this place is business, and you’re incredible at that side of it. Dad talks about it all the time.”

“I know, but sometimes I just feel like…” he started, only to cut himself off. He let out a heavy sigh that made her expression soften even more. “I don’t even know.” He shrugged, his shoulders slumping. “I just can’t do what you and Dad do.”

With a look of pure sympathy, Rio shook her head and reached up to run a hand through his hair.

“Benny, it’s not a competition,” she said, shrugging. “You don’t need to do what I do or what Dad does. You are you, and that’s the best part about you, dummy. You’re amazing because you are you.”

“You only say that because you’re my sister,” he murmured, rolling his eyes. “You’re literally obligated to feed me lines like that.”

“Please, you know damn well I don’t give a shit about obligations,” she countered, which finally coaxed a faint, grateful smile from him. “Benny, you don’t have to equal anyone, and you don’t have to best anyone. Just being yourself is more than enough. You’re great exactly as you are, with that massive brain of yours, your lanky arms, and your notorious two left feet.”

She nudged him playfully, and Benito couldn’t help but laugh, shoving her shoulder back in retaliation.

“Actually,” Rio added, her grin widening as she watched him cheep up, “you must be getting better with those feet. I heard a rumor that you’re the team captain now.”

Benito rolled his eyes, letting out a heavy, frustrated breath.

“And what good does that do now?” He sighed, completely drained. “I spent the entire year killing myself for this, just to miss the biggest game of the season.”

“Benny, you’re the best player on that field. The head coach from Montana literally came down to watch you last week. They have their eyes on you!” she urged, giving his shoulders an encouraging shake. He just shrugged, avoiding her eyes.

“I’m missing the game, Rio,” he muttered. “That’s when all the scouts show up. You know colleges recruit, they only care about the big games.”

“You still have a whole year ahead of you.” Rio shrugged, grasping for the right words, through her expression softened with deep empathy. “It’s going to work out. I promise you it will.”

Benito shook his head and exhaled sharply, shifting his weight on the mattress to face her fully, his eyes fixed on the floor.

“Can I tell you something?” he asked, his voice dropping to a near whisper. Rio nodded instantly.

“Always.”

“Sometimes… I feel like I don’t belong here,” he confessed, the whisper barely audible as his shoulders slumped. “Everything I try to do turns into a disaster. I can’t even ride a horse without breaking a damn leg.”

Rio offered a gentle, reassuring smile, squeezing his shoulder the exact way their father used to do whenever she felt overwhelmed.

“Benny, I know everyone treats you like you’re a grown man, but the truth is you’re still just a kid.” Her teasing smile made him roll his eyes, and she laughed softly. “Seriously, you’re a boy. You haven’t even finished high school! You have so much time to find your place and figure out who you want to be.”

“Come on, Rio…”

“It’s the truth! Just look at me,” she countered, gesturing to herself. He arched an eyebrow. “I’m a disaster who only just now got her life together, and I have an eleven-year head start on you. Trust me, if I could navigate my way out into what I am today, you’ll find your path too.”

“You kind of have a point.” He rolled his eyes, but a genuine smile finally broke through, making Rio smile right back. “But I always knew you’d find your way. You’re the most amazing person I know.”

It was Rio’s turn to roll her eyes.

“You only say that because you’re my brother; you’re literally obligated to feed me lines like that,” she teased, and he laughed.

“I mean it,” he said, locking his eyes onto hers, and a sudden, profound warmth settled in Rio’s chest. “You always knew exactly who you were, and you always knew this ranch was your home. You just… lost your way a little bit.” He shrugged, and she let out a soft, emotional laugh.

“And that’s fine. Sometimes we get turned around, but the only thing that matters is fighting to find our way back. And I know you will.”

Benito sighed, closing his eyes for a quiet moment. Rio could sense a lingering tension — a deeper worry or frustration he wasn’t quite ready to voice. Whatever it was, she decided not to push. She would give him the space he needed.

“I want you to have something,” she said, an excited smile lighting up her face. He opened his eyes, looking at her with genuine curiosity.

Smiling, Rio pulled the small metal chip from her pocket. She had just received it hours ago; today marked exactly three months of sobriety. Benito took the token, staring down at it in silence for a long moment. When he finally looked up, a bright, prideful smile broke across his face — a look that instantly made her own smile widen.

“I know three months isn’t a lifetime, but it’s a start,” she said, shrugging. She knew the road ahead was still long and dauting. “Think of it as a little piece of hope for the right path. I swear, mi vida, if I could do this, you can conquer whatever comes your way. You’re brilliant. You have so much ahead of you.”

Benito smiled, pulling her into a fierce, tight embrace, and Rio held on just as tightly.

Most days were an uphill battle, but it was in quiet moments like this that she knew the fight was entirely worth it.

***

Present Day

Morning irritability was customary for Rio, a ritual formed over a brutal year of watching her life slide downhill. She was always the first awake, aggressively snapping the sheets into place with a scowl before slipping downstairs before Lilia even reached the kitchen. She craved these quiet dawn hours, even if the raw sobriety of the morning irritated her.

Ever since her father started falling ill, Rio had forgotten what peace felt like. She spent all her time eating herself up inside, eventually growing so accustomed to the internal friction that she simply tuned out the rest of the world, retreating deep within her own mind. Now that he was gone, her anger had dissolved into a heavy, suffocating melancholy. She wanted desperately to scream, to let it all out, but she had forgotten how to express herself. Her words had grown so consistently harsh and biting that she had simply stopped trying — she had lost her touch, leaving her with nothing to do but torment herself. She knew she was pushing everyone away, but she also knew no one could despise her half as much as she already despised herself.

Downstairs, she choked down a dry piece of bread and pulled a beer from the fridge, wincing at the loud creak of the door. She sank into her usual armchair, staring out at the horizon as if the sky might magically yield answers to questions she hadn’t even figured out how to ask. It was still dark, but that faint lavender dawn was her favorite view — the quiet, effortless transition from night to day. Watching it, she wished people — herself, specifically — could change like that, with such natural grace.

For the first time in a long while, she hesitated to open the beer, staring intently at the can in her hand. As deeply as the fight with Benito had enraged her, his words refused to leave her head. Her brother wasn’t trying to punish her; he was just brokenhearted. And though she would never admit it aloud, not even under torture, that realization stung because she knew he was right.

Finally, rolling her eyes at her own hesitation, she popped the tab and took a long, heavy swig, letting the icy liquid burn a reassuring path down her throat.

Most days, she hated herself for throwing away a life that had taken a decade to build. But owning her failure was terrifying; it was easier to succumb to the numbness, to surrender to the comfort haze that quieted her racing thoughts. She knew she was hurting herself, but the illusion of an escape was too intoxicating to resist. She wasn’t just back at square on — she had regressed entirely.

An alcoholic never stops being an alcoholic. The standard AA introduction echoed in her mind: Hi, my name is Rio, and I’m an alcoholic. It was a mantra that tasted like ash now. Everything about recovery felt bitter, futile, and utterly foolish. Yet the irony of her relapse wasn’t lost on her.

The dependency felt larger than her, a desperate craving for a comfort she couldn’t find anywhere else. She wanted to fight it, but honestly, she felt completely depleted. Closing her eyes, she pulled out her phone and stared at the screen — a photo of her two godsons. She missed them fiercely. Those two boys had been her anchors, and now, as she felt herself drowning, she silently begged the universe for strength, if only for their sake.

Rio hated admitting weakness and always pushed back defensively, but deep down, she knew Wanda was right. In this state, she was a terrible role mode. Come on, it’s just a few beers, she would always argue, trying to placate her comadre, but the lie never stuck.

With a heavy, sorrowful sigh, her mind drifted back to the day at the winery, standing before her father’s portrait and promising him she would do the right thing. That memory haunted her now — the suffocating weight of failing to keep her word, even when she desperately wanted to be honorable. She truly wanted to try.

Nervously, Rio bit the inside of her cheek, staring at the glowing screen. She unlocked the phone, the keypad blurring slightly before her eyes. She let out a ragged breath. Maybe she could try. Just for today.

Feeling the heavy weight of her old sobriety chip hidden in her pocket, she finally placed the call.

***

Before even pulling the reins to dismount, Rio caught sight of Wanda waiting on the porch. Leaning against the doorframe, Wanda watched her with narrowed eyes — a calculated mix of suspicion and hopeful curiosity softened by the ghost of a smile. Rio rolled her eyes internally. As small she felt under that scrutiny, she refused to let her defenses crack, masking her nerves with her trademark smug indifference.

“You’ve already been drinking, haven’t you?” Wanda asked, arching a sharp eyebrow.

Rio widened her eyes in theatrical outrage, playing offended. “Good morning to you too, Wanda! What a beautiful, sunny day to see you!” she chirped with an over-the-top smile. Wanda rolled her eyes, letting out a soft laugh. “I had a beer. One. A single unit of beer,” Rio clarified, holding up a solitary index finger.

Wanda’s eyes narrowed again, tracking the gesture. “You know the rules,” she said shrugging.

“One beer,” Rio pressed. “Bring out the breathalyzer if you want.”

“Rio…”

“I know the rules, okay? I won’t drink around the boys,” Rio said, finally letting her guard drop. Her brow furrowed, her expression turning into a silent plea for grace. “I promise you, Wanda. I wasn’t lying. I genuinely miss them, and I’m not going to ruin this. Just give me a shot.”

Wanda studied her in the ensuing quiet, her expression unreadable, before her face softened into a faint smile. She nodded. “I believe you.”

“Seriously?” Rio let out a disbelief laugh, prompting Wanda to chuckle.

“Am I not supposed to?”

“No, definitely stay the course!” Rio interjected quickly, struggling to keep the pure relief out of her voice. “You absolutely should believe me. In fact, I highly encourage it.”

As Rio’s own smile finally broke through, Wanda jammed two fingers into her mouth and let out a piercing whistle toward the house.

“Twenty minutes to get dressed if you want to hang out with your madrinha!” she yelled over her shoulder. Instantly, the house erupted. Rio burst out of laughing at the familiar, chaotic chorus of “I’m coming!”, “I can’t find my shoes!”, “Mom, where’s my truck?” and “Tommy, move!” She had missed this beautiful madness so much.

“They’re all yours,” Wanda said, turning back around, and Rio offered a grateful nod. “What’s the plan for today?”

Rio shrugged. “Whatever they want.”

“And no buying them toys,” Wanda added, her tone shifting to a strict warning that earned a quiet scoff from Rio. “I meant it, Rio. You spoil them rotten.”

“Pretty sure that’s the godmother’s job description,” she murmured, shrugging again. Wanda just shook her head, a fond smile gracing her lips.

In the brief silence that followed, Rio felt suddenly naked under her comadre’s gaze. Despite the warmth in Wanda’s eyes, there was an analytical intensity to the look that made her skin prickle.

“What?” Rio asked, shifting uncomfortably.

Wanda shrugged it off. “I just know you’re putting in the work. I’m really glad you’re here,” she said softly.

Rio instantly rolled her eyes to deflect, a sudden wave of embarrassment and raw, unsettling vulnerability washing over her.

“Don’t… don’t start,” she muttered, her cheeks flushing.

Wanda let out a soft laugh, arching an eyebrow. “I’m serious, Rio. It’s a massive step.”

“Please, spare me the talk about steps,” Rio interrupted, giving a small shake of her head through a faint laugh escaped her. “You know that’s a trigger word for me,” she mocked, prompting Wanda to roll her eyes.

“Listen, jokes aside, I need to talk to you about something.” Wanda’s tone shifted, turning serious enough to make Rio’s brow furrow with a sudden spike of apprehension.

“If this is another serious talk…” Rio sighed, slumping slightly. “I’ve already hit my quota for the deep talks today.”

“I know this isn’t your favorite subject, but I can see how hard you’re trying,” Wanda said earnestly, ignoring Rio’s tired, dismissive huff. “That’s exactly why I’m bringing it up. I spoke to Benito yesterday.”

“What is this, a coordinated intervention?” Rio snapped, her defenses instantly flaring.

Wanda remained entirely unfazed, offering only a calm, understanding shake of her head. “No, so put your claws away, okay? I just wanted to…” She paused, letting out a quiet sigh. “He mentioned that the two of you are finally talking. He said you invited him out to Pedra Purpura.”

Rio let out a low grunt of dissatisfaction. “I don’t even know where we stand anymore, Wanda. We got into a huge fight last night and—”

“That changes nothing, Rio. He’s your brother,” Wanda said gently. Rio pulled a mocking face at the compassion in her voice, but Wanda pressed on. “He genuinely wants to bridge the gap, and he’s going to show up. He’s just as pigheaded as you are.”

“Well, if he’s shows up, I’ll be there,” Rio muttered, shrugging it off.

“That’s the thing.” Wanda grimaced slightly, prompting Rio to arch an eyebrow in curiosity. “You know Benito. He’s full of grand ideas, and his heart is usually in the right place, but I know how you operate.” She picked her words carefully as Rio’s eyes narrowed. “If he steps out of line, you’re going to completely shut down. And I know you’re putting real effort into this— just agreeing to see him is huge, and—”

“Wanda, get to the point,” Rio interrupted, her impatience bleeding through.

Wanda let out a heavy breath. “Beyond just fixing things with you, he wants to rebuild what he considers his family.” Rio arched a skeptical brow. “He wants to make peace with you, but he also wants you to make peace with the past. He invited Agatha.”

The color drained from Rio’s face instantly. Her chest seized up at the mere mention of the name, a violent jolt of electricity striking her core. In an instant, her mask of cold indifference crumbled into utter bewilderment. She couldn’t even process the thought; her heart hammered wildly against her ribs, and a numbing anxiety tingled all the way to her fingertips.

Of course Benito would pull a reckless stunt like that. It was entirely his style. She closed her eyes, forcing a deep breath as her thoughts began to spin out of control, blurring into a chaotic haze.

“I’m telling you this now because I didn’t want you to be blindsided. I know how delicate everything is right now,” Wanda said, her features softening with empathy.

Rio just stared back, her gaze entirely hollow. “I… I don’t…” She stammered, shaking her head. “I don’t even know what to think,” she finally admitted.

“I know he jumped the gun, but it doesn’t need to be a disaster,” Wanda urged, though Rio’s widening eyes signaled absolute disagreement. “Years have passed, Rio. You aren’t the same people you used to be, and I think it’s time you let go of this weight. Even if Benito handled it poorly, his intentions weren’t bad, quite the opposite. She was always part of the family,” Wanda added with shrug.

Rio looked down at her boots, her jaw tight. She knew that truth — she knew Agatha had been family. But facing it now, after a decade of estrangement and a grueling, daily battle to bury the memory, felt like a physical chokehold. It was agonizing to reframe Agatha as family; honestly, it was agonizing to think of her at all, which was why she had trained herself to live in complete denial — a coping mechanism bought at a very high price.

It wasn’t how it used to be anymore. The frantic, bleeding urgency of that suffocating love had long since burned out, but the residual melancholy remained. The wound had closed, but the scar still throbbed with a sharp, persistent ache.

She knew she had been cruel during their last encounter, but how could she have been anything else after everything that had happened? After all these years. How do you welcome someone back as family when they’ve become a total stranger? So much time had drifted by that Rio couldn’t even summon the sound of her voice, yet it had taken less than a heartbeat to recognize her presence — and that was the bitterest pill to swallow. Realizing that her ultimate safe haven had been permanently reduced to scorched earth.

She needed to think. Or find a drink.

Before she could form a response or open her mouth, Billy came barreling across the house toward her. Rio instinctively knelt down to catch him, her heavy thoughts dissolving as she scooped him up, smiling at his sheer euphoria and squeezing him tight. He was growing like a weed, already reaching her waist, but he was nothing she couldn’t handle.

“My turn!” Tommy yelled, sprinting up behind his brother. Rio barely had time to set the first twin down before sweeping the second into the air, the sound of the boys’ laughter blending with Wanda’s chuckles in the background.

***

No matter how much the boys entertained her, Rio felt the hours drag. The fragile optimism she had managed to muster that morning had been utterly flattened by a sudden storm of self-loathing. As if the exhausting clash with Benito weren’t enough, she was still chewing on Wanda’s warnings, paralyzed by the realization that her brother had actually decided to drag her kicking and screaming into a pit of bitter nostalgia.

She desperately wanted a drink.

It wasn’t like her to obsess over how she treated people — at least, not until recently. Something inside her had surrendered long ago, content to let the days bleed into one another in a dull haze. Sha hadn’t cared about anything as long as the ranch work got done. But ever since her father died, a heavy, stagnant ache had settled in her chest. She wasn’t exactly haunted, but she felt constantly choked, as if he were looking down from above with a furrowed brow, waiting for her to do the right thing. The weight of it crushed her because she was entirely self-aware, yet she lacked the strength to do the right thing.

She really was trying, though. The burden on her shoulders had lightened by tons while she chased the twins, kicking a soccer ball around and playing the terrible goalie, deliberately fake tripping so they could outrun her. But the pure vitality of their laughter was bittersweet. She craved more of that joy, but she knew she wasn’t stable enough to make it a permanent reality — not on Wanda’s terms. And deep down, she knew Wanda was right.

It was entirely counterproductive, but Rio hated sobriety precisely because it forced her to face herself.

By three in the afternoon, the boys still possessed boundless energy. Rio wanted more than anything to match their spirit, but she couldn’t anchor herself to be present. A heavy lethargy weighed her down, and her throat burned with a familiar, destructive thirst for oblivion. Giving up, she sank into the tall grass, stretching her legs out and bracing her weight on her hands behind her. A faint smile touched her lips as she watched the twins chase a piglet she had let loose, aggressively competing to catch it first. She wanted to lose herself in the moment, but the darkness inside wouldn’t let her. To keep from ruining their fun, she stayed right where she was — far enough from the boys to avoid drowning them in her melancholy, but far enough from the house to resist the temptation of grabbing a beer.

As the chase drifted into the distance, Rio let out a ragged breath and tilted her face toward the sky, letting the warm sunlight soothe her skin. It was a fleeting comfort. She knew she had everything she could ever need, yet the responsibility of knowing that she was the one accountable for whatever came next made her crumble inside.

A sudden tap on her shoulder broke her stride. Her defensive frown instantly melted into genuine tenderness when she turned to find the boy — Agatha’s son — staring back at her. He had a crown of thick curls, massive brown eyes, and an open, inviting smile as he sat down beside her in the grass.

“Hey, cowboy,” Rio said softly, hating how a profound warmth instantly flooded her chest when his smile widened.

Rio couldn’t quite explain why this child disarmed her so completely — though, in truth, she knew exactly why. He was six, but he carried himself with a fragile, diminutive innocence. He looked even smaller with those wide, earnest eyes, his cheeks flushed with heat and an expression brimming with curiosity and pure affection. Looking at him felt jarringly familiar, like staring directly at a mirror of her own childhood self. He was completely captivating. She found a quiet amusement in watching him adopt the identity of the ranch piece by piece — right down to his tall boots, cuffed jeans, dirt-streaked white tank top, and the red flannel shirt that perfectly matched her own.

He didn’t speak, but he pressed close, nearly leaning his weight against her side. Rio looked down at him, noticing how possessively he clutched a drawing notebook against his lap, and a soft smile crossed her face.

“I thought you were mad at me,” she murmured, keeping her eyes on him, though his focus remained locked on the paper. “You ran away yesterday.”

At that, Nicholas looked up, meeting her gaze entirely unfiltered. For a reason she couldn’t fathom, a sharp shiver ran down her spine. He simply shook his head, his smile returning.

“Then why did you run?” she asked gently. He gave a small shrug. “Are we good now?” He nodded, and she nodded back, a quiet truce established.

Right then, the piglet bolted past them, the twins shrieking in hot pursuit along the same path.

“You don’t want to join them?” Rio asked. Nicholas shook his head.

“Do you want to see my drawings?” he asked, pointing down at the cover. This time, Rio nodded fully, turning her body toward him and leaning in to look.

Puffing out his chest with a strike of pure pride, Nicholas flipped open a page in the middle of the book. Rio tilted her head, taking in the chaotic vibrant crayon strokes — remarkably detailed for a six-year-old. The drawing featured towering trees, sharp green grass, a massive brown horse, and a short-haired girl sporting a bright yellow hat.

“How beautiful,” Rio said softly, her voice thick with uncharacteristic warmth as she traced a finger over the colorful lines. “You’re incredibly talented, you know that?”

“It’s you,” he said, turning his face to look at her, beaming. Rio’s breath hitched, her features freezing as the revelation caught her completely off guard.

“Me?” she asked, a nervous, startled laugh escaping her. “Why did you draw me?”

Nicholas giggled, as if she had just asked the most ridiculous question in the world.

“Because you’re the best rider in the whole world,” he said proudly, his dark eyes flashing with pure enthusiasm. “The fastest one of all!”

Rio’s eyes widened, completely speechless. She opened and closed her mouth a few times, the defenses she spent a lifetime building suddenly failing her.

“Who told you that?” she asked, her laugh faint and self-conscious.

“Uncle Javi,” Nicky replied with a bright smile.

Instantly, the ground beneath Rio shifted. Her expression softened completely as a sudden rush of tears blurred her vision.

“He told you that?” Her voice was a fragile whisper. She swallowed hard, desperately trying to suppress the tidal wave of emotion that her father’s name — and the weight of this perfect moment — had unleashed inside her soul.

“He said it all the time,” the boy added gently. “He said you were his favorite person in the world, the one he liked the most.”

Blinking back the tears that threatened to spill, Rio let out a watery, breathless laugh and pulled the boy against her. He stiffened in surprise at first, but a moment later, he let out a giggle and threw his small arms around her neck, burying himself in her embrace. She tightly closed her eyes, trying to hide the fact that her tears were soaking into his brown curls, as a profound, aching warmth filled her chest.

Every time her father had returned from California, he would practically glow, showering Benito with praise and talking endlessly about their life there, about Agatha, and about her son — the cowboy, as Javier loved to call him. Rio had always played it cool. She would look away, indifferently pushing her food with a fork as if she couldn’t care less. But she had listened to every single word. In truth, beneath the armor of her stubborn pride, she had been deeply grateful. She was thankful he shared the details she lacked the courage to ask about, the family updates her own ego wouldn’t let her seek out.

Despite the miles and the years that detached her from her brother’s life on the coast, she had actually known a great deal. She had quietly looked at the photos, tracking the weeks her father spent away, learning what they were doing and how the boy was growing. Yet, when Javier first used to return with those stories, a bitter resentment would flare up; she felt like an outsider. It seemed like Javier only had eyes for Benito, Agatha, and the kid, leaving her forgotten to hold down the fort at the ranch. It had made her feel inadequate, as if she were merely her father’s consolation prize — the obligation he had left behind.

Never once had occurred to her that while he was out in California, her father had spoken of her to them with that exact same love and fierce pride.

Nicholas was the one to pull back, gently breaking the embrace. Rio laughed softly, wiping her forearm across her eyes to dismiss the few tears that had escaped. He beamed up at her, and the sudden whirlwind of emotion melted her defenses so completely that she felt a flush creep up her cheeks. Not knowing what else to do with the overwhelming tenderness, she simply reached out and playfully ruffled his curls.

“Can I see the rest of your drawings?” she asked, doing her best to steady the sudden tremor in her voice. Nicky nodded eagerly.

“I have a million of them!” he cheered.

Rio’s chest tightened with an involuntary affection as he snuggled tightly against her side, resting his head comfortably against her chest. She could barely focus on the pages he was flipping through. She felt clumsy and out of her depth — physical affection had never been her strong suit — yet the sheer sweetness of the moment entirely consumed her. Her arm hovered awkwardly for a few seconds, frozen in place, until she finally let herself relax and wrapped it securely around his small shoulders. The sensory overload was dizzying; her thoughts blurred, her heart hammered against her ribs, and the air left her lungs, yet sitting there with Nicholas felt entirely right. She felt a profound sense of gratitude.

He was just a little boy, but without even knowing it, he had been the first person to offer her real comfort since the day her father died. She hadn’t realized how desperately she needed to hear those words, how much she needed to be assured of her father’s love and pride. It changed everything. A gesture so small had filled the massive void she had been trying to drown.

“Nicky!”

The sharp shout made them both jolt in perfect synchronization. Breaking the quiet spell, they turned together toward the edge of the lawn, where Agatha was standing. “Your grandma is looking for you!”

A familiar knot of anxiety tightened in Rio’s stomach. She instinctively lowered her head, wishing she could simply evaporate under the weight of that distant blue gaze. But when she noticed Nicholas mimic her exactly, ducking his head with the exact same stubborn defiance, a sharp chuckle escaped her nose.

“Nicky!” Agatha called out again, louder this time.

When the boy stubbornly shook his head, explicitly pretending to be deaf, Rio bit the inside of her cheek to keep from laughing out loud.

“Your mom’s calling you, cowboy,” she whispered softly. He whipped his face toward her, his brow furrowed in pure, exaggerated frustration. “Go on. You have to listen to her.”

“Nicholas, I am not going to ask again!”

This time, Rio couldn’t contain her laughter. Nicholas scowled, but she just smiled, ruffling his hear one last time before standing up and extending her hands to pull him to his feet.

“Go,” she urged as he stubbornly stomped his boot. “You have to listen to your mother.”

He knit his brows, having a silent argument with her, and looking up, Rio saw Agatha with her arms crossed. This time, it was Agatha who lowered her gaze.

“You can show me the rest of your drawings later,” Rio offered as a truce. Nicholas weighed the offer, gave a firm nod, and suddenly threw his arms around her waist for a quick, tight hug before sprinting off across the lawn.

Rio pressed her lips together to keep from smiling as she watched Agatha’s guarded expressions melted away completely. Agatha opened her arms with a brilliant smile as her son barreled into her, catching him in a tight embrace and affectionally ruffling his hair just as Rio had done moments before.

Rio couldn’t tear her eyes away from the scene. The profound tenderness in Agatha’s face, the unforced joy in her smile — Rio realized she had never known this side of her. She had never seen the mother Agatha had become. It was a beautiful thing to see.

She must have been staring for too long, because suddenly, Agatha looked up and caught her eye. Rio froze as the weight of that intense blue gaze locked onto hers from across the yard. Her mind went completely blank. Feeling entirely foolish and awkward, Rio slowly raised a hand and gave a stiff, mechanical wave, immediately cursing herself internally for looking like an idiot. But the tension broke completely when Agatha offered a soft, quiet smile in return.

It felt like a genuine truce, and the sheer weight of it made Rio’s heart drop heavily in her chest.

As soon as the two turned toward the house, Rio let out the breath she hadn’t realized she was holding. She closed her eyes tightly as all her thoughts rushed back to her mind like a sudden jolt.

Yes, she really needed a drink.

***

Dusk was setting in, and she was expected at Pedra Purpura in just a few hours, but her conviction had entirely vanished. She felt utterly paralyzed, trapped in a relentless internal tug-of-war where each half of her brain violently pulled in an opposite direction. Deep down, she just wanted to vanish — to dig a deep hole in the ground and crawl right into it.

The grim irony of the thought brought a faint, hollow chuckle to her lips. Leaning her head back against her father’s massive marble tomb, she mindlessly spun the still-sealed bottle of vodka between her palms.

This was her first time stepping foot in the cemetery since the funeral. She had spent weeks wanting to visit just to feel close to him again, but whenever she built up the nerve, she couldn’t face the finality of it. The mere thought of coming here would seize her chest with a suffocating tightness. Stepping past these gates meant accepting a reality she wasn’t ready for — admitting that what was carved into stone was absolute, and that he was never coming back.

Tonight, however, she knew she had to face the music. Not just out of a desperate longing to feel his presence, but because she figured if she couldn’t even look herself in the mirror, she at least had to look reality in the eye.

Her mind drifted back to the exact moment the fabric of her life began to unravel: the day he collapsed in the stables last year. Rio could still hear her own echoing scream, could still feel the crushing weight on her shoulders as she and the ranch hands desperately hauled his limp body back to the house. Then cane the diagnosis. That memory haunted her waking hours. She couldn’t shake the sudden, hollow void that had opened up inside her, the violent knot in her throat, or the tears that had choked the air right out of her lungs.

She hadn’t slept a wink that night. She knew Javier well enough to know that all the medical experts in the world couldn’t force him to rest; he had made it crystal clear that he would only stop working when he was dead. He had laughed when he said it, but his humor had only triggered a deep, boiling rage inside her. To Rio, it felt like an intentional death sentence. It felt like he was actively choosing to leave her behind, choosing to die faster. Before dawn broke, she had saddled Raio and ridden out to the vineyard, hoping the cool air would clear the fog in her head. Instead, her anger completely blindsided her common sense. Before she even realized what she was doing, she was standing in the dark of the cellar, uncorking a bottle of wine.

A decade of hard-fought sobriety, instantly thrown down the drain.

She hadn’t panicked in the moment. When she finally paused to process it, she simply rationalized the relapse, telling herself she just needed to let off some steam and that mistakes happen to everyone. She kept the secret entirely to herself. But after that, she couldn’t stop, and a short time later, there was no way left to hide it.

It turned out she had spent ten years suppressing a thirst she didn’t even realize was lingering. After that first taste — the moment the alcohol hit her system and gifted her that sweet, numbing oblivion — she was hooked all over again. She craved the escape. She desperately needed a break from the weight of her reality.

“You’re probably mad at me right now,” Rio muttered against the cold marble, cracking the seal on the vodka and taking her first long swig of the day. “But honestly, dad? I’m pretty damn mad at you, too.”

She let out a dry, humorless laugh, realizing it was the very first time she had given voice to the resentment.

“If you weren’t so stubborn, you could be here right now, with me,” she said, tipping the bottle back for another heavy drink. “Was it worth it?” She looked up at the darkening sky, the stars just beginning to show. “Looking down from wherever you are, do you really thing it was worth it? Or would you choose differently if you got a do-over? Because if I could go back, I’d change everything. I never would have taken that first sip. Not again. God, I wish I could just talk to you. I need to know if you’re as consumed by regret as I am. Because, dad, it’s eating me alive.”

Rio raised the bottle for a third time, but her hand hesitated. Exhaling a long, ragged breath, she set the vodka down on the grass and leaned her head back against the tomb, staring blankly up at the sky.

“We can’t undo the past, can we?” she whispered, a faint smile breaking through her melancholy. “You always drummed that into my head. It’s a bitter pill to swallow, but I guess the truth always is.”

She closed her eyes and took a deep, steadying breath, before reaching back down for the bottle to take another long drink.

“You know that for the better part of my life, I never listened to a single thing you told me. I always had to learn the hard way, always did things my own way. But I swear to god, dad, if you could just tell me what the hell to do right now… I promise you I’d actually listen this time.”

“If he could talk, he’d tell you to pull your head out of you ass and grow the fuck up.”

Rio nearly jumped out of her skin, the sudden voice making her vault in surprise. The vodka bottle slipped from her hands, tumbling onto the grass and spilling a heavy pool of alcohol over the fresh flowers she had just laid down.

Yelena was practically doubling over at the sheer terror on her face, while Rio unleashed a rapid-fire string of every profanity she knew.

“For fuck’s sake, Yelena!” Rio barked, trying to catch her breath. “What the hell are you doing here?”

Yelena’s laughter finally began to wind down as she casually sat cross-legged on the grass directly across from her. “I think I’m here for the exact same reason you are,” she said, shrugging effortlessly. “I wanted to talk to the old man.”

Rio took a slow, grounding breath to steady her racing pulse, retrieved the bottle from the grass, and eyed the blonde with a mix of suspicion and curiosity.

“You wanted to vent to the old man?” Rio asked, arching an eyebrow. “What the hell did you do this time?”

Yelena let out a soft chuckle, but she averted her eyes a beat too quickly for Rio to miss it. “Nothing disastrous enough to make me drink my feelings away.”

Rio rolled her eyes at that, tipping the bottle back for a long swig before flashing a sarcastic smirk. “Let he who has never drowned his sorrows cast the first stone.”

“You know what? I actually used to do exactly that when I was a teenager,” Yelena countered, matching the sharp sarcastic smile while Rio tracked her with narrowed eyes.

“Color me shocked…” Rio muttered dryly.

“Oh, absolutely. I went through a massive rebellious phase. I was drinking almost every single day, and things got so toxic that my mother straight-up kicked me out. I had zero choice but to track down my sister, who was living out in the middle of fucking nowhere,” Yelena continued, amused by the shifting look in Riandra’s eyes. “Can you even picture it? Leaving the great NYC to live on a ranch in the middle of nowhere?”

“I’m willing to bet you despised every second of it,” Rio murmured, her eyebrow arching again.

Yelena laughed. “I completely loathed it,” she admitted with a drastic grimace, prompting Rio to let out a quiet laugh before taking another drink. “I flew in, and my sister had to drive forever to pick me up because this godforsaken place doesn’t even have an airport. What kind of civilized town lacks an airport?” she mocked, making Rio chuckle again. “It was a nightmare, I swear. When we finally arrived and I realized a single family essentially owned the entire place, I was just like what kind of medieval fiefdom did I just stumble into?”

This time, Rio laughed genuinely, the bitterness momentarily slipping away.

“You should have just hitched a ride out of there,” Rio pointed out with a sarcastic shrug.

Yelena nodded in agreement. “Trust me, I tried. I packed a bag, stole my sister’s car, and ended up stranded on the side of the highway out of gas,” she said, suppressing a giggle while Rio shook her head at the memory “A few minutes later, my sister’s best friend pulled up and absolutely ripped me a new one, just tore me to absolute shreds. Can you believe that? I drove back completely silent, taking the beating.”

“You must hate that little bitch,” Rio ironized, though a smile tugged at her lips.

“At first, I hated her guts,” Yelena confessed. “But even though she rode me hard, she ended up taking me under her wing. I have no idea how she managed it, I didn’t think it was even possible, but she made me to see the good in this place. I actually fell in love with it.” She spoke with complete, unvarnished sincerity.

Rio felt her eyes prickle with sudden warmth and quickly looked away.

“I used to carry so much rage because nothing ever went the way I wanted. I felt like a misfit everywhere I went,” Yelena said gently. When Rio looked back, she saw her friend’s face soften with deep affection. “But she had this profound calm, this beautiful way of looking at the world. She actually listened to me, and I think she was the very first person who ever did. She was a former alcoholic.”

“An alcoholic is always an alcoholic,” Rio murmured, repeating the bleak mantra with a heavy dose of sarcasm.

“A recovering alcoholic,” Yelena corrected firmly but playfully. “She had been sober for a long time, and she taught me that drinking to escape or bury your pain is just a cheap way of lying to yourself.”

“She sounds pretty stupid,” Rio spat out of irony, tilting the bottle back for another heavy swig.

“Actually, she’s the wisest person I’ve ever known.”

“Now you’re just making shit up.” Rio rolled her eyes, but Yelena merely held out an open palm, a silent demand for the bottle.

“You know damn well I’m right,” Yelena said with a pointed gaze. “You’re wiser than that, Rio. You really are the wisest person I know, so please, quit being a dumbass, at least for today.”

Letting out a defeated sigh, Rio surrendered the bottle. The moment Yelena took it, she stretched her arm out, placing the vodka far out of Rio’s reach on the grass.

“What’s really going on, Rio?” she asked softly. Rio sighed again, resting the back of her head against the cold marble to stare up at the sky. “This isn’t just about your father. I know you too well.”

“I don’t even know, Ye,” Rio whispered, her eyes drifting back to her friend.

It was the honest truth; she couldn’t pinpoint a single trigger because it was everything hitting her at once — a relentless flood.

“Just talk to me,” Yelena urged with a shrug. “Say literally anything. Maybe if you voice it, things will finally make sense inside your head.”

“That’s impossible,” Rio laughed bitterly. “My head never stops; I can’t put anything in its place. I think about everything at the same time, I feel everything at the same time, and it’s horrible. It’s fucked up. I am so fucking fucked up.”

“What is all of this that you’re feeling?” Yelena asked with immense patience.

Rio let out a long, ragged breath, finally burying her face in her hands. “I don’t know how to deal with feelings; I never have,” Rio admitted honestly, her voice trembling. “And it’s just so much at once, you know? My dad… everyone back at home… I just… I don’t know.”

“Everyone back at home…” Yelena mused, her thoughtful tone immediately drawing Rio’s sharp gaze. “Let’s break it down then, starting with your brother.”

Rio rolled her eyes instantly. “Don’t start. You’re not my shrink.”

“Well, you clearly need one.”

“Shut up,” Rio murmured with a hint of impatience, shaking her head.

“Look, I know having him around throws you off, but honestly? I’m just going to lay it out: you two are a pair of incredible stubborn mules,” Yelena said, making Rio’s eyes widen in genuine offense. “Yes, absolutely. You’ve spent years keeping up a fight that doesn’t even exist, and all because you both miss each other.” Rio opened her mouth to cut in, but Yelena pushed right past her. “He misses you. He literally told you so, and it’s useless to deny that you feel the exact same way. You know you do. Why are you so furious about that? Why do you hate yourself so much for wanting him around? He wants you too! So drop the fucking pride. Your dad is gone, Rio, but your brother is standing right in front of you. Go throw everything you feel in his face then give him a hug and boom it’s over.”

“You talk like it’s easy,” Rio countered, rolling her eyes.

“Because it is!” Yelena shot back in exasperation. “I’m not saying the emotions are simple, or that reality isn’t messy, but stripped down, it really is that basic. He’s here, you’re here, and neither of you has forever. So yeah, it’s simple. It’s hard, but it’s simple: talk to him. Tell him the whole truth. Scream, fight, whatever, but talk. Just bleed it out. I swear to god, once you purge all of this, a massive weight will lift, and you’ll realize all you actually want is to hold onto him.”

Rio felt a suffocating knot tighten in her throat as a wave of hot tears blurred her vision. She loathed the realization that, at the end of the day, it truly was that simple — all she had to do was something, anything. But that was the real trap. Never in her entire life had she felt so completely paralyzed.

“And this isn’t just about him; this goes for Agatha too.”

“Please…” Rio’s voice cracked into a thin, broken whisper. Defeated, she buried her face in her hands, entirely unable to meet Yelena’s piercing gaze as the tears finally spilled over.

“It’s the truth, Rio,” Yelena pressed. “How did your dad always put it? We can’t undo the past, but the now is ours to write.”

“He’s not here to say it anymore,” Rio spat through gritted teeth, her shoulders shaking as she wept into her palms.

“Exactly. He isn’t. But you are, and you get to decide where you go from here. You can either keep eating yourself alive from inside out, or you can scream it all out and finally breathe again. You always pinpoint everyone else’s choices, Rio, but what about yours? You have to choose to live. You can’t just let life run over you. You’re carrying so much inside… Just let it out, okay?”

After a few seconds, Rio wiped her face with her hands and looked back at her with a defeated expression, feeling more vulnerable than ever. She knew that if she put the wall back up right now, things would stay exactly as they were. But at the same time, she hated admitting that she was finally letting herself be seen for who she truly was.

“And what the hell am I supposed to do?” Rio asked, her voice cracking under the strain. “Just go scream in everyone’s face?”

“If that’s what it takes, then yeah,” Yelena answered instantly, tossing out a casual shrug. “If you need to scream, scream. If you need to break down, break down. Just be honest with yourself about what you’re actually feeling.”

Rio fell completely silent. Her feelings were moving too fast for her to put them into words. That had always been her biggest problem — she never knew how to explain what was going on inside her. Everything just turned into a messy knot in her chest. No matter how deeply she felt, the words never came out right. Whenever she tried to talk, she ended up using her words like weapons. Because she didn’t know how to express her pain, her strong emotions would shock her system and turn her cold. She was sharp and harsh, inside and out, so she almost always ended up hurting the people she loved whenever she tried to explain how she felt.

But looking at the tomb, she knew she had to try. She owed it to herself, and she really owed it to her father. If she could turn back in time, she would have fought to tell him exactly how she felt. She wouldn’t have stayed quiet, poured another drink, and pretended everything was fine when they both knew he was dying.

“Do you miss it?” Yelena’s voice broke through her heavy thoughts. Rio blinked, looking at her in confusion. “Do you miss your brother and how things used to be?”

Rio just nodded, completely defeated.

“Then why the hell are you still sitting here for when they’re waiting for you at Pedra Purpura?"

Chapter 17: truce

Chapter Summary

TW: this chapter contains scenes of domestic violence, so if that’s a trigger for you, please read with caution

Chapter Notes

hey, we’re back!!! this chapter is a total rollercoaster, so strap in for the ride and enjoy the slowest slow burn in history but trust me, it will burn!!! see you in the notes at the end :)

See the end of the chapter for more notes

“I hate you for what you did and I miss you like a little kid” — Motion Sickness, Phoebe Bridgers

***

For over an hour, Agatha paced the room in a blur of restless energy. She was on her third or fourth outfit change, each return to the mirror punctuated by a frustrated grunt. Her clothes felt wrong, her hair looked worse, and with every passing minute, Benito and Kate offered another round of complaints about her unnecessary nerves.

As if she didn’t have every reason to be on edge.

The mere thought of sharing a room with Rio again tied her stomach in nervous knots. It wasn’t about Rio herself, but the sheer weight of their history — a chaotic lifetime abruptly buried when they both agreed to pretend the other had never existed.

Alex insisted it was about the love they once shared, but Agatha knew better: it was about the trauma. It was about how deeply they had wounded each other — a damage Agatha had never forgiven herself for inflicting. Rio had hurt her through reckless choices, sharp words, and self-destruction, but Agatha was hardly innocent. She had broken Rio’s heart and refused to let her heal, constantly pulling her back only to shatter her again with promises she lacked the courage to keep. Theirs wasn’t a romance; it was tragedy. Agatha knew that because it still ached inside her. It had never stopped aching.

For years, she had watched Rio spiral to rock bottom — drowning in festering resentment, suppressed rage, and enough alcohol to make drinking her only constant in life. While Rio pulled the trigger on her own undoing, the destruction tore Agatha apart because she loved her. She knew she wasn’t the sole cause, but she couldn’t deny that the wreckage of their relationship fed the storm raging in Rio’s chest.

Even after realizing her marriage to Tessa was a mistake, Agatha knew that turning back time wouldn’t have saved her and Rio. They were never going to work — not as they were. There had been too many years of fighting and heartache, each attempt ending in absolute disaster. Agatha couldn’t stomach the thought of hurting Rio for the rest of their lives, nor could she bear to watch her wither in a frustrated, unhappy existence. Selfish as she had been, Agatha finally let go because she couldn’t bear to see Rio suffer for the fantasy of a love that brought only pain. She was crushed under the weight of a story that was doomed from the start.

Severing ties wasn’t driven by a desire to erase Rio, nor lack of love. The years Agatha spent away from the ranch weren’t because she didn’t miss her or genuinely wanted the distance. She walked away precisely because she loved her too much. She knew thar proximity would make it impossible to resist a bond that was destroying them both. Unable to live with her share of the blame for the mess Rio’s life had become, Agatha stepped aside to give Rio the life she deserved, she refused to let Rio surrender her future to a failed past.

Walking away was the hardest choice Agatha ever made — but it didn’t mean she loved Rio any less.

Agatha had spent years trying to erase Rio from her mind, but she never stopped worrying. She wondered about Rio’s days, whether she was truly happy, and if she had managed to put the past behind her in a way Agatha never could. She continually justified the distance, holding onto the reassuring updates from her godfather that Rio was finally okay. That was all Agatha ever wanted: the certainty that Rio was whole.

Her nerves weren’t born out of dread. The truth was, she longed to see her. More than anything, Agatha wished they could speak as equals, lay the past to rest, and forge a new path where they could be in each other’s lives again as friends.

Yet, she knew it wasn’t fair — not to Rio, and not to herself. Agatha felt entirely undeserving of forgiveness and had no right to ask for a truce. She knew this invitation was just another one of Benito’s meddling schemes, which only fueled her anxiety. The last thing she wanted was to intrude Rio’s space more than she already had.

They might have become strangers, but Agatha knew Rio too well. She knew how Rio processed her pain: cornered by her feelings, she would shut down, bottle everything up, and drown it in a drink. Agatha refused to trigger that cycle again. She had been a burden for far too long; she wouldn’t be the spark that ignited another fire.

She had every reason to be on edge, and every reason to refuse. But Benito and Kate wouldn’t let it go.

“My god, Agatha! It’s not a date, you don’t need to stress over what you’re wearing,” Benito muttered, his impatient tone laced with amusement that sent a flush of pure stress to Agatha’s ears.

Agatha — having just emerged from the bathroom for the thousandth time, now adjusting her earrings in front of the mirror while wearing a simple light-blue sundress — glared at him, her nostrils flaring as she huffed in irritation.

“I shouldn’t be worrying at all, because I shouldn’t even be going,” she shot back.

Benito rolled his eyes while Kate slumped her head back against the sofa in utter boredom.

“There’s nothing more to discuss, you were outvoted,” Kate murmured. “You voted no, we voted yes. Majority wins.”

“You two are both stupid children without a single grain of common sense!”

“Agatha, stop being dramatic,” Benito clicked his tongue, flippantly waving a hand that made her eyes widen in disbelief. “It’s a family gathering. You’re family.”

“I wasn’t invited!” Agatha practically shrieked, her arms dropping to her sides in complete exasperation as she swept her hair into a massy bun, casting anxious glances at the mirror to judge the effort.

“I invited you!” Benito declared, flashing a smug smile.

“And does your sister know that?” Agatha shot back, her brow arching sharply.

“Details, details,” he countered with a tilt of his head, earning another loud huff from her.

“Look, let’s get down to reality,” Kate interrupted before the argument could spiral further. Clasping her hands in her lap, she turned full attention to Agatha. “You don’t have any plans to go back to California, so you can’t dodge Rio forever.”

“She’s dodging me too, and it’s been working out great so far,” Agatha muttered with a careless shrug, sitting on an ottoman to slip into her shoes.

“And how long do you honestly think that will last?” Kate pressed. “You practically live in the same place now. Like it or not, you share a family. Eventually, you’ll have to talk.”

“It doesn't have to be tonight,” Agatha offered with a weary sigh. “I’m not saying we’ll never speak again, but barging into her space like this feels completely unfair.”

“You’re not barging in. I invited you,” Benito reminded her.

“Fine then,” Agatha let out a dry laugh. “I don’t think it’s fair for you to barge into her space, especially when she’s finally giving you a chance to rebuild your relationship.”

Benito’s eyes widened. He flashed a frantic look at Kate, gesturing for backup, but she merely shrugged.

“She has a good point,” Kate admitted with a grimace, making Benito exhale in sheer annoyance.

“This is ridiculous,” Agatha said, shaking her head as she stood. “I’m changing back into my pajamas. You two go on ahead. I’m staying out of it.”

“No, no, no!” Benito scrambled, pulling out his phone and frantically tapping the screen. “I’m calling the voice of reason. She’ll set you straight.”

“Don’t you dare—” Agatha warned, diving to snatch the phone, but the call connected on the very first ring.

“This better be a life-or-death situation, because I was two minutes away from starting Law & Order,” Alex’s voice snapped impatiently over the speakerphone, drawing a frustrated groan from Agatha.

“It’s not!” Agatha shouted, lunging again as Benito dodged her, darting around the room to keep the phone out of her reach. “It’s just Benito throwing a fit!”

“Is that Agatha yelling?” Alex asked, her interest clearly piqued. Benito called out a loud affirmative. “Oh, now I definitely want to hear this.”

Accepting defeat, Agatha threw her hands up, grunted, and collapsed onto the sofa next to Kate. When Benito slid into the cushion beside her, she shoved him pettily before locking her arms across her chest.

“Okay, listen,” Benito began, taking charge of the call. “Rio invited us to Pedra Purpura for a family night, but Agatha is throwing a full-blown tantrum and refusing to go.”
