“That’s not how it happened,” Agatha said, finally managing to snatch the phone away. “Rio invited Benito and Kate,” she emphasized sharply. “Benito lied to me, claiming she included me, when in reality she has no idea he asked me to come.”

“You’re family!” he argued in exasperation, ignoring Agatha’s furious glare while Kate bit her lip to stifle a laugh. “Your presence is implied!”

“Isn’t Pedra Purpura a bar?” Alex asked, met by a duo of affirmative grunts from the room. “It’s a bar. Nobody needs an invitation to go to a bar. You just walk in.”

“Okay, she actually has a point there,” Kate grinned, prompting Agatha to roll her eyes.

“That’s not the issue, Alex, and you know it,” Agatha pressed. “I tried talking to her once and it was a complete disaster. She made her feelings about me being here crystal clear. Tonight is about her and her brother, it’s not fair for me to tag along. I know how she is, and no matter how much Benito insists this is a brilliant idea, it’s going to backfire on him.”

“Agatha, you tried talking to her on the day of her father’s funeral, did you honestly expect open arms?”

“I don’t even know why I’m talking to you,” Agatha muttered impatiently. “You’re just as childish as these two.”

“Hey!” Benito and Kate protested in unison, earning only a cold huff from Agatha.

“Agatha, how much longer do you think you can stay on this ranch dodging her like the plague?” Alex asked, her tone softening. “It isn’t sustainable for either of you. Sooner or later, you have to talk.”

“Thank you, Alex!” Benito chimed in. “That is literally what I just said.”

Agatha let out a long, heavy sign of defeat.

“I’m serious,” Alex continued. “You’ve been there for a month or so, and every time we speak, it sounds more and more like you want to stay. Like it or not, your lives are intertwined again. It’s inevitable. You live yards apart, your mother treats her like a daughter, and she’s baked into your family. You can’t pretend she doesn't exist. Eventually, your paths will cross, and you’ll have to face each other.”

Of course Agatha had thought about that — she just forced the reality out of her mind every time it surfaced. The last thing she wanted was to overstep.

“I just don’t want to force it,” Agatha murmured. “If she wants to talk, I’m right here. I’m open to it, I’ve already tried, but I shouldn’t impose myself or crash her place without knowing if she’s okay with it.”

“Didn’t you two talk today?” Kate chimed in, causing Agatha to let out a nervous chuckle.

“We didn’t talk,” Agatha muttered, rolling her eyes as a sudden flutter bloomed in her stomach at the memory. “She waved, I smiled. That was it.”

“See?” Benito grinned. “She doesn’t hate you!”

“I doubt she’d scream at me in front of my son,” Agatha countered, raising an eyebrow.

“She was with Nicky?” Alex asked, her voice instantly dripping with gossipy curiosity.

“You have no idea,” Kate chuckled. “He adores her. Follows her around all day.”

“The apple doesn’t fall far from the tree, does it?” Alex laughed from the speaker. Before Agatha could interject, her friend pressed on. “Seriously, Agatha, that’s even more reason to try. She’s already part of Nicky’s life.”

“Alex, I—”

“Kids, run along and find something else to do so I can talk to her alone,” Alex interrupted smoothly. “Adult conversation time.”

Benito and Kate groaned, attempting to object, but Alex relentlessly shooed them off over the line. Huffing in surrender, Benito finally caved — though he made a point to warn Agatha he’d be back in twenty minutes and expected her ready to leave.

“I need you to be completely honest with me,” Alex said, her tone suddenly serious. Agatha offered a quiet hum of agreement; she really had no choice, given that Alex knew her better than anyone. “What are you going to go? Do you actually plan on coming back, or are you moving somewhere else to start fresh with Nicky?”

That was the million-dollar question — the very thought that had been keeping her awake for weeks. Agatha hadn’t planned on moving to Darby. In fact, she hadn’t planned anything at all; she had simply bolted on a sudden surge of courage. When she drove off with her life packed into her car, her only absolute certainty was that her marriage was dead and she would never cross that threshold again. Everything else was a total blank.

During her first few days at the ranch, she had considered settling somewhere else — maybe another city in California — to find a manageable compromise with Tessa for Nicky’s sake. As much as she wanted her ex-wife to vanish, Tessa was still her son’s mother, and Agatha wanted to avoid an ugly fight she knew she couldn’t afford to lose.

She certainly hadn’t planned on feeling at home. Agatha had spent her youth running from this place, but now, everything felt different. It was more about her own growth than the town itself, yet it had been years since she felt this grounded — free, genuinely happy, and completely calm. It was good to be back on the ranch surrounded by family. Even better was watching Nicky thrive — uninhibited, healthy, and happier than she had ever seen him.

She hadn’t planned on staying, but now, she couldn’t bear the thought of leaving. She was finally right where she belonged.

“I never thought I’d say this, but I really love it here,” Agatha admitted with a soft, nervous chuckle. “It’s not just the ranch, it’s how I feel here. I don’t think any other place could give me this sense of home. You should see Nicky, he loves this place. I’m happy here, Alex. I’m happy seeing him flourish.”

“Then own it. It’s your home now,” Alex said softly, her smile practically radiating though the receiver.

“I never imagined this would happen. I didn’t come here to stay,” Agatha murmured, sinking into the sofa cushions and letting her eyes drift. “It just… happened.”

A quiet beat passed before her best friend let out a heavy sigh.

“You’re not going to like what I’m about to say,” Alex warned. “But you’re not on vacation, Agatha. If this is home now, you need to start building a life for your stability and Nicky’s. Tessa is refusing to sign the divorce papers and constantly blowing up your phone. Do you really think she’s just going to let you walk away? She’s already threatened to take this to court if you stay.”

“I know…” Agatha exhaled sharply, rubbing her temples. “I just didn’t want it to get this ugly.”

“We’re talking about Tessa, of course it’s getting ugly,” Alex countered with a trace of disdain. “You’re a lawyer, Agatha. You know she’ll build an ironclad case if you don’t pull yourself together and take control of the narrative.”

“And how am I supposed to do that right now? I can barely keep my head above water!”

“Life doesn’t pause while you figure things out. You need to make a move, find work, enroll Nicholas in school, set up his therapy, and get out of your mother’s basement!” Agatha grunted in response, but Alex pressed on. “Tessa is a top prosecutor at one of the biggest firms in California. She knows stability wins custody battles, and she can prove she has it. You need to build your arsenal: document every moment she neglected him, contact his former nannies, pull his school records. It’s a fight, Agatha.”

“I am going to fight, you know it. No one is taking my son from me,” Agatha declared, her voice hardening. “I was just… naive, I guess. I didn’t want to believe she’d drag us through the dirt like this.”

“You were the only one holding out hope,” Alex murmured, her eye-roll palpable over the line. “I know you’ll fight for him, and I’ll be right beside you in the trenches every step of the way.” Agatha’s posture softened with unspoken gratitude. “I know you’ll win, but you have to start moving.”

“I will,” Agatha nodded to the empty room. “I was an idiot to think there was a gentler way out. You’re right.”

“Good. Now that we’ve established the ranch is your home now, you need to accept the package deal: Rio is going to be in your life.”

Agatha groaned softly. “Do we really need to go back to that?”

“Come on, Agatha…” Alex let out a soft laugh. “You can’t run from her forever. You already tried that, remember?”

“As if I could forget…”

“I know you haven’t. You never did,” Alex said gently, prompting a heavy sigh from Agatha. “She has always mattered to you. I know everything that went down between you two was a disaster, but that’s in the past. You’re not the same person you were back then, and neither is she. Besides, neither of you really has a choice, you’re going to have to coexist.”

“That doesn’t make it any easier,” Agatha murmured, closing her eyes. “I deeply regret how things ended, and how stupid and selfish I was. But I can’t just assume she’s okay with it. I can’t simply walk up to her and say hey, can we be friends? It’s been too long, Alex.”

“Exactly. It’s been years,” Alex offered warmly. “It was awful, but it passed. Even through the worst of it, you never stopped caring about her, and I’m certain she never stopped caring about you, either.” Agatha let out a breath of quiet disbelief, but Alex pressed on. “You will always matter to each other, Agatha. You can’t just erase history.”

Agatha was at a loss for words. With her eyes shut, a familiar tightness gripped her chest. She was terrified that her presence would bring Rio pain, but what she kept hidden — even from Alex — was how much it hurt her, too. It felt like staring at a photograph from the happiest moment of her life, consumed by the crushing certainty that she would never feel that way again.

The truth was, Agatha didn’t know if she could bear having her worst fears confirmed: that Rio truly didn’t want her around, or that nothing remained between them except rage and resentment. If that was the reality, she didn’t know if she could stay. The ranch wouldn’t feel like home anymore.

“I don’t want to force myself onto her, I really don’t. But it’s hard,” Agatha admitted softly. “I don’t know if I’m ready for this. I don’t know if I can handle the truth.”

“You don’t have a choice. It’s going to happen eventually, so why not now?”

“What if I show up and it’s an absolute disaster?” she whispered, her voice laced with insecurity as her fingers massaged her temple.

“Then you leave and try again another day,” Alex said smoothly, as if it were the easiest thing in the world. “If it goes south, you accept it and wait for her to make the next move. But the point is, it’s going to happen sooner or later. Why keep putting it off? What I said before applies here too, you need to stop hiding and start making things happen.”

***

Three Years Ago

Agatha had called more than twenty times, only to be sent straight to voicemail every single time. She probably shouldn’t have left such furious, curse-laden voice messages, but Tessa had no right to pull a stunt like this. Agatha knew it was pure retaliation — a petty punishment for leaving the house the day before without asking permission. It was completely unfair, and Tessa knew it, which made her behavior all the more calculated. Agatha had even tried calling her in-laws, but no one picked up. She was on the verge of losing her mind.

Things hadn’t been good between them for a long time. In truth, their marriage had never been the fairy tale Agatha insisted on painting it as; she had simply clung to the illusion because the concept of their life together looked picture-perfect on paper. Deep down, she had noticed the red flags long before the wedding — a persistent warning whisper in her mind that she ignored for the sake of the dream. Agatha had always accepted the excuses. She wanted to believe Tessa would be better, that she wanted to be better, and that her volatile outbursts were merely temporary. But with each passing day, that hope further out of reach.

For three days and nights, Agatha had been stranded at home alone with their son while Tessa vanished without trace, offering nothing more than a flimsy excuse about an urgent work trip. It was insulting — as if Agatha hadn’t worked at the exact same firm, as if she didn’t have enough contacts to know it was a poorly constructed lie. She was utterly exhausted. While she loved her son more than life itself, he was not an easy child; he required constant, intense attention and meltdowns were triggered by the smallest things. All Agatha wanted was a little support. She needed her wife — the mother of her child, for god’s sake — to step up, share the burden, and be a steady presence. But Tessa was never there.

Exhausted and profoundly lonely, Agatha had just wanted a night to unwind: a glass of wine, a listening ear, and a space where she could speak freely without walking on eggshells. That was why she had spent the previous evening with Alex, her best friend. Yet the moment she walked through the door that night with Nicky, she found Tessa waiting on the couch with crossed arms, narrowed eyes, and a ice-cold expression. Without a word, Tessa let out a sharp, sarcastic huff and retreated straight to the guest room — not even sparing a glance at Nicholas, as if her own son were invisible.

Normally, Agatha would have chased after her to smooth things over, but she was burned out. She was sick of being blamed for the paranoid fantasies brewing in her wife’s head, sick of carrying the heavy, constant guilt of feeling like she did everything wrong. So that night, she didn’t follow.

When Agatha woke up this morning at nine, the house was completely empty, no sign of Tessa, and no sign of Nicholas. It was nearly three in the afternoon. She couldn’t care less about her wife disappearing — she was used to that — but not knowing where her son was or if he was safe was driving her to frantic madness.

Tears of sheer panic streamed down Agatha’s face as she dialed her wife for the thousandth time, just as the front door swung open. Instantly, she saw her little boy — his face flushed, eyes swollen, and nosy runny from crying. Agatha dropped to her knees on the floor, and Nicholas sprinted into her arms, burying his face in her neck and wrapping his little arms tightly around her, sniffling softly.

“It’s okay, my love,” she whispered, swallowing the tremor in her voice as she closed her eyes in overwhelming relief. “It’s okay, mommy’s right here.”

“My god, so dramatic,” Tessa muttered.

If looks could kill, Tessa would have dropped dead on the spot when Agatha looked up. Her wife didn’t seem the least bit remorseful; she simply rolled her eyes.

“Sleepy, mommy,” Nicholas whimpered, his face still pressed against her collarbone.

Agatha nodded gently, kissing the top of her son’s head, but kept her ferocious gaze locked onto her wife’s cold blue eyes — which stared right back, unimpressed, with a lazily arched eyebrow.

“I have no idea why you’re looking at me like that,” her wife tossed out with a light, dismissive huff, causing Agatha’s jaw to set tight as her eyes narrowed into slits.

“Are you sleepy?” Even at the peak of her fury, Agatha’s tone transformed into gentleness as she addressed her son. Nicholas nodded, rubbing his eyes. “Do you want mommy to put you to bed?” He nodded again, and she kissed his crown, running her fingers through his soft brown curls.

“Agatha—” Tessa started, but Agatha cut her off instantly, raising a sharp index finger.

“You stay right there,” she commanded, her voice low and unwavering. “I am putting him to bed, and then we are going to talk.”

Tessa merely shrugged and shook her head. It was her signature move — whenever Agatha tried to stand her ground, Tessa reframed her boundary as an overblown dramatic display.

Agatha walked slowly toward her son’s bedroom, gently swaying her body to soothe him. Thumb in mouth, Nicholas blinked heavily with exhaustion. His swollen eyelids bore the unmistakable signs of a long crying spell — a sight that never failed to break Agatha’s heart.

Gently, she lowered him onto the mattress and pulled the quilt embroidered with little horses up to his chin, tucking it neatly around his small frame into a cozy cocoon. A faint smile touched her lips as she looked down at his drowsy face.

“What did you do today?” she asked softly, sweeping his dark hair away from his forehead.

“Grandma’s house,” he murmured around a wide yawn.

Agatha let out a breath she hadn’t realized she was holding, relieved.

“And why are you crying?” she asked gently. “You love grandma’s house.”

“There was too many people,” he grumbled, his tiny brow furrowing. “Too noisy and momma didn’t want to leave.”

Swallowing hard, Agatha hid her growing concern behind a reassuring smile. “She just wanted to spend time with her mommy, sweetheart.”

“But I wanted my mommy,” Nicholas said, reaching up with both hands.

Agatha knew the gesture well — it was his purest way of showing affection. She leaned down, letting his small palms frame her face, and rested her forehead against his, looking into the deep brown eyes she cherished above everything else. Whenever he did this, an overwhelming sense of peace washed over her.

When he lowered his hands and tucked them back under the blanket, Agatha kissed his forehead.

“Mommy’s right here now. You’re home,” she whispered, settling the blanked around his shoulders. “Take a nice nap, and when you wake up, I’ll still be here.”

“Mommy,” Nicky whined cutely as she began to stand. Agatha immediately paused, giving him her undivided attention. “Sing the song for me,” he pleaded with his lovely eyes.

Agatha broke into a warm smile and nodded. It was Where the Skies are Blue — Javier’s favorite song, which he played on his acoustic guitar whenever he came to visit. Ever since Nicholas first heard it, he demanded it every time he fell asleep.

“You’re gonna leave, it ain’t gonna break my heart, mama…” she began softly, her voice hushed and soothing as she stroke his hair. She watched his eyelids grow heavier. “I’ve never seen nobody quite like you…” A faint smile touched his lips as sleep finally pulled him under. “And if you ever change your tune, or the world’s got the best of you, you can always find me where the skies are blue…”

She kept singing until his breathing settled into a deep, rhythmic pattern. Her little angel. Leaving a gentle kiss on his forehead, she stepped away quietly, pausing at the door for one last look before silently pulling it shut behind her.

The moment the latched clicked, the tenderness drained from Agatha’s posture. Her shoulders squared, her pine stiffened, and she took a stabilizing breath to brace herself for the collision ahead.

When she stepped into the living room, she found Tessa lounging on the couch with a glass of wine. Tessa had recently cut her hair into a sharp neck-length bob, and when she first went platinum blonde, Agatha had found it striking. But looking at her now — detached and lost in thought, wearing a baby-blue silk shirt with rolled sleeves, wide-leg linen trousers, and hands heavy with gold rings — all Agatha saw was calculated superficiality. She wondered, not for the first time, how every drop of warmth she once felt for her wife had evaporated so completely.

“What were you thinking?” Agatha demanded, her voice cutting through the quiet room.

“What are you talking about?” Tessa replied, having the nerve to look bewildered.

“What am I talking about?” Agatha scoffed, a bitter laugh escaping her throat. “I woke up to an empty house! My son was gone! What the hell were you thinking?”

“Oh, so you can take him wherever you want whenever it suits you, but I can’t enjoy a morning with my parents?” Tessa shot back, her tone laced with sharp indignation.

Agatha stared at her, stunned into silence for a fraction of a second before shaking her head.

“A morning? You vanished with him for half of the day without a word!” Agatha snapped, her frustration boiling over. “I don’t care about you taking him to see your parents, Tessa! The issue is that I woke up, he was gone, and I was left entirely in the dark! No note, no text, and you ignored all my calls. Do have any idea what you put me through?”

“Of course I didn’t answer, I was with my parents! I wasn’t going to sit there staring at my phone every two seconds!” Tessa snapped, her voice rising in irritation as she slammed her glass onto the table. Stepping directly into Agatha’s personal space, she glared down at her. “You were asleep when I left, and I didn’t plan on staying long. Stop being so hysterical!”

“And you couldn’t leave a note? You couldn't send a simple text?” Agatha shot back sarcastically/ Her eyes narrowed into cold slits. “Do you have any idea what you put me through, Tessa? Hours! A whole damn day not knowing where my son was or if he was safe!”

“What could have possibly happened to him?” Tessa countered loudly, throwing her hands up in exasperation. “I took our son to see his grandparents!”

“I didn’t know that!” Agatha shouted back, matching her volume.

“I didn’t plan on being gone long!” Tessa practically yelled, the harsh authority in her voice making Agatha flinch. “Besides, what’s the big deal? You take him out all the time without giving me a play-by-play.”

“So that’s what this is about? You’re punishing me for being a present mother while you’re absent? Is that it? What was I supposed to do, go out and leave him home alone?”

“Punish you?” Tessa spat the words with pure disdain. “Why on earth would I want to punish you? When have I ever punished you for anything?” Agatha wet her dry lips, letting out a breath of utter disbelief. “Not everything revolves around you, Agatha. I’m his mother, too.”

“Of course it’s not about me,” Agatha murmured, a bitter, humorless laugh escaping her chest. “Is anything in this house ever about me?”

“Of course you’re going to play the victim,” Tessa scoffed, rolling her eyes. “As if you don’t live like a queen on my dime, getting whatever you want, whenever you want it. My god, life must be so terribly hard for you!”

“I don’t live on your dime because I want to,” Agatha said, swallowing back her pride. “I don’t work because someone actually has to raise our child.”

“And that is exactly why I work my ass off!” Tessa roared, her face flushing red with rage.

“And you work so hard, don’t you?” Agatha threw the words back like venom. A mocking smile curled her lips as Tessa’s eyes narrowed. “I’m sure you get completely exhausted on all your business trips fucking all the whores you play house with.”

Agatha didn’t even have time to blink before Tessa’s palm cracked violently across her face.

The impact left her cheek burning, radiating a blinding string. Agatha froze, her breath hitching in her throat as her hand flew to her face. Sudden teats blurred her vision.

Tessa, now trembling, stared at her wife with wide, horror-struck eyes.

“My love, I’m so sorry!” Tessa blurted out, her voice choking as she instantly closed the distance between them. Agatha remained completely numb, paralyzed by the shock. “I’m so sorry, my god, I’m so sorry, baby!” Tessa cried, tears welling in her own eyes as she cupped Agatha’s burning face and pressed their foreheads together. “I shouldn’t have— I just— God, baby, forgive me. Please, forgive me,” she pleaded, the words tumbling out in a desperate rush. Agatha couldn’t speak; she couldn’t move. “I didn’t mean to, I—” Tessa stammered, shaking her head frantically as she peppered kisses across Agatha’s cheek and temple. “I just lost my head! I would never cheat on you, baby, I would never hurt you. Never! I love you, Agatha, more than anything in the world, I swear. I lost control, I’m so, so sorry…”

Tessa kept babbling, her tone shifting to a frantic whisper, her eyes wide with palpable panic. It was a barrage of pleas Agatha felt powerless to process. She stood catatonic as her wife declared her love, whispered sweet promises, and swore — just as she always did — that it would never happen again.

When Tessa finally wrapped her arms around Agatha’s waist, burying her face into the crook of her neck, while weeping and begging for forgiveness, Agatha just stood there, motionless as a statue.

***

Once again, Tessa had vanished on another sudden work trip. Agatha would never admit it out loud — not even under torture — but her wife’s absence brought a profound sense of relief.

Agatha had reached a point in her life where pretend was second nature. Most days, she hid behind a practiced smile the moment she stepped outside her door, barely aware of her true feelings. Today, however, her smile was real. She was finally getting to spend time with her family, and god knew how desperately she needed to be around the people she loved.

It was Alex’s birthday, though the party wasn’t until that evening. Her best friend had begged for a full godmother-and-godson day with Nicholas as her present. Agatha, who rarely liked being away from her son, readily agreed; Alex was the person she trusted most in the world, and Nicky had been practically bouncing off the walls with excitement. With her entire day wide open, Agatha finally allowed herself to unwind, a faint, genuine smile gracing her lips as she strolled along the beachfront promenade.

The moment she stepped inside Casa Vidal, Agatha couldn’t contain her joy. Kate, Benito, and her godfather were sitting at a porch table overlooking the beach, laughing together over glasses of wine. When she greeted them, the trio broke into wide grins and rushed over to engulf her in a warm hug. It was exactly what she needed; she had missed her fiercely. Benito had just returned from a three-month study abroad program in France, Kate had spent the early summer with her family, and it had been too long since Agatha had seen her godfather.

Javier wrapped his arms around her in a tight embrace. Looking up at him, Agatha felt an instinctive wave of tenderness. He was still the same massive, smiling man with a booming, welcoming voice, though he now sported a full graying beard to match his hair, his caramel skin deeply bronzed by the sun. God, how she had missed him. All of them.

“Where’s my cowboy?” Javier asked the moment she sat down, causing Agatha to let out a soft laugh.

“He’s spending the day with Alex,” she answered, accepting a glass of wine as Javier’s expression melted into a slight pout.

“I miss him so much.”

“He’s going to go insane when he finds out you’re here,” Kate added between sips.

“Sometimes I think you love him more than me,” Benito grumbled, drawing laughs from the table.

“Well, of course I do! Don’t you know a grandfather’s love for his grandkid trumps his love for his own children?” Javier teased with a broad smile. “At least Agatha gave me a grandson. What about you? When are you going to grant me that blessing?” he poked at his son, who rolled his eyes.

“For your information, I already have twenty-four kids,” Benito replied with a smug air that made his father shake his head in amusement. “And that number is only going to grow. I’m probably the biggest sperm donor in all of California.”

“You’re a freak,” Agatha muttered over her glass.

“And where all these kids on the ranch? Because I haven’t met a single one.”

“It’s anonymous, they’ll never know,” Kate said with a chuckle.

“I don’t know why you guys tease me so much about it,” Benito muttered with a shrug. “People get to be happy having children they couldn’t otherwise have, and I leave my legacy behind without the burden of raising a kid. It’s a win-win situation.”

"¡Dios mío! ¿En qué fallé contigo?” Javier groaned in a good-humored despair. “I’ve already given up hope on Rio, but I still hold out hope that you two will give me a few grandkids,” he said, pointing between Kate and Benito. The pair exchanged a look and burst out laughing

“Dad, how many times do I have to tell you that we’re not dating?”

“You’re just in denial,” Javier dismissed with a wave of his hand. “Time will prove me right.”

“Whatever keeps you happy, dad…” Benny muttered, rolling his eyes as he took another sip.

“Okay, I’d really prefer to stop talking about your sperm,” Agatha said, scrunching her nose at Benny, who playfully stuck his tongue out in response. Rolling her eyes, she turned back to her godfather. “I want to hear about you. How are things at the ranch?”

“I was actually just talking about that before you walked in,” Javier said with a relaxed smile, leaning back in his chair. “Things are great, better than ever, honestly. We just built new stables at the racetrack, and more people are moving into town. Business keeps booming.”

“That’s great,” Agatha said, her smile widening. “Benny mentioned you’re releasing another line of artisanal wines this year. I hope I get a sample for my collection.”

“Of course, tesoro,” he said warmly. “Rio created an entire collection inspired by the seasons. I think it’s her best work yet. I’ll gladly bring you a few bottles.”

Agatha smiled, brushing past the sudden tightness in her chest at the sound of Rio’s name. It happened every single time — that bittersweet sting of loving someone who had become a stranger, the strange grief of mourning a person who was still very much alive. Whenever Rio crossed her mind, Agatha wondered if she would ever truly move on.

“Speaking of Rio, how is she?” Benito asked with a ghost of a smile, his brown eyes lighting up with expectation. Agatha knew that look all too well; she felt that same spark herself.

“She’s doing great. I couldn’t be prouder,” Javier beamed. Agatha couldn’t help but smile along with him. “Actually…” he reached into his pocked and pulled out a small silver token, his smile deepening. “She hit ten years of sobriety this week.”

As the conversation swirled around Rio, Agatha drifted into her own thoughts — her gaze wandering toward the distant horizon where the sky met the sea. She wondered what the sky above Rio looked like on the ranch right now. It was so surreal to be so close yet so impossibly far, learning about Rio’s life without being a part of it. Still, a quiet warmth washed over her knowing Rio was okay — that she was genuinely happy.

Agatha had always wanted that for her. And every time she thought about it, she felt a little happy, too.

***

Present Day

Even when it was just a sketch on paper, Pedra Purpura was her ultimate pride — the physical embodiment of a dream and a sense of fulfillment unlike anything else. The moment it opened, it became her sanctuary: a space uniquely her own that reflected her from head to toe.

It was a silly thought, but opening those doors felt like opening a piece of her soul to the world. And as stubborn as she was, hiding behind a suit of chrome armor, she genuinely hoped Benito would walk through them. She wanted him there, even after everything she had said, even after trying so hard to push him away.

Rio found a bitter irony in how often she craved the very things she claimed to despise. Her default impulse was to push people away and run, when deep down, all she wanted was to hold them close and stay. She couldn’t speak her truth without hurling the stones that had hardened inside her over time.

Terrified of losing again, she preferred to hide. Emptiness was easier to manage than the pain of longing — nothing was more frightening than the could grip of nostalgia.

Rio felt everything too intensely. Her emotions overwhelmed her, stripping away her common sense and leaving her disoriented. She was furious at her own yearning and terrified of what she couldn’t control. More than anything, she wanted to break free from the grief that had haunted her for years: longing for how things used to be, for her mother, for Agatha, for Benito, and for her father. She missed a time when love hadn’t decayed into sorrow, leaving behind nothing but the chill of an empty room and the gloomy certainty that nothing would ever be the same.

She wanted to do the right thing, but she lacked the strength. Rio was a coward through and through, masking a mountain of fear behind a sharp exterior. She was terrified that if she lost the anger protecting her, she would be left with nothing but raw, aching pain.

She was trying — perhaps not enough, and certainly not correctly, but she was giving everything she had in that moment. She wanted things to work out, yet felt entirely undeserving of it. She had been waiting for Benito since eight in the evening; it was now past ten, and he still hadn’t shown up.

Rio sat in her office, submerged in silence. She was grateful for the soundproof walls, which isolated her from the chatter, laughter, and country music echoing through the winery downstairs.

Slumped in her swivel chair, numb from half a bottle of vodka, she stared at the photograph hidden in her desk drawer: an old portrait of herself grinning from ear to ear with a young Benito on her back and Agatha by her side, smiling so wide her eyes crinkled shut. That picture was tangible proof of the longing consuming her.

She knew she had been cruel and felt awful for it, but grief hardens a person. Rio had petrified to the point of a stone. Deep down, she knew no one was to blame, but bludgeoning others with fault was easier than crumbling from the inside. It wasn’t fair to Benito, and it wasn’t fair to Agatha.

She desperately wanted Benito to arrive, but as for Agatha, she was unsure. The thought of her was jarring. Knowing Agatha was so close felt surreal after years of convincing herself she was merely a ghost — an intangible shadow haunting her memories. Now, that she was real again, Rio didn’t know what to feel, and that uncertainty terrified her.

Yet beneath the fear, she wanted to make amends. She wanted to lift the crushing weight off her chest.

“This is the first time I’ve ever walked in here without finding you out on the floor with everyone else.”

Olivia’s voice made Rio slam the drawer shut, spinning her chair toward the door. The police officer stood in the doorway with arms crossed, leaning against the frame. A ghost of a smile touched her lips, though her brow was knit in quiet concern.

“How did you get in here?” Rio asked, deflection the woman’s searching gaze.

Olivia smirked, flashing a badge from beneath her jacket. “I told them I had a warrant,” she teased, earning an amused huff from Rio as she rolled her chair back to let Olivia perch on the edge of the desk.

“Of course they let you in,” Rio muttered with an eye roll that amused the officer.

“It’s not their fault you show me off everywhere,” Olivia replied with play-acted arrogance. “They probably think I’m the first lady or something.”

“Do they know you’d rather walk the plank than date me?”

“I can’t say, but I know the feeling is entirely mutual,” Olivia grinned.

Rio laughed softly, resting a hand on Olivia’s knee. “And that’s why I love you,” she offered with a charming smirk, watching her friend roll her eyes.

“In all seriousness, though,” Olivia’s tone softened into genuine concern. “Why are you hiding in here?”

“Rough day, I guess,” Rio murmured, looking down at her hands. “I tried— Everyone said I should reach out now that Benny’s back, so I…” she paused, chocking slightly on the words, unaccustomed to opening up. “I invited him tonight, but he didn’t show.”

“What do you mean he didn’t show?” Olivia asked, a confused smile tugging at her lips as Rio let out a heavy sigh. “He’s downstairs.”

Rio’s eyes snapped up, her heart slamming against her ribs like an electric shock.

“He’s here?” she whispered, stunned. “Alone?”

“With two women, I think,” Olivia nodded.

Rio gripped her armrests so tightly her knuckles turned bone-white. The blood drained from her face as a wave of paralyzing anxiety washed over her.

He was here. Which meant Agatha was here, too.

She couldn’t hide in her office feeling sorry for herself anymore; they were both standing right downstairs. Her excuses were gone. Benito. Agatha. Her mind short-circuited as a tremor ran through her hands.

“He’s right there,” Olivia said with a soft chuckle. “Are you going to sit here, or are you going downstairs to talk to him?”

***

“I still think this is a terrible idea,” Agatha muttered, her eyes locked on the three shots of tequila lined up on the marble bar.

It had taken nearly two hours and several generous glasses of wine for Agatha to finally yield to the idea of coming to Pedra Purpura. Benito had been sweating with anxiety, practically pleading in desperation for them to leave before his sister assumed he had chickened out. Even with the glaring certainty that this was a terrible idea — one that could permanently ruin the fragile reconciliation between the siblings — Agatha ultimately caved.

Perhaps it was one of her most selfish impulses in recent memory, because the raw, unavoidable truth was that despite her terror, anticipation sizzled inside her all the same. Deep down, she wanted to go. And who could blame her?

Yes, they shared a mountain of baggage and an entire trail of debris swept under the rug over the years. But before everything broke, they had been something good. They had been everything, and that kind of bond isn’t dissolved by the dust of time. Rio would always be a force of nature in her story — and Agatha would always love her, one way or another. Rio was carved into every piece of who Agatha was; she was part of her very existence, even in her absence.

Agatha had been to a few branches of Casa Vidal — three, to be exact: Los Angeles, which had become her sanctuary near home; Paris, during an anniversary trip; and New York, on one of Tessa’s business ventures. Though distinct and tailored to the luxury of each city, they all shared the same sleek, refined concept.

Pedra Purpura, however, had absolutely nothing in common with them. Yet even though she had walked in blind, the place felt uncannily, exactly as she had imagined.

Far from the cold minimalism and polished elegance of the other branches, Pedra Purpura shed sleek sophistication in favor of deep, comforting warmth. The rustic, raw-stone facade opened into an interior bathed in golden light, where warm wood and rock walls embraced crowded tables of people laughing without restraint. No one held back for appearances here: conversations were boisterous and laughter flowed freely against the lively rhythm of country music. The atmosphere exuded a palpable human warmth — a thick, welcoming embrace of home. Everything about it screamed Rio’s presence; Agatha could feel her soul pulsing in every single detail. It was breathtaking.

Her chest was so tight with nerves it was almost laughable, but there was nowhere left to run. Squeezed between Kate and Benito at the bar, the three of them were about to knock back their second shot of tequila under the silent agreement that liquid courage was the only thing capable of dulling the knot in their stomachs.

“To terrible ideas!” Kate grinned, raising her shot. Benito and Agatha followed, Agatha rolling her eyes before throwing it back in a single gulp, her body shuddering at the bite of the liquor.

“If she stops talking to you after tonight, I’m taking zero responsibility,” Agatha muttered, pointing a finger at Benito.

“I’m aware and I’ll take full responsibility,” he raised his hands in surrender, coaxing a laugh from her.

“I know this is completely out of nowhere, but can I ask something?” Kate chimed in unexpectedly. She was on her third shot, having already downed a few glasses of wine before arriving, and a tipsy gleam was taking over her eyes. “I just can’t get over the name…” she mused softly. Agatha let out a heavy sigh while Benito stifled a laugh, ordering another round. He needed the courage, too. “Like— why Pedra Purpura? What’s the point of the name? Is it a secret code or something? What’s the meaning? God, the curiosity is killing me.”

“Sometimes you’re worse than Yelena,” Benito teased.

“I’m serious!” Kate insisted, her eyes widening.

“I’d be really grateful if you just dropped it,” Agatha said with a tight, pleading smile.

“Why?”

“Kate, think about it for a second,” Benito chuckled, resting an arm on the counter as he turned to his fiancée. “Pedra Purpura. A purple stone. What is a stone that’s purple?”

Agatha buried her face in her hands, snatching Kate’s shot and knocking it down her own throat just as Kate opened her mouth to answer. Kate’s expression instantly fell into a silent, apologetic grimace.

“Geez…” Kate murmured with a nervous chuckle. “I bet that’s not awkward for you at all.”

“Oh, not in the slightest! I’m loving every second,” Agatha replied through gritted teeth.

“Rio!” Benito shouted suddenly, throwing his arms up in a exaggerated wave of tipsy enthusiasm, his cheeks flushed red.

Involuntarily, Agatha turned her entire body to follow Benito’s gaze, her heart dropping and squeezing tight as if it were about to burst.

Rio was right there, in the flesh, just a few paces away. Agatha had caught glimpses of her since returning to the ranch, but she hadn’t truly been able to look at her until now. Seeing her up close brought a painful comfort — a double-edged sensation that felt like a punch to the gut.

Rio had hardened with the passage of time. Her shoulders no longer carried their former lightness, and her old, carefree demeanor had given way to a rigid, guarded posture. Expression lines framed a grave countenance, and her brown eyes, though lacking their past warmth, still burned intense. She wore what seemed like a rehearsed smile, coming across more like an awkward grimace. She appeared mature and nearly impenetrable, wrapped in a layer of harshness Agatha had never expected her to possess.

This was a side of Rio she had never known. Now, more than ever, a bitter certainty settled in Agatha’s chest: she truly didn’t know her anymore. A deep sadness washed over her as she took that in, even if she knew it was only fair — Rio didn’t know her anymore either.

It was jarring to realize that Rio was now a stranger who held all her secrets and knew her entire life — a stranger she had once loved more than anything in the world.

“You came,” Rio said to her brother, her expression a mix of guarded joy and disbelief, laced with the faint hint of a smile. Agatha tracked every single micro-expression on her face.

“Of course I came!” he grinned, opening his armes at the exact second Rio extended her hand.

They instantly swapped — she opened her arms while he held out his hand. Both broke into laughter, and Agatha offered a faint, sympathetic smile. In the end, Rio just shook her head and settled for a firm, affectionate squeeze on Benito’s shoulder, earning a genuine grin from him.

“Kate,” Rio greeted her with a warm smile, but Kate didn’t give her time to overthink, pulling her into a enthusiastic hug that made Rio’s eyes widen as her body went rigid. Everyone laughed, including the brunette beside Rio — Olivia, whom Agatha had only just noticed. “I know we haven’t really talked properly since you arrived, but I hope that changes tonight.”

“It’s totally fine,” Kate said with a shrug. “It’s been a tough time for both of you, so all that matters is where we go from here.” Rio nodded in agreement.

Finally, Rio’s eyes landed on her, and Agatha felt her entire body go rigid. Contrary to her dread, Rio’s lips curled into a quiet sort of smile, her brows knit in an expression Agatha knew all too well: a truce. Agatha smiled back, giving a small, surrendering shrug.

“Hi,” Agatha said faintly.

“Hi,” Rio replied, her shoulders dropping slightly.

“Hi!” Olivia piped up enthusiastically, waving to the group.

Rio shook her head as if snapping out of a trance. “Right, sorry!” she said, turning to the brunette, who watched her with an amused smile. “Everyone, this is Olivia, one of my dearest friends. And Olivia, this is my brother, Benny whom you already know,” Rio introduced as the two shook hands. “This is my sister-in-law, Kate. And this is Agatha.”

“Agatha! You’re the Agatha?” Olivia asked with a bright smile, pointing at her before giving Rio a playful look. “Your Agatha?”

“She’s not— She’s not my Agatha,” Rio stammered, flushed and visibly embarrassed. Agatha lowered her gaze, her cheeks flushing hot with anxiety. “She’s married. To her wife. She has a wife. And a kid! She’s married and has a kid with her wife.”

“I think she gets it,” Benito interjected with a forced smile, his eyes widening to tell his sister to stop babbling. Catching the hint, Rio fell silent and nodded.

“It’s nice to meet you,” Agatha rushed to say before Rio could open her mouth again, extending a hand to Olivia, who smiled and shook it.

“You’re quite famous around here,” the officer teased. Agatha let out a faint chuckle and nudged Kate’s elbow, silently begging her with a look to change the subject.

“So, Rio,” Kate chimed in smoothly, breaking the tension. “Do you have a table for us?”

“Of course!” Rio answered instantly, gesturing for them to follow.

“At least now we know for sure that Rio doesn’t hate you,” Benito whispered as they headed toward the back of the venue. Agatha glared at him with lethal intensity, looking ready to strangle him on the spot.

They settled at a round table, private and tucked away from the main crowd, offering a scenic view of the starry night over the distant hills. Benito sat first, placing himself between Rio and Kate. Agatha sat beside Kate, sandwiched between her and Olivia, who was seated right next to Rio.

Because the table was small, she and Rio were essentially sitting face-to-face.

Rio stared at her without pretense, measuring her with an intense gaze. Agatha held her eyes, unsure how to react yet completely incapable of breaking contact. Once again, just as it had always been, their eyes acted like magnets drawing each other in. Great, Agatha thought, a shiver trailing down her spine. Not awkward at all.

“It’s really nice in here,” Benito broke the silence, scanning their surroundings with an impressed smile on his face. “Different from the others, in a good way.”

“Yeah,” Rio agreed with a nod. “Pedra Purpura is more of my own project. The rest was dad’s idea, I just stick to the wines.”

“The most important part, I’d say,” he said with a laugh, making her roll her eyes; as always, Rio was still completely incapable of taking a compliment. Agatha found it endearing, but kept quiet. “I think this one is my favorite.”

“It’s my favorite, too,” Rio admitted, and both siblings shared a genuine smile. “But I want to hear about you guys,” she added enthusiastically, gesturing toward Kate and Benito. She was clearly a but tipsy; apparently, they weren’t the only ones who had needed liquid courage to face the night. “How did you meet? How long have you been together? Before you got here, I didn’t even know you two were a thing.”

Agatha averted her gaze, pressing her lips together into a neutral mask as she accepted a glass of wine from the waiter. Kate and Benito exchanged a brief look and burst into laughter. Agatha wanted to laugh, too.

“We’ve been together since—”

“I think—”

They spoke over each other and laughed, while Rio watched them with genuine interest, completely detached from any lingering heavy air as she took a sip from her glass.

“It’s hard to pin down when it started, exactly,” Kate answered, and Benito nodded. “We were in the same class, became best friends, and… It just kind of happened.”

“Yep, it just kind of happened,” Benito echoed, lacing his fingers with hers on the tabletop. Agatha took a quiet, deep breath, biting her lip to keep from laughing. This really was a terrible idea.

“Actually, I think dad mentioned you guys before,” Rio murmured, narrowing her eyes and scratching the back of her neck as she searched her memory. “But I thought you were just friends.”

“It wasn’t planned,” Benito said, flashing a warm smile at Kate. “It just happened.”

“And how are the wedding plans coming along?” Olivia joined in, smiling at the couple, who exchanged another glance.

“With everything that happened, we put things on hold, but we don’t want to wait too long to set a date,” he replied, and Rio nodded in understanding.

“I don’t know what you were originally planning, but I think I would be amazing if you did it on the ranch. There’s plenty of space, and a celebration would do us good. It’ll be nice to celebrate something positive after everything,” Rio said, her gaze drifting as if saying those words took an extra toll on her.

“Yeah,” Benito agreed softly. “It’d be a great way to mark a fresh start.”

“Are you planning on staying?” Olivia asked with genuine interest, and this time Rio and Benito locked eyes. He gave a faint nod, and Agatha caught the wave of relief that washed over Rio’s face, along with the deep affection shining in her eyes.

“I don’t know how, but he managed to land a total catch,” Rio muttered to Olivia, using her glass to gesture toward Kate. “She grew up on a farm,” she added, making Olivia look impressed.

It was obvious how comfortable Rio felt around Olivia, as if her mere presence put her at ease. As strange as it felt, Agatha was genuinely happy about it — knowing Rio had someone to lean on, someone she trusted and could be herself around.

“It’s a welcoming change of peace,” Kate shrugged. “I love Los Angeles, of course, but for me, nothing beats the peace of a ranch. I love the routine, the animals, morning horse rides… Honestly, I’ve loved every second since I arrived.”

“Unbelievable,” Rio said with a wide smile. “How did you managed to get her to put up with you, pendejo?”

“I really don’t know,” Benito laughed. “But I agree with her. It’s a great change. I never pictured myself living on the ranch, but I think I just needed some perspective on myself and what I wanted to do with my life. I missed it. It feels good to be home.”

“What about you, Agatha? Any plans to stay?” Olivia asked, and in that exact second, Agatha felt Rio’s gaze lock onto her. Her breath hitched.

“I’m just enjoying it for now,” she lied — there was no need to make the moment any more awkward than it already was. “I just needed a breath of fresh air.”

“Her wife probably misses her by now,” Rio murmured softly. There was no usual sharpness in her tone; she offered it casually, like a passing observation.

Agatha felt Kate and Benito’s eyes dart toward her, accompanied by a sudden, rigid stiffness in her own posture.

“The good thing is she has plenty to keep her busy,” Agatha muttered, clearing her throat before taking a long gulp of her wine. “She works a lot, hardly ever at home.”

“What about you two?” Kate showed mercy, shifting the spotlight toward Rio and Olivia. “Are you together?”

Rio and Olivia exchanged a look before bursting into laughter, shaking their heads in unison.

“We’re good friends,” Rio answered, casting an affectionate glance at the police officer, who threw a casual arm around her shoulders. “More than friends sometimes, but friends above all else.”

A sudden wave of awkwardness washed over Agatha. Averting her gaze, she downed the rest of her wine in several long gulps, reaching for the bottle in the center of the table to refill her glass.

“I’m not big on relationships, I’ve never been one to commit,” Olivia shared with a shrug. “I’m married to my job, always travelling… I don’t like feeling tied down.”

“And I’m just terrible at relationships,” Rio murmured with a roll of her eyes. Agatha felt her cheeks flush hot as she caught Kate watching her carefully.

“You dated plenty over the last few years, though,” Olivia pointed out, prompting Benito to arch his brows in curiosity. Agatha stayed silent, hanging on every word.

“Just passing the time, I guess,” Rio said with an air of mild boredom. “Nothing serious, except once, but it didn’t work out.”

“With the French girl, right?” Benito asked, snapping his fingers as the memory clicked.

Rio narrowed her eyes, intrigued. “Yeah, Camille. How did you know that?”

“Dad told me,” Benito answered with a grin, drawing a soft laugh from his sister. “He thought you two had a real shot. He liked her a lot. You were together for a while, weren’t you?”

“A year and a half, I think.” Rio knit her brows, tracing the timeline in her head. “I met her at a race abroad; her dad was one of my sponsors. She was sweet, loved the sport.” Rio smiled, looking back on it fondly. Slightly tipsy, Agatha wondered if Rio remembered their past with that same soft affection.

“Why did it end?” Kate asked.

Rio shrugged. “She spent most of her time here, but she wanted us to move to France,” she explained, a touch of nostalgia in her voice as she looked down at her glass. “We called it off. The ranch is a non-negotiable for me.”

Agatha knew that all too well.

“After you two split, dad said he lost all hope of getting grandkids from you,” Benito laughed. Rio joined in. She was noticeably drunk — not slurring, but clearly fueled by the alcohol to speak with an effortless unguarded ease.

“He used to ride my ass about it, but to be fair, I gave him reason to hope,” she admitted, a wistful smile lingering on her lips. “I always wanted kids, wanted to build a family… It just didn’t pan out. Now I must act my own age.”

“Oh, come on!” Kate chimed in. “You’re still young!”

“You guys are young,” Rio countered. “After this wedding, I expect at least a couple of kids running around the ranch. Two or three, the more, the merrier.”

Kate almost choked on her wine, quickly masking it with a laugh.

“Let’s save that conversation for down the road,” Benito cut in, though Rio shook her head in fond disbelief. “Besides, there’s no shortage of kids on the ranch right now.”

“Nicholas loves the ranch,” Agatha blurted out daydreamily, her eyes widening a fraction as she realized she had spoken aloud. Suddenly, Rio’s dark eyes were burning into hers once again.

“Really?” Olivia asked softly. “How sweet! Has he been here before?”

“No, but Javier always filled his head with stories. Benito, too,” Agatha added with a mock glare, though Benito just chuckled. Rio wore a soft smile, and at the sight of it, a gentle warmth bloomed in Agatha’s chest. “He always wanted to come, and now he’s like a kid in a candy store. I barely see him during the day; he’s constantly exploring.”

“He’s a good kid,” Rio said softly. Agatha smiled, caught completely off guard by the genuine tenderness in Rio’s tone. “You can tell you’re a great mom.”

Agatha froze, entirely unprepared for the compliment. Her brows drew together as a wave of deep emotion hit her, flooding her chest with a comforting heat. She hadn’t realized how desperately she needed to hear those words — especially from Rio.

“He’s obsessed with you, by the way,” Kate offered mercifully, rescuing the beat of silence.

Rio chuckled, a light flush rising on her cheeks as she shook her head, a little sheepish. “I found out today. He told me.”

“He told you? With actual words?” Agatha blurted out in a flurry of disbelief.

Rio gave her a puzzled laugh. “How else would he tell me?”

“He’s a boy of very few words,” Benito interjected, and Agatha thanked him with a quick glance.

“Yeah, I picked up on that,” Rio said warmly. “But he’s sweet, a good kid.”

The conversation lightened, unlocking bit by bit as glasses were emptied and refilled around the table. Rio had sent for a few bottles from her private cellar, and from the quiet safety of her corner, Agatha observed her with veiled admiration — captivated by the fluid, passionate way she spoke, making it unmistakably clear how deeply she loved her craft. It was a beautiful side of Rio, one Agatha hadn’t witnessed up close in years, and watching it now filled her with a quiet, lingering warmth.

The initial awkwardness still hung in the air, but it slowly dissolved, chased away by uninhibited laughter and the way Rio gradually let her guard down around her brother. They unspooled old family memories, laughing with sweet nostalgia over childhood antics. Agatha surrendered to the laughter too, chiming in with a nostalgic affection that comforted her from the inside out. With every story, the shattered pieces within her seemed to gently fall back into place, reminding ger of who she really was — and how things used to be.

She had never imagined she would share those memories with Rio again in such a casual, lighthearted way — floating back to a simpler time, when the greatest challenge in their lives was merely crossing the threshold before sundown.

“And Agatha’s nickname was Rapunzel!” Benito blurted out through loud, drunken laughter.

Agatha’s cheeks flushed crimson. She hid her face in her hands with a chuckle, looking up just in time to catch Rio sending a faint, knowing smile in her way.

It felt good to reminisce without the suffocating weight of the pain those memories usually carried — as If they were simply found moments rather than fragments of the chaos they had both become. Of course, the recollections still carried sharp edges, but seeing them shape into something beyond grief offered profound comfort.

“Please, you don’t need to drag that back up…” Agatha murmured bashfully, letting out a soft laugh as the rest of the table joined in the amusement.

“Come on, Rapunzel!” Kate chimed in, her speech slurred as she gave Agatha a playful pat on the shoulder. “I want the whole story!”

“Because our parents wouldn’t let the two of them sleep in the same room,” Benito explained.

Rio’s locked eyes with Agatha’s once more, both blushing and pressing their lips together at the heat of the memory. God, that had been buried for so long. Agatha couldn’t even remember the last time things had felt this effortless — how happy she used to be.

“So Rio would climb the almond tree and sneak through her bedroom window,” Benito continued. “Then one day, Evanora went to wake Agatha up, caught them red-handed, and chased Rio down the driveway with a broom!”

It was Rio’s turn to bury her face in her hands, her cheeks burning bright red with embarrassment as she laughed and quickly took another long gulp of wine. The entire table roared. Agatha took a slow sip of her own drink, needing to stay fueled on liquid courage.

They carried on sharing stories, the evening turning into a tribute to the good old days and the wonderful years they had spent with Javier. Benito recounted his father’s visits to California, the wild tales he used to tell, and the trouble they would get into. Agatha shared sweet moments Javier had spent with Nicholas, while Rio, wearing a wistful smile, recalled memories of the two of them on the ranch — the endless hours spent side by side, dreaming up projects and bringing them to life. Agatha couldn’t remember the last time her heart had felt this light.

“I think he would’ve loved this,” Rio murmured thoughtfully, her eyes wandering over everyone at the table. “All of us here together… laughing, talking…”

“No fighting or crying,” Benito added, barely holding back a smile. Rio smiled back, and so did Agatha.

“He used to say this was all he ever wanted,” Agatha remarked softly, her gaze drifting as her finger traced the rim of her glass, lost in thought. “A full house, all of us together again…”

“He’s probably looking down with a huge smile on his face right now,” Rio said. This time, when their eyes met, they simply shared a quiet, lingering smile.

“A toast,” Benito announced loudly, raising his glass high. “To dad. It was a good life, he was a great man, and I’m really glad we’re doing this. I’m sure he’s happy wherever he is.”

Everyone raised their glasses in unison. For the first time in years, Agatha felt completely at ease — at home.

Before long, everyone was thoroughly tipsy, swimming in easy laughter and carefree banter. It felt remarkably natural — as if sitting together like this was second nature, something they did every day. Agatha couldn’t stop smiling. Rio was smiling too, throwing her head back and laughing loudly in a way Agatha hadn’t seen in a lifetime, which only made Agatha’s grin widen.

“Rio!”

Everyone turned toward the shout. A man stood a few tables away, calling out to her with an acoustic guitar in his hand.

“No, no! Not tonight!” Rio shouted back, shaking her head. Almost instantly, the entire room erupted into playful boos and groans of disappointment.

“Come on, Rio!” several voices chimed in, but she adamantly shook her head.

“What’s going on?” Benito asked, intrigued. Rio waved a dismissive hand, treating it like nothing.

“Rio sings sometimes,” Olivia offered quickly. “Loads of people come to see her.”

A chanting chorus of “Rio! Rio! Rio!” swallowed the entire room. Agatha took in the scene with quiet fascination. Rio had always been shy, guarded and reserved; picturing her stepping onto a stage to perform in front of a crowd like this felt entirely surreal.

Perhaps it was the alcohol, or the sudden urge of nostalgia, or simply that warm, comforting sense of home she hadn’t felt in years — whatever it was, Agatha genuinely wanted to watch her perform.

“Why don’t we sing together?” Benito suggested. Rio’s eyes widened in instant rejection. “Come on, let’s do it! For dad!” he pressed, his brows knitting in a desperate plea that draw a shy, reluctant groan from his sister. “He always loved us singing together…”

After minutes of hesitation — and relentless badgering from every corner of the bar — Rio finally caved.

The crowd erupted into cheers and wild applause as the siblings wove their way through the tables toward the small stage. Agatha watched with rapt attention; it felt as though she were meeting Rio for the very first time. This was a side she had never been allowed to see, and witnessing how deeply adored Rio was by these people brought a surprising, quiet warmth to her chest.

With a bashful tilt of head, Rio avoided the room’s collective gaze as she perched on a tall barstool while servers adjusted two microphones. Besides her, Benito tuned the acoustic guitar with a wide, triumphant grin.

“You’re going to love this!” Olivia said excitedly to Kate and Agatha. “She’s amazing.”

Agatha already knew that; she had spent a lifetime listening to her sing.

“You guys are making a complete fool out of me tonight,” Rio murmured into the microphone, coaxing a wave of warm laughter and applause from the audience. Shaking her head shyly, she turned to her brother. “What do you want to play?”

“You know exactly which one,” Benito said. Agatha froze the second his fingers struck the opening chords. “Dad’s favorite.”

No. No. Please, no.

The peaceful, comforting atmosphere evaporated into thin air as Agatha’s stomach twisted into tight knots.

“Benny…” Rio murmured, visibly uncomfortable. Agatha felt her heart squeeze painfully inside her chest, cold sweat coating her palms. “Come on, pick another one.”

“Come on, Rio! It’s for dad,” he urged, restarting the strumming pattern. “You’re gonna leave, it ain’t gonna break my heart, mama…” he began, turning to Rio, who let out a long, heavy sigh.

“I’ve never seen nobody quite like you…” she joined in, her eyes softly closing.

“And if you ever change your tune, or the world’s got the best of you, you can always find me where the skies are blue,” they sang together, exchanging a brief smile.

Hands trembling, Agatha could no longer see clearly through the thick wall of tears blurring her vision. Her heart throbbed with an agonizing ache, and in a single heartbeat, every drop of comfort she had felt vanished beneath a crushing, unbearable weight.

***

Sixteen Years Ago

Another year had drawn to a close, bringing Agatha right back to where she always ended up. She desperately wished things were different, but the pull was beyond her control — no matter how far she wandered, returning home always meant sinking back into Rio’s arms.

This time, though, felt a little different.

Guilt weighed heavily on Agatha’s chest over her situationship with Tessa, which had grown far more serious than she cared to admit. It was just as agonizing to witness Rio’s state — to realize Rio was trapped in place because of her, ignoring letter after unanswered letter but forever waiting for Agatha to come back to her.

Of course they had rushed into each other’s embrace the moment Agatha set foot in Darby, but for once, they actually talked. They finally confronted the elephant in the room without the night devolving into screaming matches, tears, and shattered hearts.

In truth, Agatha was already heartbroken. She desperately wanted Rio to understand her side and commit to what they shared, but knowing that was an impossible dream, they had to accept reality, painful as it was. Rio’s heart was equally broken — Agatha could see the quiet grief in her eyes — yet she carried a new, strangely comforting calm. With sad, gentle eyes, Rio conceded that there was nothing more they could do.

They loved each other deeply, but life had dealt them a familiar hand — some people are meant to fall in love, but not to end up together.

“You’re not staying for New Year’s?” Rio asked, strumming her acoustic guitar. She was sitting between Agatha’s legs, her head resting against Agatha’s chest.

Agatha let out a heavy sigh, her fingers weaving through the soft strands of her brown hair.

Agreeing to call it quits hadn’t actually stopped them from clinging to one another. Neither had the strength to walk away. As much as they had rationalized the tragedy of their situation, they couldn’t just say goodbye as if their history meant nothing. Deep down, Agatha carried a fatalistic certainty that no matter how many times they parted, they would always find their way back to each other.

After their long talk, they had walked hand in hand to the lake on the far side of the ranch, spending hours tangled in quiet, comfortable embrace as the sun spilled across the horizon and slowly sank.

“You know I never stay,” Agatha replied softly, tilting her head down to meet Rio’s upturned gaze. Looking into those endless brown eyes made her melt — a deep ocean of love in which she was always eager to drown.

“You could stay this time.”

“It’s better if I go. You know it is.”

Rio sighed and shifted, turning around to sit directly in front of her with her arms resting across the guitar in her lap. Agatha knit her brows in a silent plea, begging her not to reopen that wound tonight.

“Do you think one day you’ll ever be able to choose me over her?” Rio whispered in a barely audible voice. There was no venom or bitterness in her tone — just a quiet, profound sadness that tore Agatha apart. “That one day you’ll choose us?”

“Rio…” Agatha pleaded, the name slipping out like a painful sigh.

“I know,” Rio said gently, full of understanding. “It’s not about her or me. It’s about what you want for you like, your hopes and dreams. I get it. It’s just hard to accept.”

“I know,” Agatha echoed, equally heartbroken, reaching out to stroke Rio’s cheek. Rio leaned into the touch, closing her eyes tenderly.

“We’re a mess,” Rio whispered, a faint smile breaking through her melancholy.

“I know. Sometimes I wonder how we even ended up like this,” Agatha murmured.

Rio shook her head, lost in thought for a moment before a genuine smile took over. Agatha arched an eyebrow, catching the spark of playful amusement in her eyes.

“You know what?” Rio asked softly.

“What?” Agatha smiled back, already sensing a cheeky remark coming.

“Our mess,” Rio said, a soft chuckle escaping her nose, “reminds me of the old man’s song.”

“No…” Agatha laughed, shaking her head. “Not that song, please! He plays it every single day; I don’t know how you endure it!”

“I’m serious!” Rio insisted, positioning the guitar properly as her fingers hunted for the right chords. “If you actually listen to it, it’s out exact story.”

“Rio…” Agatha rolled her eyes, affectionate and exasperated.

“It could be our song,” Rio insisted, striking the opening chords. Agatha shook her head, unable to hide the fond smile as she watched her play. “You’re gonna leave, it ain’t gonna break my heart, mama. I’ve never seen nobody quite like you… and if you ever change your tune, or the world’s got the best of you, you can always find me where the skies are blue…”

Agatha smiled as Rio sang. Though her heart felt completely shattered, she was utterly helpless against Rio’s charm. Sitting there, watching Rio sing with that silly grin, Agatha felt that familiar fatalism wash over her again — the quiet promise that, somehow, eventually, things would find their way right.

“Wanted to change, turn into what you want, mama. And I would have given all of my best to you,” Rio sang, beaming as Agatha reached out to stroke her face mid-melody. “So if you ever need a fool who will give a love so true, you can always find me where the skies are blue…”

“You are such an adorable dork,” Agatha whispered, gently plucking the guitar from her lap.

Rio burst into open laughter, leaning in to cup Agatha’s face in her hands.

“How can you always manage to make me smile in moments like this?” Agatha asked softly.

“Because I love you,” Rio said, her smile pressing against Agatha’s lips.

Agatha’s brows knit in a tender, helpless smile. Shaking her head, she pulled Rio in by the nape of her neck, sinking into a deep, sweet kiss where both of their smiles melted into one another.

***

Present day

It was all happening too fast — too intense, too weighed down by memories — and not even the dull hum of alcohol could pull her mind from its tailspin.

The warmth of the moments they had just shared sourly curdled, turning into a sharp, physical pain in her chest and leaving a bitter taste in her mouth. It was the taste of everything she had surrendered: the most beautiful love she had ever known, and the tenderness she had let slip through her fingers. Far beyond romantic love, she mourned the lost warmth of her former safe haven, forced to confront the chilling reality that she no longer truly knew the person who had been her favorite human being for years.

It had been easier when she kept it all buried, fooling herself into believing the past was dead and gone. But facing it all at once — in a violent, overwhelming flood — made the world tilt beneath her feet. A sudden wave of nausea washed over her, making her feel as though she might throw up at any second.

Ignoring the bewildered looks and muffled questions from Kate and Olivia, Agatha bolted for the exit. Submerged in her own mind, her face was already slick with tears.

“Agatha! Wait!”

She was already halfway down the sidewalk when Rio’s voice cut through the air. Squeezing her eyes shut, Agatha cursed herself for crying. She froze, shaking her head, but within seconds felt a tender hand touch her shoulder.

Hesitantly, Agatha turned around, keeping her eyes glued to the pavement. When Rio’s gaze locked onto hers, Agatha watched her features soften into a look of restrained affection. Agatha sighed, shaking her head helplessly.

“I’m sorry, I— I shouldn’t—” Agatha stumbled over her words, completely disoriented. “It’s just that—”

“I know. It’s too much all at once,” Rio murmured softly. Agatha’s eyes widened in profound relief as the truth of those words hit her. “It’s too much for me, too.”

“Yeah…” Agatha agreed faintly. “It’s a lot.”

In that moment, Rio looked a little more like the woman she used to know. Her eyes softened with a familiar tenderness that made Agatha heart squeeze even tighter. Rio took a deep breath, nervously scratching the back of her neck as if weighing every word. Agatha couldn’t help but take her in, realizing that beneath Rio’s hardened exterior, so much remained unchanged. It was comforting, familiar and agonizing all at once.

“I wanted to apologize,” Rio said, her voice catching in her throat as though she were fighting herself to speak. Agatha froze, her eyes widening in disbelief. “I’m so sorry for how I talked to you at my dad’s funeral. I just—” She cut herself off, taking a steadying breath. “I’m not good with words, you know that.” Agatha did know. “I shouldn’t have spoken to you like that.”

Rio shrank her shoulders, and Agatha felt her heart twist.

“None of if was true.” Rio added. “You’re always welcome here. You’ve always been part of this family, and I never should have said those things. I was just angry.” Tears began to pool in those deep brown eyes. Agatha nodded silently, understanding completely as fresh tears welled in her own eyes. “I know that doesn’t excuse what I said, but… I was just so angry.”

“I know,” Agatha whispered softly, offering a faint, gentle smile. “I know you were angry. It’s okay.”

“No, it’s not,” Rio breathlessly replied, her tone heavy with sadness. “I can’t even remember the last time things were okay, but it isn’t your fault, and I shouldn’t have lashed out. I wasn’t even angry at you— I was just angry. So, I’m sorry.”

“Of course I forgive you,” Agatha sighed, tilting her head. “And even if you had been angry with me, I would still forgive you.”

“I was never angry at you, Agatha. For a long time, I actually tried to be, but I never could,” Rio admitted softly.

Agatha wept, but this time out of pure relief, as if a crushing weight had finally been lifted from her shoulders.

“It wasn’t anger,” Rio continued. “It was— I don’t know what it was, but it was never anger.”

“I want to apologize, too,” Agatha whispered. “I’m really, really sorry.”

“You don’t need to apologize, Agatha, I—”

“No, please. I really need to say this,” Agatha interrupted, raising a hand to gently stop her.

Rio nodded, keeping her gaze lowered yet attentive.

“I am so sorry. For everything. I never wanted—” Agatha choked back her words, swallowing hard as she shook her head. “I’m sorry. For everything. I truly am.”

“I know you are. I am too,” Rio replied softly, Her calm, composed tone was almost disarming, yet deeply comforting because Agatha could tell it was completely genuine. “I know things ended badly between us, but it’s in the past, Agatha. I’m not that person anymore, and neither are you. And I don’t hate you. I never could.”

“Thank you,” Agatha whispered, exhaling a breath she hadn’t realized she was holding. “I really needed to hear that.”

Rio offered a faint, tender smile.

“It’s good having you here,” she admitted. “My dad would be happy.”

“I’m happy to be here, truly,” Agatha said, brushing away her tears with the tips of her fingers. “I’m glad we’re talking. I know we’ve changed and we can’t turn back the clock, but I don’t want to keep pretending you don’t exist.”

“Yeah. It’s weird, isn’t it?” Rio let out a soft chuckle that drew a wet laugh from Agatha, who nodded in agreement. “I’m glad, too. I really wanted to put all of this behind us. You’ll always be a part of the family, Agatha. You are family. This place is yours too, and it always will be.”

A wave of profound relief washed over Agatha, filling her with a comforting warmth. Impulsively, she threw her arms around Rio, pulling her into a tight, fierce embrace — a hug born of pure gratitude for this moment and everything they had once shared. She felt Rio stiffen for a fraction of a second before her arms wrapped around Agatha in return, both of them softening into the hold. It felt like coming home, like stepping back into a long-lost sanctuary. She hadn’t realized how desperately she needed it.

When they finally pulled apart, their eyes locked for a moment before they both burst out laughing. It was awkward, but in the best way possible — the two of them, wiping away tears and laughing together, sharing a genuine good moment after so many years and so much pain.

It wasn’t just a truce — they had finally raised the white flag.

“Thank you for this,” Agatha said.

Rio gave a soft shrug. “I think we both needed it.”

“Yeah,” Agatha agreed. “I guess we really did.”

Chapter 18: roots

“And the Years passed like scenes of a show [...] Looking backwards might be the only way to move forward” – The manuscript, Taylor Swift

***

Rio had always struggled with ambiguity, which made her despise the very notion of self-awareness. Her mind was strictly literal and objective, built on the simple premise that things were black and white — a thing was what it was, and nothing could ever be two conflicting things at once. But awareness was agonizingly complex, peeling back layers like an endless onion, and Rio hated layers.

It unfolded into a dizzying spectrum of definitions, forcing her to see herself at opposite extremes of the same situation and feel a dozen contradictory things about a single fact. To Rio, that was terrifying. She hated emotions, hated introspection, and above all, hated anything she couldn’t control.

Deep down, she knew awareness meant turning her gaze inward — confronting who she was, what she had done, and the harsh clarity of her own actions. Because she possessed this self-awareness, she couldn’t hide from herself. She saw her best and her worst, recognizing the weight of her unjustified anger and bitter resentment. She understood that all the fury she projected outward was actually directed at her own reflection. Since before her twenties, she had known the truth: she was the problem. And what hurt the most was knowing it was entirely her fault that everything had slipped through her fingers.

Yet the cruelty of awareness didn’t stop at self-reflection. If acknowledging her own failure was the only obstacle, she might have found a way to shrug it off and cope with hitting rock bottom once again. The true nightmare lay in its other facet: the moral compass that weighed relentlessly on her shoulders, demanding she distinguish right from wrong.

While self-awareness forced her to face the darkness of rock bottom, her conscience compelled her to look sideways and see who she had dragged down into the abyss with her. That was where her literal mindset completely shattered. If a thing could only ever be one thing, how could she simultaneously be a hostage to her own demons and the tormentor of the people who loved her?

As Shakespeare famously wrote, thus conscience does make cowards of us all. It was this moral burden that robbed Rio of her soul’s only relief: the sweet comfort of ignorance. Stripped of sleep day after day, she could no longer move forward without looking back. Remorse showed her no mercy, forcing her to replay every cutting word and destructive choice in an endless loop, watching the damage of her actions reflect in the eyes of those who had only ever tried to save her from herself.

It was a layered torture — the worst kind imaginable. Without the clarity of conscience, she wouldn’t have cared about the pain she left in her wake, comfortably lying to herself and outsourcing the blame to the world. Instead, being trapped by both sides of her awareness felt like gripping a knife by the blade: she watched other people’s blood drip onto the floor, but it was her own hand that was bleeding. It was neither objective nor literal; it was absolute hell on earth.

Yet, she had to admit that last night had made the weight on her shoulders feel a fraction lighter.

Throughout her years of sobriety, Rio had learned the true value of forgiveness and its liberating power. To move forward, she had left a lot behind, including old grudges, which was how she had managed to find peace for so long. Though her pride would never let her try to fix things, the anger was gone. Not toward them, anyway. She had finally understood that what you cannot control shouldn’t be allowed to control you through resentment. She had let it go and rarely looked back.

The only person Rio had never been able to forgive was herself, and that remained an unbearable burden. Even beneath the numbness of alcohol, the guilt had always been bitter and suffocating, driving her back to blaming everyone else for what she knew, deep down, was entirely her own fault. It was a vicious cycle that led straight back to rock bottom, yet in some twisted way, it had hurt a little less than the truth.
