Still, last night had felt good. Incredibly good. It was a feeling she hadn’t realized she was starving for, but one she needed more than anything else. It was comforting to have her brother so close, to talk, to watch him smile, and to laugh about the past instead of screaming and pointing fingers. It had been good to see Agatha — to speak the truth, to accept that there was no longer any blame between them, and to leave the past where it belonged. For just one night, it had felt good to stop hurting others and herself. It had felt good to simply teel the truth.

Rio was no fool, however. She knew it wouldn’t be long before the taste in her mouth soured again and she retreated behind her familiar walls of anger and resentment. Just thinking about it made her mind begin to spiral, and everyone knew what happened when she spent too much time trapped inside her own head. She would end up ruining everything, like she always did.

“It’s been a while since I’ve seen you like this,” Natasha’s voice broke through her thoughts. Rio turned her gaze toward her best friend, instantly relaxing into the peaceful, steady rhythm of Raio’s trot.

Before Rio had slipped back into her old habits, the two of them used to ride horses together every morning, just like this. It was a ritual that brought them both comfort. Just before dawn, Rio would meet her at the stables, and they would share a thermos of black coffee as they rode through the fields toward the highway, skirting the edge of the city. They spent hours on those quiet mornings watching the sun rise and the city awaken alongside them. Sometimes they talked, sometimes they rode in absolute silence, but they never missed a day.

Rio couldn’t even explain what had made her call Natasha this morning; she had just done it. And though she would never admit it out loud, she felt profoundly comforted when her best friend accepted the invitation without a single hesitation. She truly needed this.

“Like what?” Rio asked with a faint smile, stretching out her back. “Sober in the morning?” she murmured, raising an eyebrow as Natasha let out a soft laugh.

“I was going to say peaceful, but yeah, that too.”

“I’m picking up the twins today to make the most of the weekend,” Rio murmured, glancing away as she tried to mask an inexplicable unease. “I don’t want Wanda yelling at me, I know the rules well enough.”

Natasha offered a quiet, understanding nod. “You could always just accept a compliment without killing the vibe,” she said with a light shrug. “It’s good to see you sober in the morning, and it’s good to see you at peace. You don’t have to justify having a good day.” Rio narrowed her eyes playfully, fixing her with a dry look. “If it’s a good day, let’s just be grateful for it.”

“You have such a way with words…” Rio muttered. Natasha pressed her lips together, instantly recognizing the smirk forming on her friend’s face. “Ever considered becoming a preacher?”

“You’re impossible. I honestly don’t know why I bother,” Natasha said, rolling her eyes.

“Because I sign your paychecks,” Rio replied deadpan. For a split second, they locked eyes before bursting into laughter. “Thanks, though. For trying.”

“See?” Natasha shot back with a triumphant wave. “You’re actually thanking me! When was the last time that happened? Is this a miracle? Am I witnessing a miracle right now?”

Rolling her eyes, Rio pulled gently on her horse’s reins, closing the distance so she could reach out and shove Natasha’s shoulder just to mess with her. Natasha simply laughed, uncorking the thermos of coffee to pour a cup for Rio, who readily accepted it, before pouring one for herself. They rode on in comfortable silence for a while, gazing out at the horizon with their hands warmed by the steaming cups. It was nice. Rio couldn’t quite explain it, but even with the familiar dark clouds brewing inside her, right there beside Natasha, she felt a sudden flicker of hope.

“Seriously, though,” Natasha broke the silence, turning a warm, thoughtful gaze toward her. “It’s really good to see you having a good day.”

Rio didn’t reply, letting her lips curve into a faint, understated smile. She didn’t want to ruin the moment — she didn’t want to admit that, despite all her effort, it still felt like she was falling short. She knew she wasn’t out of the woods yet. She stayed quiet because, as much as she doubter herself, she desperately wanted to believe it, too.

Yet god, her throat burned for a cold beer. Her palms were slick with sweat, and chill prickled the back of her neck. As Natasha turned her attention back to horizon, Rio looked down at her own hands, noticing her knuckles locked in a white-knuckled grip on the reins. Slowly, that familiar, restless irritation began to claw at her chest.

“So…” Natasha spoke up again, and Rio could have kissed her. She really didn’t need to be left alone inside her own head right now; any distraction was a blessing. “How was yesterday? Are you going to fill me in or what?”

“Yesterday?” Rio feigned innocence, but Natasha just narrowed her eyes and shook her head.

“Don’t even start,” Natasha warned with an arched brow, prompting Rio to let out a defeated sigh.

“Yelena told you, didn’t she? Unbelievable. That girl has a mouth the size of a sieve, I swear to god—”

“Yelena knew and I didn’t?” Natasha interrupted, feigning offense. “She didn’t tell me a thing, it was Wanda.”

“Of course it was,” Rio muttered, rolling her eyes and nearly smacking her own forehead. “You and your sickeningly healthy marriage where secrets are illegal.”

“What can I say?” Natasha shrugged with a mock-smug smile. “I’m a lucky woman.” Rio only rolled her eyes again, though Natasha caught the faint twitch of amusement playing at the corner of her mouth. “Now, onto what really matters: how was yesterday at Pedra Purpura? I know your brother was there, and Agatha, too. Wanda mentioned that you were the one who invited them.”

“I didn’t invite Agatha,” Rio shot back, but Natasha merely offered an indifferent grunt.

“Yeah, I heard that part too which is exactly why I want to know how it actually went.”

Rio drew in a long breath, letting the air rush out so heavily that her shoulders visibly slumped. It was a complete double-edged sword; honestly, she couldn’t even untangle what she was feeling.

“Would you think it’s weird if I said it wasn’t bad?” she confessed, shrinking slightly under her friend’s sharp, attentive gaze. “Because it honestly wasn’t. It was… normal, I guess? I don’t really know…”

“Normal?” Natasha echoed, her tone laced with curiosity as Rio nodded thoughtfully.

“Yeah, normal… familiar, you know? It felt like no time had passed at all, and not in a terrifying way either. It’s weird, isn’t it? It was—” Rio caught herself, bitting her tongue right before she slipped up and said it had actually been good. “Yeah. Just normal.”

“Yeah, definitely weird,” Natasha murmured with a nervous chuckle. “But like… good-weird, seeing it wasn’t a disaster.”

Rio could see the mountain of questions practically screaming behind her best friend’s eyes, and she silently thanked her for choosing to give her breathing room instead of prying. Normally, Rio would lock everything away and throw away the key, but right now, she desperately needed to unburden her mind.

“Everyone was hammered, which definitely helped,” she admitted, catching a fleeting flash of disapproval cross Natasha’s face. But Natasha shook it off a second later, conceding that it was a fair point given the circumstances. “We talked about my dad and spent most of the night just reminiscing, you know? It wasn’t as agonizing as I thought it would be. It was… good, actually,” she confessed, exhaling a heavy breath as if physically shedding an anchor of weight. “It’s just so hard facing the fact that he’s gone that I never let myself think past the grief. I never allowed myself to remember all the good things.”

Natasha’s expression softened into deep compassion, and she offered a gentle nod. Rio pressed her lips into a thin line and shrugged — talking about it scraped against old raw edges, yet somehow, she felt oddly comforted.

“There were just so many things hitting me all at once, so many feelings crashing into each other that I—” Rio cut herself off, swallowing hard as she took a steadying breath. “It’s just weird.”

“And how are you feeling about all of it now that the booze has completely worn off?” Natasha asked carefully, her striking green eyes tracking every micro-expression on Rio’s face.

“Relieved, I suppose,” Rio admitted, and Natasha offered a soft, encouraging smile. “I really missed my brother. I don’t think I ever let myself admit that out loud because it sounds so stupid, doesn’t it?” Her voice hitched slightly on the edge of vulnerability, but Natasha instantly shook her head.

“It’s not stupid at all, Rio,” she said gently. “He’s your brother, of course you missed him. And for the record, he misses you, too.”

“That’s precisely why it sounds stupid, why couldn’t I just say it? Why couldn’t I just admit it?” she murmured. Natasha gave a helpless shrug, searching for the right words. “He’s a grown man, but he’s still such a goofball, just a kid a heart,” Rio added, drawing an understanding affectionate laugh from her friend. “It felt like not a single day had gone by, like he hadn’t gown up, and like she had never left.”

Natasha let out a long whistle, her face twisting into a thoughtful grimace that prompted a soft shake of the head from Rio.

“It’s weird, isn’t it?” Rio asked, her brows knit in frustration. Natasha mirrored her expression, her heart tightened with sudden apprehension as she looked into Rio’s bewildered brown eyes.

“Look, you can’t just erase history,” Natasha began cautiously, her hesitation showing she wasn’t entirely sure how to tread. “A lot has happened, and a massive amount of time has passed, but the truth is…” She trailed off, exhaling a heavy sigh. “You love them both.”

Rio dropped her gaze as if physical impact had followed the words.

“It’s messy because, yeah, everything fell apart, but you all still matter to each other. It’s just… good to see you slowly realizing that, each in your own way.”

Admitting it felt surreal — the realization that, despite everything, Agatha was still someone she… loved. In fact, confronting the reality of Agatha in the present tense was deeply unsettling: Agatha, alive and breathing, standing in her town, woven into the fabric of her life, and acknowledging to herself that she still held weight. That she ever stopped holding weight. It was terrifying and liberation all at once, because for years, Rio had buried that truth in the darkest, most locked-away corners of her soul. Yet it remained undeniably true: Agatha mattered to her.

Rio thought back to all those trips over the last thirteen years, flying out to California just to visit Alex and fish for updates, desperate to know it Agatha was okay. If she was happy. Agatha was important. She always had been, and it was deeply frightening to accept that perhaps she always would be.

Once again, Rio found herself cornered by ambiguity. Loving someone like that after so much time, after oceans of pain and wounds that still occasionally throbbed beneath the scars — it defied her rigid, black-and-white worldview. It was the ultimate proof that a single thing could be a million contradictory things at once. It hurt, it terrified her, but at the same time… it brought a strange comfort.

Perhaps that was why she felt so unmoored. The night before had been an ocean of grey areas, completely devoid of logic or safe ground, sending her spinning through a maddening storm of conflicting emotions. Yet, standing face-to-face with Agatha after all this time — speaking her truth and watching the matching truth reflect back in those eyes — had finally dissolved a fraction of the heavy anchor she’d been dragging around. It was living proof that Rio hadn’t survived that heartbreak alone, hadn’t loved in a vacuum, and hadn’t suffered by herself; they had both been carrying the exact same weight. And against all odds, something fragile and good had survived the wreckage. Something resilient enough to outlast the distance, the bitterness, and even Rio herself, with her ruthless, self-sabotaging talent for destroying everything she loved.

Yes, it was undeniably strange, but for the first time, it offered a faint glimmer of light at the end of the tunnel. If they could somehow salvage something meaningful from the wreckage of the past, perhaps she was capable of fixing the rest of it — or at least the most fractured pieces of herself.

“So, are things actually good with your brother now?” Natasha asked. Rio, still lost in a tangle of competing thoughts, simply let out a long breath and nodded. “Come on, you said it was good. Weird” — Natasha playfully emphasized — “but good!”

“I think so,” Rio murmured with an uncertain shrug, the lingering fear of messing things up still chewing at the edges of her mind. “He’s staying at the farm, and we’re going to run things together… I guess it’s a start,” she conceded finally, flashing a weak, hesitant smile that drew an approving nod from Natasha. “I really did miss him.”

“I know you did. You love pretending you’re made of stone, but I know you better than that,” Natasha said, wrinkling her nose affectionately. Rio let out a soft laugh and rolled her eyes. “You’ve got a soft heart, Rio. You’re a nightmare to deal with, but you’re a softie.”

“He’s changed, but in the best way possible,” Rio pressed on, deliberately brushing past her friend’s teasing. “He’s not that quiet, closed-off kid anymore, you know? He’s confident, funny and genuinely sweet all at once… He reminds so much of my dad, in a way that just… comforts me.” Rio trailed off, her voice softening into a contemplative cadence as her thoughts drifted.

Recognizing this rare, unguarded moment of vulnerability, Natasha stayed quiet and simply nodded, giving her space to keep going. “You really have to see it, the way he talks, the sound of his laugh,” Rio added, a genuine smile breaking through. “He’s happy… It’s a genuinely beautiful thing to witness.”

“And it’s even more beautiful watching you feel happy for him,” Natasha observed, noticing the introspective shift in Rio’s posture. “It’s good to see you actually admitting it, letting yourself feel something real.” At that, Rio rolled her eyes. “I know you think it’s a cheesy cliché, but it matters, Rio. I honestly think you needed this, just allowing yourself to feel for once.”

“It’s more than that, I think,” Rio continued, her voice dropping into a reflective tone that instantly silenced Natasha in quiet surprise. “I know it was only one night, but it felt… it felt like I was getting to know a completely different person. Seeing his fiancée, watching the way they talk to each other and look at each other with so much tenderness… it’s wonderful, but it also makes me painfully aware of all the years I missed, all the parts of his life I still don’t know.”

“I’d bet anything he feels the exact same way about you,” Natasha said gently, reaching across to give her shoulder a reassuring squeeze. “But that’s not what counts right now, Rio. You’re both here, and you’re back in each other’s lives. What matters is what you do from this moment on, showing up for each other and finally letting yourselves be brother and sister again.”

Rio nodded vaguely, her gaze drifting back to the horizon. She fell silent for several minutes, seemingly entirely lost in her own thoughts. Sensing that this conversation was merely a piece of much larger, shifting puzzle in her friend’s mind, Natasha let out a heavy sigh.

“Did you get to talk to Agatha? Just the two of you?” she asked, her face twisting into a reluctant frown. Rio turned to look at her, her reflective expression instantly dissolving into a faint laugh.

“What?” Natasha snapped impatiently, rolling her eyes.

“Every single time you say her name, you make that exact face,” Rio murmured with a soft smile, gesturing to the sour expression her friend was wearing. “I really thought you’d be over that by now.”

Natasha rolled her eyes again and offered a defensive shrug.

“My bad. I know it’s none of my business, but I was there too, Rio. When everything went up in flames, I was right there every step of the way,” she muttered, dropping her gaze. “I hate dragging up the past, but it’s kind of impossible to pretend it doesn’t matter now that she’s actually back.”

“It’s not her fault,” Rio said with a calm serenity that caught her best friend completely off guard, though was not malice in her surprise. “I was there too, Nat. You’re right, I hate looking backward as much as anyone, but…” Rio exhaled softly. “It isn’t fair to pile all the blame on her shoulders, especially when I played my part. I know it’s not her fault. It never was. And yeah, I know I talked your ear off complaining about her for years, but that wasn’t fair either. She made her choices, but I made mine, too.”

As the words left her mouth, they felt like barbed wire tearing her throat. The truth always had a way of cutting deep, no matter how many years you spent trying to swallow it.

“So you actually talked?” Natasha pressed, steering the conversation back on track. Rio let out a quiet breath and nodded.

“I apologized.”

‘You did what?” Natasha’s eyes widened in disbelief, but Rio simply gave a calm nod.

It wasn’t a reprimand or a judgment; Natasha was genuinely stunned that Rio had actually swallowed her pride enough to say sorry. It almost made Rio laugh because, honestly, she had been just as shocked with herself. Still, it was the right thing to do — she had promised her dad she would.

“I apologized for the way I spoke to her, for the things I threw in her face—”

“Okay, you really were a jerk at your dad’s wake,” Natasha interrupted, shaking her head. “I’m not her number-one fan by a long shot, but yeah, all of that was completely uncalled for.”

“Yeah, I know,” Rio admitted with a sigh. “I was furious, and… I just did what I always do,” she added with a helpless shrug. “But she didn’t deserve any of that, which is why I apologized. I didn’t want—” She cut herself off, drawing in another steady breath. “I never wanted us to turn into something toxic in each other’s lives.” Seeing Natasha open her mouth to argue, Rio hurried on. “And she apologized, too. For everything.”

“She apologized?” Natasha echoed, genuinely startled. Rio nodded. “Wow. Never thought I’d see the day.”

“Honestly, she didn’t even have to, but it felt good to hear. It was good for me… just to talk to her.”

Natasha studied her for a few long seconds, her expression deeply thoughtful. Rio merely shrugged, holding her friend’s gaze until Natasha finally let out a soft sigh.

“If it was good for you, Rio, that’s all that matters.”

“I think I just have to… accept it, you know?”

“Accept what?”

“Everything.”

Natasha stayed silent, clearly at a loss for words. And that was fine. Rio wasn’t entirely sure she had the right vocabulary either — of if any words could possibly make sense of the moment. She barely knew how to process her own thoughts and feelings, let alone translate them into speech.

Yet it had been so much more than a simple truce. It was something she could feel deeply, even if she couldn’t neatly package it into explanations. It felt like watching a movie years ago and only now understanding the ending. And stories were like that: whether you liked the outcome or not, it wasn’t a choice. It wasn’t something she could rewrite, only accept. Whether it brought her comfort or confusion didn’t matter.

Her brother was happy. Genuinely happy. He had truly found his footing, carrying a steady, radiant light wherever he went alongside a heart that was impossibly large. Now, he had found love and was preparing to marry an incredible woman. He was happy. Agatha, too, had made her choices. She was fulfilled by the life she had built — successful, living in the city of angels, and raising an wonderful son. She was happy, as well. That was simply the reality of it, and for Rio, the only path left was acceptance. Because despite how completely everything had spiraled out for her control, a part of her had always wanted precisely that: for them to be happy.

Sometimes, she wondered if she would ever find that kind of happiness herself.

Even on her best days, Rio always carried a lingering sense that something was missing. After a decade of sobriety, she was objectively fine; she had nothing to complain about and had achieved everything she had once set out to do. Yet life still tasted a bit flat, lacking the vibrancy she had once imagined. That hollow ache of incompleteness had shadowed her through even her finest moments. She wondered if she would ever figure out what left her feeling so empty, of if she would someday manage to fill that space with something that made the rest of it make sense.

“Natasha,” she broke the silence, prompting her best friend to turn her way. “Do you consider yourself happy?”

Natasha, mid-sip of her coffee, simply raised her eyebrows in surprise. Normally she would deflect with a dry joke, but the quiet gravity in Rio’s expression told her this was entirely serious.

“Yes, I do,” Natasha answered honestly. Rio nodded, watching her with a quiet, curious anticipation. “I married the woman I love, I wake up beside her every single day, and I have two kids I adore more than anything in the world. I’ve got my sister back, reclaiming a piece of family I never thought I’d see again. And I genuinely love my job. I spend every day working alongside my best friend who refuses to read a single contract and since she owns the company while I handle the logistics, I happen to give myself quite a few raises.”

That drew a soft, genuine laugh from Rio.

“You’ve more than earned them,” Rio said with a warm look before offering a casual shrug. “And you know I couldn’t care less about the money.”

This time, Natasha couldn’t hold back her amusement.

“Only a filthy rich person would say shit like that,” she accused, pointing a finger at Rio, who just laughed and shrugged again.

“What? Aren’t you filthy rich yet? Go ahead and give yourself another raise, I’ll sign it up.”

“Rio, for the love of god!”

The two of them dissolved into laughter as their horses ambled forward at an easy, rhythmic pace. The silence that settled between them afterwards was entirely comfortable. Rio gazed out at the horizon, lost in quiet reflection, completely unaware of the soft, concerned look Natasha was casting her way. Rio simply had too much swirling inside her to notice.

“You deserve to be happy, too, Rio,” Natasha said quietly.

Rio snapped her gaze back to her, her eyes instantly locking onto her friend’s with a sharp, questioning look. “You deserve it just as much.”

***

Agatha hadn’t even bothered to get up; she had been writing relentlessly since the moment she woke. Ever since her arrival at the farm, writing had transformed into a sacred ritual — a private sanctuary where she could pour out every hidden feeling and unspoken word. It was deeply liberating to express herself without fearing retaliation or shame, a quiet habit making each day feel a little lighter.

The previous night had taken a turn she never could have anticipated. She had spent so many years nursing the heavy burden of her shared past with Rio that she had never once considered the possibility that Rio might have actually moved on. Agatha had felt so overwhelmingly guilty over how things ended that she always assumed Rio felt the same, blaming her just as fiercely. But the truth was, the guilt she carried wasn’t solely about Rio — in fact, it had far less to do with Rio and everything to do with herself.

Agatha felt this crushing weight because, deep down, she was drowning in regret. She regretted most of the choices she had ever made. That remorse had been eating her alive for years, so she had subconsciously preferred to project it, convincing herself of Rio’s lingering resentment just to give herself a concrete excuse to feel guilty. It was far easier to embrace the comforting armor of being hated than to face the raw, naked reality: she simply resented herself for the life she had chosen.

It was a strange kind of guilt — not agonizing or sharp, just profoundly sad. Agatha was so accustomed to forgiving everyone else’s flaws that the necessity of forgiving herself had never even crossed her mind. It was a dauting mountain to climb, but the could finally see how desperately she needed it to move forward and start over.

For years, she had trapped herself in endless loops of what-ifs, never stopping to accept a simple truth: what’s done is done, and history could never be rewritten. Nothing would change unless she finally left the past behind. She needed to move forward. She needed to forgive herself. It was an agonizingly difficult process, and all she wanted was for it to be just a little bit easier. Yet, after the revelations of the night before, she was beginning to realize that even if it hurt, it was possible.

Years of accumulated guilt had been instantly absolved by the mere look in Rio’s brown eyes. It was almost ridiculously simple — bordering on the absurd — how deeply she had needed to hear that it wasn’t her fault, that the past was dead and buried. She had needed to know that everything was okay, that what happened was truly behind them. She hadn’t even realized the true magnitude of that hunger until she felt as though a literal ton had been lifted off her shoulders.

Now, however, to truly walk into tomorrow, she had to embrace the present instead of endlessly martyring herself over yesterday. Yes, she was allowed to regret her past choices, but she couldn’t keep carrying the crushing weight of the world, not when she knew she had tried, at all costs, to do the right thing. It was time to accept reality and own her story: she had been a victim, she had been forced to run away to survive, but she had finally found her way home, and for the first time, she could genuinely see hope in the future. For the sake of the present and the promise of a lighter tomorrow, she had to take action. Alex was right. She needed to step forward, focus entirely on Nicholas, build a real life on the farm, and, dear god, she desperately needed to move out of her mother’s basement.

When her phone rang, she snatched it up instantly, eager to tell Alex that she was ready — that the time had come to finally let it all out. She was done merely surviving; she was ready to start living.

“Agatha?”

Her entire body locked up. It wasn’t Alex.

“Agatha, are you listening to me? What is your problem? I’ve been waiting for you for a month, and you don’t even have the decency to answer your phone?”

“Tessa…” she murmured, her breath catching in her throat.

“Agatha, I said I would give you some space, but this is crossing every single line!” Tessa’s voice spiked, and Agatha instinctively squeezed her eyes shut, drawing in a sharp breath. “You won’t talk to me, you ignore my calls… what on earth is going on? My love—“

“Don’t call me that,” Agatha interrupted through gritted teeth. “I didn’t answer your calls because I refuse to speak to you, Tesse, not until you sign the divorce papers.”

Agatha held her breath at the sound of her wife’s harsh, sarcastic laugh.

“Are you seriously still pushing this idea? For the love of god, honey, get a grip!” Agatha ground her teeth again, her hands trembling slightly against the phone. “What on earth do you want from me, Agatha? I’ll give you anything, but it’s time to put an end to this breakdown of yours. Do you have any concept of what I’ve been enduring?”

“What you’ve been enduring?” Agatha scoffed.

“Yes, Agatha! What I’ve been enduring! What you are putting me through! I’m sitting here without my wife, without my son, having lost my entire world! And I can’t keep inventing excuses for you disappearance, telling people you’re traveling, of that you’re just clearing your hear after you godfather’s passing. You need to come back home, Agatha! Look at what you’re doing to me, I’m a complete wreck!”

“I’m the one who’s been destroyed, Tessa!” It was Agatha’s turn to let her vice rise, cutting through a tired, performative sigh from the other end of the line. “I’ve been falling apart for years while you couldn’t care less. I’m not coming back. I am never coming back, not with you. But the moment you sigh the divorce papers, we can talk and work out a custody arrangement for Nicky, seeing as you’ve suddenly decided he matters to you.”

“Listen to the things you’re saying, my love…” Tessa whimpered, and all Agatha felt was a hot surge of fury flush across her face. “Just come home, Agatha. I’ll find the best therapist in the world for you, I promise. You just need to pull yourself together.”

“I genuinely do need a therapist, but not for the reasons you think”

“Agatha, are you even hearing yourself right now? Look at what’s coming out of your mouth…” Tessa deployed that suffocatingly condescending tone that made Agatha’s jaw ache. “I know your godfather’s death shook you up, but this spiraled completely out of control. You need professional help to manage this crisis.”

“Tessa, I’m not going to—” she started, but Tessa ruthlessly cut her off.

“I don’t want to fight, Agatha, and I know you don’t either. You despise fighting, and so do I. Honey, I hate fighting with you, you know that, but what choice do you leave me? I’m trying everything I can to help, but you refuse to let yourself be helped.”

“If you want to help so badly, Tessa, sign the damn divorce papers,” she fired back with unyielding resolve. “I promise I’ll speak with you the moment that’s settled.”

“You don’t actually want this, Agatha, we’ve already been through this conversation,” Tessa purred in that sweet, sickening cadence that masked the iron fist of her demands. Agatha knew that tone all too well. “I just want you back home. I just want us to be a real family again, just like we’ve always been, but you’re making this impossible by refusing to see reason. I’ve done everything in my power, Agatha. I gave you space, I waited patiently without interfering, but I’ve reached my limit. You need to come home before I’m forced to take drastic measures.”

“Are you threatening me?” Agatha choked out, hearing Tessa release a heavy, theatrical sigh.

“Why do you always have to twist every single word I say?” Irritation dripped from Tessa’s voice. “Why do you constantly manufacture drama where none exists? I’m trying to fix our family, Agatha, but you’re fighting me every step of the way.”

“You can’t fix this, Tessa!” she nearly screamed, hot tears finally spilling over her lashes. “There is nothing left to fix! It’s over, Tessa.”

“Agatha, you have two weeks. I’m not giving you an inch more than that.” Tessa’s voice dropped into a chillingly resolute finality, prompting Agatha to shake her head violently as she wiped her cheeks with her forearm. “If you refuse to make the right choice, I’ll have to make it for you, and I have a strong feeling you won’t like the outcome of it.”

The line clicked dead before Agatha could even draw a breath to reply.

Her hands shook violently, her vision blurring behind a fresh wall of tears. It felt as though she had just been doused in freezing water. Pulling a pillow into her lap, Agatha buried her face into the soft fabric, sobbing as the material slowly darkened with her grief. She hadn’t wanted to cry, hadn’t wanted to unravel like this, but her body seemed to bypass her mind entirely, utterly exhausted by years of buried anguish.

She knew fighting it was useless; the only way through was to surrender to the tears. She needed to purge the poison, to let whatever was drowning her spill out into the open. To build a new life, she had to stop running from the ugly truths, the pain, and the wreckage. She was done lying to herself; she had to face things exactly as they were and accept the unchangeable past. She needed to forgive herself so she could finally take a step forward.

After a long while, she drew in a deep, shuddering breath. She refused to let Tessa rob her of her fresh start — not after everything she had clawed through just to reach this place. She was done merely surviving, and no matter how terrifying it felt, she wanted to live. She wanted to take those first tentative steps toward the light. The suffocating silence, the swallowed cries, the hollow lies that glossed over broken moments, the painful, plastered-on smiles — she was leaving all of it behind.

She needed air, and so she took it. She stayed curled in the exact same position for long minutes, breathing deeply until her racing pulse began to slow. She didn’t force herself to stop crying; she let it run its course until her body felt impossibly lighter. Finally, she stood, made her way to the small bathroom, splashed cold water over her face, and drew in a breath fueled by a quiet, newly anchored strength. She was ready to move forward.

Stepping out of the basement stairs onto the sunlit porch, Agatha leaned her forearms against the weathered wooden railing, closing her eyes as she let the warm rays and the gentle breeze wash over her face. She knew her features were blotchy and swollen from the tears, but it felt right. It felt safe. She soaked in the quiet lightness of the day — a stark, beautiful contrast to the heavy shadows she had carried for so long. It was the lightness of finally being home. When she opened her eyes, a soft smile curved her lips at the sight of Kate, just yards away, crouching in the grass beside Nicholas, who was grinning wildly as he tried to catch the wind with a homemade kite. Her friend gesture encouragingly toward the sky, and her son nodded eagerly, his messy curls catching the light, his eyes alive with focused, uncontainable joy.

Agatha felt a profound warmth bloom in her chest, as if she were being wrapped in an embrace from the inside out. Every time she saw him like that — smiling and unburdened — she knew she was making the right choice, both for herself and for him. They were home now, and that was all that truly mattered. Eventually, everything would be okay. As impossible as it felt to rationalize everything in that exact same moment, she believed it; piece by piece, little by little, everything was going to be okay.

“Sweetheart, is everything okay?” Agatha heard her mother’s voice drift up from behind her. The moment she spun around, she saw Evanora’s face twist with immediate distress, reaching out to rub a comforting hand across her shoulder. “Agatha, why are you crying? What happened?”

“It’s nothing, mom,” she murmured, quickly scrubbing the back of her hand across her face. “I just—”

“Did something happen back home?” her mother interrupted, her voice sharp with alarm. “I was just coming out to see if you were awake yet. Tessa called, and I—”

The name hit Agatha like an electric shock. In a fraction of a second, every ounce of lightness drained from her body, her eyes widening in a panic that only deepened the raw concern stamped across her mother’s features.

“Tessa called you? She called here? What did she say?” Agatha rushed the words out, breathless, but her mother merely shook her head, trying to soothe her.

“She was just worried, honey. Said you weren’t picking up your phone, and I told her you were probably still sleeping, but that I’d let you know she called.”

“What did she say, mom? Did she say anything else?” she pressed frantically, making her mother’s brow furrow in confusion.

“Honey, she just wanted to know if everything was alright,” Evanora replied in a gentle, compassionate tone, rubbing her daughter’s arms. Agatha let out a shaky breath, letting her head drop. “What is going on, honey? What aren’t you telling me?”

Agatha simply shook her head, burying her face in her hands as fresh tears blurred her vision all over again. Evanora sighed, a heavy weight sinking into her chest as she rubbed her back, caught in a haze of worry and uncertainty over how to help.

"Come here, my love," her mother murmured softly, guiding her gently toward the house with a protective hand pressed against her back. "Come inside, I'll get you a glass of water. Everything is going to be alright, sweetheart."

Ever since she had first crossed the threshold of the farm, Agatha had been dodging this exact moment. She knew that, sooner or later, she would have to face her mother and tell her the truth. She needed to explain why she was here, because the reality was simple: she had no plan of leaving. It was just another hidden truth she had been burying, another suffocating secret she was terrified to release into the open. But now, she realized she had run out of road.

Alex was right — life didn’t hit pause just because she was trying to sort herself out; she had to take charge and make things happen. And if she was genuinely going to start over, if she was ever going to accept reality and let herself heal, the very first step had to be absolute honesty with her mother.

Evanora pulled a pitcher of water from the fridge and poured her a glass. Agatha took it, sipping slowly, feeling entirely cornered yet unable to look away from the deeply apprehensive gaze fixed on her.

“Agatha, I didn’t want to pry, but I know something is wrong,” her mother said gently, prompting Agatha to look up with a faint, surprised frown. “I’m not blind.”

“Mom, I never—”

“I know,” Evanora interrupted in a soothing tone, reaching across to wrap her daughter’s hand securely within her own. “A few days after you godfather’s wake, I noticed things were out of sorts. You practically moved into the basement, you stopped mentioning how things were going at home, and you never said a word about Tessa…” At the mere mention of her wife’s name, Agatha drew in a sharp, rattling breath, and Evanora tilted her head, watching her with a perceptive, searching gaze. “I didn’t want to crowd you, I thought it was best to give you space. But now I’m genuinely worried.”

“Mom, I…” Agatha tried to begin, but her voice fractured, and she let out a heavy, defeated exhale. “Tessa and I… we…” She broke off, choking as her throat tightened completely. “Mom, I asked for a divorce.”

The instant the words left her mouth, pure shock swept across her mother’s expression, blurring Agatha’s vision with a fresh surge of tears. Yet, when she looked into her mother’s eyes, there was no shadow of judgment — only the deepest, most unconditional concern.

“Oh, sweetheart, I am so sorry…” her mother whispered, her face falling, but Agatha fiercely shook her head.

“Don’t be. It was the best decision of my life. You have no idea how desperately I needed to do this.”

“Honey, I didn’t even know that was a possibility between you two,” her mother said, her eyebrows pulling together in a conflicted mix of confusion and worry. “I know we sometimes go stretches without seeing each other as much, but you always insisted everything was fine. I genuinely thought…”

“I never wanted you to see it any other way. I didn’t want you to think everything had fallen apart,” Agatha confessed, her shoulders slumping. “I lied because… because I desperately wanted to believe it was fine, too— that sooner or later, things would fix themselves. I didn’t want you to see that I had been sleepwalking through a lie this entire time, and—”

“Honey, I am so heartbroken that you felt like you couldn’t be honest with me…” Evanora interrupted, shaking her head as she pulled her daughter into a tight, protective embrace. Agatha immediately rested her head against her mother’s shoulder, letting out a ragged sigh as long, comforting fingers stroked through her hair. “All I have ever wanted for you is happiness, real genuine happiness, my angel. I am so sorry, my love.”

“I wanted to believe it was real too, you know?” she murmured in a fragile, broken voice, pulling back just enough to look at her mother in the eyes and seeing an understanding nod in return. “She isn’t who you think she is. She isn’t even who I thought she was. It was so agonizingly hard, mom… I spent years idealizing everything, always reaching for more, always trying harder because I genuinely thought… I thought I deserved it all. I thought I just had to swallow it and take it, because it was the price of my own choices.”

“Oh, sweetheart…” her mother whispered, her brows knitting together in deep compassion as she reached out to cup Agatha’s face. Agatha closed her eyes, leaning into the warmth of the touch and drawing in a ragged breath. She needed this more than words could say. “I am so sorry, my love. I am heartbroken that you even think that way, because it isn’t true. I can see the exhaustion in your eyes, the heavy burden you’ve been carrying and none of it is right. No matter what happened, I know who you are. I know you never deserved to suffer like this.”

"I truly thought I deserved it," she confessed, her gaze dropping to the floor. "But it eventually reached a point where I simply couldn't breathe anymore, where I couldn't keep going... Not with Nicky, not while I watched him slowly shrink into himself day after day..."

"What did she do to you, Agatha?" her mother asked in a fierce whisper, locking eyes with her while holding her face in a protective grip.

Agatha felt her throat seize entirely, leaving her capable of nothing more than a slow, defeated shake of her head as she averted her eyes.

“I ran away… I asked for a divorce and ran away,” Agatha whispered, her voice barely carrying across the room. “And I refuse to go back, mom.”

Her mother's expression melted instantly, shimmering with unshed tears. Evanora nodded, pressing a lingering kiss to Agatha's forehead before taking her hand once more, gazing at her with a fierce, unwavering tenderness meant to offer both comfort and absolute safety.

“You never have to return. You have a home right here,” her mother said softly, smoothing away the worry lines on Agatha’s brow and letting her exhale a lifetime of held-in breath. “You are home, honey. And I’m here, I’ll always stand by your side, no matter what comes next.”

"She refuses to sign the divorce papers," Agatha murmured, and in a flash, the tenderness on her mother's face hardened into protective resolve. "I need to build my life here from the ground up. I need to get things in order, find a job, arrange proper treatment for Nicky, get him into school, I—"

“I know these aren’t the ideal circumstances, but nothing in this world could make me happier than having both of you here with me,” Evanora interrupted gently, drawing a soft, trembling smile from Agatha. “We’ll figure it all out. Everything can be mended in time, what matters is that you’re safe here now. As for the rest, we’ll take it one step at a time.” Agatha nodded, inhaling deeply. “You have the house Javier left for you, and I have more than enough to help you get back on your feet. I have no doubt you’ll find your footing here.”

“Mommy?”

Agatha nearly jolted out of her chair, her heart leaping into her throat at the sound of her son's voice. She spun around instantly to see him standing nearby, his small forehead furrowed in deep concern. He reached out a hesitant hand to touch her cheek, gently wiping away a stray tear while searching her eyes, his tender, confused brown gaze filled with worry at the sight of her crying.

Nicholas had come so far since their arrival at the farm. He was more affectionate, more expressive, actively engaging in daily routines, and it had been a long time since he last suffered a nervous breakdown or a crushing crying fit ending in aggressive spasms and screams. And though silence remained his default, there were rare, unexpected moments when he would softly offer a word or two. Every single time it happened, Agatha felt a healing warmth ripple through her chest.

"Hey, sweetie," Agatha whispered, her voice cracking as she quickly brushed away her tears. He merely shook his head, placing his small palms over hers, studying her with a silent, questioning intensity. "Everything is fine, sweetheart. I just needed a little comfort from my mom for a moment."

“Are you hurt?” he asked, gently pressing his forehead against hers. Agatha clamped her lips together to hold back the overwhelming wave of fierce emotion that washed over her every time he spoke. She offered a weak smile and, with a slow, deliberate movement, slid her chair back — a silent invitation that he accepted without hesitation, climbing straight up into her lap.

"Just a little," she whispered like it was a grand secret, prompting him to lift his eyebrows in a silent inquiry. "Right here," she murmured, guiding his small hand to the left side of her chest and pressing it flat against her heart.

Nicholas nodded as if he truly understood, leaving Agatha utterly captivated by the profound empathy and care radiating from his soft brown eyes. Even wrapped in his silence, she felt entirely understood and deeply sheltered. He looped both arms securely around her neck, resting his head heavily against her shoulder, and Agatha finally let out a long, shuddering breath. The relief was so immense, so weightless, that she simply closed her eyes and rested her cheek against his messy curls.

When she glanced up toward her mother, Evanora was watching them with a soft, beatific smile. In that quiet fraction of a second, Agatha knew deep within her soul that everything was genuinely going to be okay.

***

Alex's words continued to echo in her mind like a steady drumbeat of encouragement. Agatha knew she was right. After the emotional upheaval of that morning, she felt more certain than ever of what she had to do: she needed to plant her feet and reclaim her life, even if it meant building it all over again from the ashes.

There was no more room for mourning the wreckage of yesterday. It was time to make peace with herself and take that first step forward. That resolve was what had brought her here, standing on Wanda’s porch, her fingers locked tightly around the hand of her son. Nicholas looked wary of his unfamiliar surroundings, chewing nervously on the inside of his cheek as he kept his eyes glued to her.

The door swung open a moment later, revealing Wanda looking entirely at ease in a breezy crochet dress, sunglasses pushed up onto her head. Behind her, a small blur darted past, accompanied by the muffled echoes of a playful sibling squabble and the bright laughter of the twins. It was deeply comforting to see the warm, joyful sanctuary her friend had built; Agatha couldn’t suppress a sudden, sharp pang of longing — it was everything she had ever dreamed of having.

Wanda’s face lit up in genuine surprise the instant she spotted her, though a soft, welcoming smile quickly curved her lips.

"Agatha? What a pleasant surprise!" Wanda greeted her warmly.

"I'm sorry for dropping in out of nowhere, but I was hoping—"

“Oh, stop right there,” Wanda interrupted with a dismissive wave. “Get in here. I’m not up to anything, just soaking up some sun by the pool.”

Agatha stepped across the threshold hesitatingly, a knot of shyness tightening in her chest, though her old friend clearly felt no need for formalities.

"A pool, huh? Aren't we fancy," Agatha quipped in a quiet, awkward attempt to break the tension. Wanda let out a soft laugh as she clicked the front door shut behind them.

"Ever since Nat made partner with the Vidals, I've basically evolved into a trophy wife. Can you believe it?"

Taking in the interior, yes, Agatha could easily believe it. The space was open and expansive, featuring elegant ceramic breeze blocks that subtly partitioned the rooms. A grand staircase swept upward, offering a clear view of the upper hallway in a style that bore an undeniable resemblance to the Vidal mansion. It was breathtakingly modern yet cozy, retaining all the rustic charm of the countryside.

“I actually spoke to Benito the other day and meant to swing by the farm. I’ve been dying to see you, it’s been ages,” Wanda said, her voice softening with affectionate nostalgia. Agatha gave a quiet nod, exhaling slowly.

"Yeah, it really has." Agatha shrank back slightly, her palpable awkwardness immediately caught by Wanda’s sharp, perceptive eyes. "I... look, I genuinely wanted to talk to you. It's been way too long, and..."

"Why don't we take this outside?" Wanda gently cut through her stumbling words, her knowing gaze making it clear she understood this wasn't just a casual social call. "Nicky can hang out in here with the boys," she offered, already letting out a sharp whistle that brought her sons running at the first signal.

Agatha felt her son instinctively press closer behind her legs, darting nervous glances between Wanda, the approaching boys, and the open doorway, though the twins were already greeting them with curious, friendly grins.

"He's a bit shy," Agatha murmured uncertainly, but Wanda only offered an understanding smile and a reassuring nod.

"Yeah, I noticed," she replied warmly. "But I'm sure the boys will be on their best behavior, right? Nicky is new here and could use some friends," she added, turning to her sons. "How about you guys put on a cartoon in the living room while Agatha and I catch up outside? And no yelling," she warned, pointing a finger at them. "If I hear a single loud noise, neither of you is going to your godmother's house today."

"Do you want to watch Horseland?" Billy offered with a friendly smile. Nicholas looked up at his mother, who offered an encouraging nod.

With tentative steps, he followed the other boys. The twins immediately started chattering excitedly about the show, trying to draw him into the conversation. Nicky stayed cautious, glancing back and forth between them as he hugged his stuffed horse tightly to his chest.

Wanda led her through the house to the back patio, which opened onto a sprawling yard featuring a sparkling pool, a barbecue area, and citrus trees lining the edges. There was a custom-built treehouse and other handmade wooden toys, painted in bright, cheerful colors.

They settled at a small round table right by the water.

"Wine?" Wanda offered with an inquiring eyebrow, prompting a soft, grateful smile and a nod from Agatha. It felt just like old times.

It really had been too long, and Agatha knew she bore the blame for the distance between them. They had managed to stay connected for a few years — Wanda had even attended her wedding, and they kept up the tradition of exchanging letters and holiday gifts. Agatha had been genuinely thrilled by the news of her friend's engagement. Despite the physical separation, their bond had never truly frayed. Things only shifted after Wanda's wedding, when Tessa flatly refused to travel to Darby, and Agatha ultimately surrendered to keep the peace.

Back then, she had still tried to look on the bright side, even when the cup was empty. She ended up retreating from everyone, cutting herself off from her entire life at the farm. As agonizing as it was, a part of her couldn't deny that her wife had a point; it wouldn't have been fair to keep returning to a place that served as a constant battleground for their marriage. Agatha had made her choice and accepted the fallout, but the bitter truth was that she missed it terribly — not just her friend, but a huge piece of the life she had left behind.

Opening up after all these years wasn't easy. Yet Wanda had a way of making her feel instantly at home, effortlessly bridging the gap of time and distance. Wrestling with her own lingering resentment, Agatha slowly began to find a fragile peace in forgiveness — both from the people who loved her and, most importantly, toward herself.

It was far from an easy conversation. She lost count of how many times she broke down in tears, but with the help of a few glasses of wine, she finally managed to share the heavy truths she had kept locked away for so long. She told her everything — or at least the parts she had processed, because there were still corners of that marriage too dark to speak aloud, memories she couldn't force herself to relive just yet.

Agatha laid it all out from the start: how blindingly perfect it had once felt in her head, building an empire with Tessa, holding the world in the palm of their hands, sharing a dream life with someone who seemed to crave the exact same things. It was an illusion so airtight that it blinded her to the red flags flickering from day one — the creeping possessiveness, the subtle gaslighting that always left Agatha holding the blame when things went wrong, the quiet expectation that she make herself smaller so Tessa could shine, the underlying message that she was fundamentally flawed and should be endlessly grateful for Tessa's infinite patience. Tessa had cast herself as her savior, and for a long time, Agatha had swallowed the lie whole.

Then came graduation, the moment Agatha longed to throw herself into her career rather than tie her identity entirely to a relationship. Tessa had insisted, pulling strings and ensuring her father hired her. Agatha couldn't say no — not when Tessa had moved mountains to give her what she wanted. But nothing came without a price, and every gift turned out to be a debt she spent years paying off with pieces of her own soul. When Agatha finally started making a name for herself — outshining Tessa in the process — the real war began. The belittling comments, the sabotage driven by an ego that couldn't bear a rival, even under the same roof. And finally, the relentless push for a child. Agatha hadn't wanted one, but Tessa wanted it badly enough that Agatha folded, desperate to believe that building a family would magically smooth over the cracks. Every time Tessa talked about a baby, she softened, turning sweet and attentive, bringing back the golden glow of the beginning. So Agatha took a chance.

Then Nicky arrived, and the battlefield simply shifted to his needs, endless shouting matches over what was best for their son. The way Tessa spoke about him, looking at him during his meltdowns as if Agatha's gentle parenting was a disease to be cured. The way Tessa began withdrawing after his birth, treating her less like a wife and more like a failed domestic servant — a role Agatha had never signed up for.

She poured it all out to Wanda, who listened with tear-filled, understanding eyes, gripping her hand in a steady, grounding show of solidarity. For the first time in as long as she could remember, Agatha felt a strange, terrifying sense of release. She felt light. She had needed this more than she realized.

"Agatha, I am so deeply sorry..." Wanda murmured, her face crumpling with empathy as she squeezed her friend's hand tighter. "No one should ever have to endure that, god... I am so sorry, truly. I had no idea. I always thought..."

"Everyone thought so. Hell, I thought so too, for a long time," Agatha admitted, staring down at her lap. "But I just couldn't take it anymore. I... I really couldn't. Not with Nicky..."

"Agatha, you endured it for far too long," Wanda said, fixing her with a steady, compassionate gaze. Agatha sniffled, quickly wiping away her fresh tears. "What she did to you... it was abuse on so many levels that I... I honestly don't even know where to start," Wanda stammered, her voice thick with a mix of fierce exasperation and deep affection. "I can't even begin to wrap my head around how hard it must be to carry all of that, to try and make sense of the wreckage. But I am just so damn glad you finally broke free, that you're actually here."

"It's not easy. God, it really isn't," Agatha confessed, and Wanda offered an understanding nod. "But ever since I arrived, I feel like things are starting to click back into place, you know? After all those years I spent running away from this town, I know this probably sounds ridiculous, but I finally feel like I'm home."

"It doesn't sound ridiculous at all. Whatever you thought you wanted back then... Agatha, none of that dictates who you are today. Just look at everything you've survived. You're making the right choice now, carving out your own space and starting over from scratch. There's nothing foolish about that. Quite the opposite."

"I just feel like I threw away so much time, you know? Like I lost years of my life living a lie and—”

"I know it's heavy, and it's definitely not something that vanishes overnight," Wanda gently cut in, her tone soft and unwavering. "This is a fresh start, Agatha. It is never too late for that, or to give yourself a second chance. You need to give yourself grace and time to heal. Yes, you lost a lot, but look at you: you're standing right here on your own two feet. This isn't the time to keep staring in the rearview mirror. You have to look forward, to yourself, and to your son, who needs you more than ever."

"I know," Agatha agreed, straightening her shoulders as she drew in a deep, stabilizing breath. "That's why I'm here. I want to do things the right way and put my life back together. I want to stay; I want to build a real life here."

"Well, you're talking to the right person," Wanda said, a genuine smile breaking through. Agatha offered a small, watery smile back, reaching across the table to squeeze her friend's hand. "The school term just kicked off, but I can easily get Nicholas enrolled. And you don't need to worry about a thing, we have several neurodivergent students and a fantastic, dedicated team heading up support."

"Wanda, I don't even know how to begin thanking you..." Agatha started, but Wanda dismissed it with a quick wave of her hand, brushing it off as nothing.

"He needs proper, specialized care, Agatha," Wanda pointed out gently, and Agatha nodded in quiet agreement. "He needs consistent support, the right activities to encourage socialization, and tools to help him stay regulated. His silence could stem from a dozen different things, and only a qualified professional is going to truly know how to unlock that for him."

"I know that, but with Tessa, it was a brick wall. She never accepted it, always shutting down any possibility of getting help."

"Well, she isn't here, and she's no longer your problem," Wanda assured her firmly, helping the last of the tension drain from Agatha's shoulders. "There is an incredible neuropsychologist in the area named Dr. Jennifer Kale. She's brilliant and specializes in neurodivergent care. Her office isn't right in town, but it's less than an hour away. I can pass along her number; if I drop my name, I'm sure she can squeeze him in."

"I want to get started immediately. He needs this. I can already see how much he's blossomed since we got here, but I know he needs professional guidance to keep going."

"Of course, I'll text you her info," Wanda said with a warm smile, though Agatha didn't miss the lingering shadow of concern in her eyes. "But you need help, too, Agatha. You can't heal if you keep all of this locked inside. You need a therapist of your own right now.”

Agatha flinched slightly, pulling back into her chair as a sudden wave of vulnerability washed over her. But she knew her friend was right. She had grown so accustomed to swallowing her own pain and letting her feelings be minimized that the mere thought of opening that Pandora's box felt terrifyingly raw. Yet, deep down, she knew it was unavoidable.

"I'm sure Dr. Kale can recommend someone great, but you have to be willing to do the work for yourself, too."

"I know," Agatha sighed, her shoulders slumping. "I know I have to, and I will."

"You’re not alone in this, Agatha.”

***

Between the past few days, Rio had already maxed out her lifetime quota of heavy, soul-searching conversations. Vulnerability was simply not in her vocabulary; opening up left her feeling completely exposed, raw, and utterly uncomfortable. Still, nobody could accuse her of not trying. Here she was — stone-cold sober in the middle of the afternoon — gearing up for another weekend with her godsons.

If she let herself overthink it for even a second, she knew she’d spin her horse right around, gallop back home, and tear open a fresh case of beer. To drown out the creeping dread, she hummed a low tune under her breath as she tied Raio to the front fence.

She didn't even need to bother knocking. The moment her boots hit the top step of the porch, Billy threw the front door wide open, his face splitting into a massive grin that instantly dragged a smile out of her.

"Are you guys ready?" she asked, catching her godson as he launched himself into her, affectionately burying his face right in her stomach.

"I haven't packed my backpack yet," he confessed with a sheepish grimace. Rio let out a long-suffering sigh and shook her head.

"What have you guys even been doing all day? I told you I was coming," she grumbled, though it melted into an affectionate eye-roll as he yanked her inside the entryway, screaming at the top of his lungs for his brother to grab his gear and get down here.

"Where is your mom?" she called out, though her question was swallowed by the sound of pounding footsteps as the two boys scrambled upstairs.

Rio shook her head with a faint chuckle and wandered down the hall, her fingertips trailing lightly over framed photos of the boys. Because she was practically part of the furniture here, the house always wrapped around her like a second home. Wandering into the kitchen, she yanked the fridge door open, only to bite back a groan at the sight of half a dozen cold beers — the exact brand Natasha always kept stocked. Grinding her teeth in silent frustration, she shoved the door shut and grabbed a bottle of water instead.

"Hey!"

The sweet, familiar voice startled her, whipping her around in a single fluid motion. Rio's face softened into an involuntary smile as she came face-to-face with Nicholas, those massive brown eyes staring right up at her. He looked the picture of a little boy: flushed cheeks, wild curls tumbling into his eyes, and a small, crooked smile playing on his lips as he rocked back and forth on his heels.

"Hey there, cowboy!" she greeted, twisting the cap off her water bottle and affectionately ruffling his unruly hair, which only made his grin widen. "What are you doing in here?"

Nicholas just gave an uncertain shrug, prompting a soft, understanding chuckle from Rio.

"Are the boys treating you okay?" When he gave a vigorous nod, Rio mirrored the gesture with a satisfied nod of her own. "Did you bring any of your drawings to show them? I bet they'd lose their minds over how cool they are."

"I forgot," he muttered, his gaze dropping to the floor in sudden deflation. Rio's brow furrowed with instant empathy as she offered a warm, reassuring smile.

"But look what I brought," he piped up, eagerly holding out a battered, stitched-up plush toy.

The moment Rio’s eyes landed on the rag horse, a wave of pure nostalgia washed over her face. It was Benito’s old toy — her mother had stitched it together when he was little, and he had named it after Agatha’s favorite horse, the only one he’d ever dared to touch. Good grief, she hadn’t laid eyes on this thing in years; she had no idea it even still existed.

"Where on earth did you dig this up?" she asked, turning the worn fabric toy over in her hands with a faint, bemused smile.

"It's mine," he answered with a proud little shrug. Rio laughed softly. Of course it was.

"You really have a thing for horses, don't you?" she asked, dropping her knees to the floor so she was eye-level with him. Seeing those big brown eyes light up as he nodded fiercely sparked a sudden, brilliant idea in her chest. "Have you ever actually ridden one?" When he shook his head furiously, Rio's grin stretched wide. "Do you want to? I came with Raio.”

Rio couldn't hold back the laugh bubbling in her throat as the boy's entire face illuminated. He nodded so hard his head bobbed, bouncing up and down on his toes with wide-eyed, electric excitement. Before she could even stand, he reached out and grabbed her hand, taking total command and practically dragging her toward the door, glancing back over his shoulder every two seconds with a grin that threatened to split his face.

"Hold on, cowboy, we need to slow down," Rio chuckled in a warm, teasing tone, resting a steadying hand on his small shoulder as he stopped to stare up at her with fierce concentration. "He doesn't know you yet, so we have to take it easy. Horses can be a little skittish."

Nicky tilted his head, a tiny crease forming between his brows as if the concept was entirely foreign to him. She couldn't help the fond laugh that slipped out.

"Come here," she murmured, opening her arms wide. He didn't hesitate for a fraction of a second, marching right into her embrace and throwing an arm securely around her neck. A profound, unprompted warmth bloomed in Rio's chest; she couldn't even explain the sheer weight of it, but knowing she had his trust felt like winning a prize she didn't deserve. "He gets nervous easily, but he's a good boy. You'll see."

With Nicky still in her arms, Rio walked over to the horse, extending a hand to stroke its velvet muzzle and running her palm gently along the crest of its mane. Glancing back down, she noticed the boy keeping his hands safely tucked against his chest, entirely unsure. With an encouraging nod, she coaxed him forward. Carefully, Nicholas reached out a small hand and brushed his fingertips against Raio’s nose, bursting into a delighted laugh when the stallion let out a soft huff of breath and leaned into the touch.

"He learns who you are by your scent," Rio explained.

The moment she spoke, Nicholas leaned in further, planting both hands flat against the horse's snout. Raio responded by tilting his massive head straight into the boy's touch, rumbling softly as he nuzzled against the small hands in search of more affection.

"He likes you!"

"I like him!" Nicky blurted out, his face breaking into a wide, ecstatic grin that left Rio utterly charmed.

Truthfully, Raio was one of her most high-strung animals — arguably the most volatile on the farm. She had rescued him years ago from an illegal racing circuit alongside a handful of broken, mistreated horses, and winning his trust had been a long, grueling battle. The others had settled into farm life eventually, but Raio remained fiercely loyal to her and her alone. Even breaking him in had felt like a form of punishment, but once they conquered that hurdle, they became an unbreakable unit; she had never ridden a horse so blindingly fast or fiercely loyal.

To this day, she was the only human he tolerated. He rejected every other handler on the property, vets included, usually throwing a fit at the mere approach of a stranger. Rio had braced herself for a long, tedious process of getting him used to a child. But instead, Raio had melted like a gentle giant in Nicholas's presence, sniffing him with meticulous care and nudging him affectionately.

"Let me just tighten the girth on the saddle," Rio instructed, showing the boy how the equipment worked so he could follow along with wide, attentive eyes. "He likes you, but I'm going to hold onto you the whole time, alright? You've never been on a horse before." She kept her tone reassuring, and he gave a solemn nod. "If he gets spooked, I promise I won't let you fall. Okay?"

Nicholas nodded, a proud little smile tugging at his lips. Shifting her grip, Rio locked her hands around his waist and hoisted him smoothly up into the saddle.

For an absolute beginner, the boy took to it with uncanny naturalness. Rio beamed, entirely captivated as she watched him instinctively wrap his legs securely around the saddle so as not to startle the animal, clutching the reins while she kept one hand anchored to Raio's back and her other arm locked firmly around the boy's middle.

"He's the fastest one here, isn't he?" Nicholas asked, twisting around to pin those bright, intelligent brown eyes on her. Rio nodded with an affectionate smile.

"Yes, he is, but today we're just taking it—"

"Nicholas!"

Agatha's frantic shriek cut through the air like a bolt of lightning. Before Rio even had the chance to pivot around, Raio bolted upright, rearing high on his hind legs in a blind panic that sent Rio tumbling ungracefully backward into the dirt.

"My god! Riandra! Have you lost your mind?!"

Scrambling up from the grass, still dusty and uncoordinated from her sudden spill, Rio threw her hands up defensively to block Agatha as the woman charged furiously toward the stallion.

"You're going to spook him!" Rio warned, stepping squarely into her path, but Agatha looked entirely unhinged, her blue eyes wide with terror.

"Riandra, my son—"

"Damn, he's actually good," Rio muttered under her breath, a flash of genuine awe hitting her as she looked back up at the boy. Nicholas was sitting tall, his small hands gripping the reins with steady, instinctive control, perfectly steadying the horse as it huffed and stamped its hooves before immediately falling back in line. "Not just anyone could handle that—"

"Have you completely lost your marbles?" Agatha barked, pointing an accusatory finger straight at her chest, her pupils still blown wide with adrenaline. "He has never ridden a horse in his life, Rio! He almost fell off!"

"You're the one who scared Raio!" Rio fired back on the defensive, rolling her shoulders as she stepped forward to lift Nicholas out of the saddle. Agatha sputtered, opening and closing her mouth in sheer disbelief as she raked her eyes up and down Rio's dirt-stained figure, completely flabbergasted to see the boy lounging happily in Rio's arms with a massive, triumphant grin. "He wasn't going to fall, I had him the entire time."

"I saw you holding him with your ass in the dirt while my son was practically launching into orbit!"

"Well, he didn't fall, did he?" Rio shot back with a smug, unapologetic grin. "Kid's a natural, seriously." She shifted her gaze down to Nicholas, who was beaming proudly against her chest. "You've got some serious talent, you know that, cowboy?"

"Rio, I swear to god—"

"I was never going to let him drop, Agatha, I swear to you," Rio interrupted, her tone softening into quiet sincerity as she met the other woman's blistering stare. "I was locked onto him the second we got up there. Raio only panicked because you came screaming across the yard, but I would've taken the fall ten times over before letting a hair on his head get touched."

The sheer intensity of that piercing blue gaze locked onto hers made Rio's breath catch, sending a sharp, electric shiver racing straight down her spine. It felt as though Agatha wasn't just reading her face, but stripping her entirely bare — probing the depths of her soul to decide whether she was worthy of belief. It was deeply unsettling, yet tangled with a strange, aching familiarity that turned Rio's stomach completely inside out.

Finally, Agatha let out a long, heavy breath, as if physically gathering the pieces of her composure, and turned her face away.

"Come along, Nicky," she murmured to her son, dropping her hand. Rio carefully set him down, but the boy immediately clamped his small fingers around her belt loop. "Nicholas..." She sighed, but he stubbornly shook his head.

Looking down with a sudden flash of awkwardness, Rio cleared her throat and gave his messy curls a playful ruffle, easily drawing those big brown eyes up to meet hers.

"You know you have to listen to your mother," she said softly, her voice dropping into an affectionate cadence. He pouted, but gave a reluctant nod.

"Who wants to come grab some cookies before we head over to godmother's?" Wanda's voice chimed in from the doorway where she stood with the boys, breaking the charged stillness of the yard.

"Go on," Agatha urged gently. Nicholas nodded grudgingly, dragging his feet as he shuffled toward the house. Rio had to bite the inside of her cheek to keep from laughing; the kid was more skittish than a green-broke colt.

"He can come along with me and the boys, if he'd like," Rio offered.

"No, he cannot," Agatha shot back instantly, spinning around with a rigid expression. "Rio, he has literally never been on a horse in his life!"

Rio's brow furrowed and she swallowed hard, a sudden, sharp pang of guilt hitting her ribs. She hadn't meant to cause a panic; quite the contrary. She did this all the time, coaching kids safely at the track, and she knew he would have been completely secure. It had been Agatha's shrieking that startled the animal — though she was smart enough not to throw that in her face. Still, she knew Agatha's overprotective streak all too well, and could only imagine how fiercely amplified it was when it came to her son.

"Agatha, I would never put him in danger. I would never let anything happen to him," Rio said quietly, watching the lingering doubt war across the other woman's features. "He likes horses, and he was just showing me some sketches of Raio the other day. I thought it would be fun, and he wanted to try. I wouldn't have let him drop."

"I know. I know you," Agatha admitted, exhaling a shaky breath as she shook her head. Rio arched a brow in quiet surprise, realizing that beneath all the wreckage, the trust between them wasn't entirely dead. "It's just..." She sighed, and Rio patiently waited. "He's not used to any of this. He's fragile with new things, and I... I panicked! I was terrified! He's so little!" she confessed in a rush of raw exasperation, drawing a soft, sympathetic chuckle from Rio.

"You were little once, too. You were his exact age when you rode my dad's horse." The words stopped Agatha dead in her tracks, her blue eyes snapping back to lock onto Rio's with a sudden, shining spark, as if a long-buried door had just flown open. "My dad didn't let you fall, and I wasn't about to let anything happen to him, either."

In that instant, the invisible magnetic pull between the vast ocean of blue and the deep abyss of brown snapped back into place. It was unsettlingly familiar, wrapping around them with a warmth and a jolt that felt entirely impossible, like recognizing a language you'd forgotten you spoke. They stared at each other, raw and unguarding, neither of them quite conscious of the gravity pulling them in. It was a silent dialogue, a quiet, desperate attempt to read the lines carved by time. A strange, unfamiliar shiver danced across the back of Rio's neck.

Agatha cleared her throat, blinking hard as she abruptly dropped her gaze, pulling herself out of the trance. Rio blinked right along with her, clearing her throat and offering a stiff, awkward nod. When they tentatively looked up again, both of them traded a small, hesitant smile.

"Listen... about yesterday," Rio muttered awkwardly, rubbing the back of her neck as she searched for footing. "Everything I said stands. You're always welcome here, and... I'm really sorry for the way I came at you when you first got back, and—"

"It's fine, really, Rio," Agatha interrupted gently, her expression entirely serene, drawing a deeply relieved breath from Rio. She hadn't realized how heavy the doubt was, worrying that Agatha might have dismissed it all as the loose-lipped sentimentality of a drunk. "What I said came straight from the heart, too."

"So... we're good?" Rio asked awkwardly, giving a vague little gesture between them. Agatha nodded.

"Yes. We're good."

"This is weird," Rio murmured with a self-deprecating huff of laughter, prompting a quiet, breathy exhale from Agatha. "But... nice. I guess. It's good that we're good."

"Is it really okay with you that we're good?" Agatha countered, a single eyebrow lifting as a playful, knowing spark danced in her eyes, drawing a soft, helpless laugh out of Rio.

"Yeah. I wanted this, I think it matters. You matter. You always will."

Agatha offered a polite, grounding nod, which Rio mirrored instantly. "Well, I should probably..." Agatha started, taking a step backward and gesturing toward the house.

"Wait," Rio murmured, and Agatha paused, turning back with an inquisitive arch of her brow. "I don't know how long you're planning on sticking around, but... you should bring Nicky down to the racetrack sometime." She shrugged casually, though her eyes betrayed her hope. "We run kids' riding classes for all skill levels, and I'm around most days. I think he'd really like it. I can bring a calmer horse out for him, I know he doesn't have his own."

"No, he definitely doesn't," Agatha laughed softly. "Thanks for the invite, Rio. I'll think about it."

"I really think it'd be good for him," Rio added quietly. "He's got a natural feel for it. I think he'd have a blast."

"I'll consider it," she replied with genuine warmth, offering a weak, grateful smile. "Thanks, Rio."

"Don't mention it."

"I guess I'll see you around, then," Agatha said, giving a small shrug before turning back toward the house.

Rio stood rooted to the spot, keeping her eyes fixed on the door long after it clicked shut behind her. She couldn't fully untangle it, but standing there with Agatha after all these years was both agonizingly disorienting and achingly comforting. She had braced herself for the aftermath to taste like ash and bitterness, but it didn't. It was entirely different. Brand new.

God, Rio really hated new things.

***

As soon as she unlocked the front door, Agatha couldn't help the familiar eye-roll as Nicholas marched right past her — arms locked tightly across his chest, a dramatic pout carved onto his face — stomping upstairs without so much as a glance in Lilia's direction. Normally, she would have cracked down on the attitude immediately, but lately, she was learning that discipline required timing. As much as she needed to check his behavior, she also had to help him self-regulate before the frustration spiraled into a full-blown meltdown.

"What set him off?" Lilia asked, her voice laced with amusement as a quiet smile twitched at the corner of her mouth. "He was practically bouncing off the walls when you two headed out this afternoon."

Agatha exhaled an amused, long-suffering sigh, following her aunt down the hallway and sinking into one of the chairs at the dining table.

"Turns out my son has officially fallen head over heels for Rio Vidal," she replied, flashing a dry, sarcastic grin that instantly coaxed a laugh out of Lilia, who settled into the chair next to her and gave her shoulder a comforting squeeze. "She rolled up to Wanda's place with a horse, let him climb right on, and now I'm public enemy number one because I dared to end the greatest day of his life."

"He really is hooked on her, isn't he? I think it's utterly precious," Lilia murmured fondly, earning another heavy-lidded roll of the eyes from Agatha. Just what she needed. "She's wonderful with kids, though. You really ought to watch her down at the racetrack, children flock to her from everywhere, just like that little storm trooper," Lilia added, gesturing toward the stairs where Nicky had vanished.

"She actually mentioned it,” Agatha murmured thoughtfully, turning the idea over in her mind. "Said I could bring Nicky along."

Lilia's brows shot up in genuine surprise.

"You two are actually talking?" her aunt asked, so unguardedly curious that Agatha gave her head a slightly self-conscious shake. She wished the topic didn't carry such gravity, that hearing their names woven together didn't still drag an anchor of nostalgia behind it.

"Yeah, I suppose so," she shrugged. As much as the air had cleared between them, Agatha couldn't quite bring herself to call it normal. It was just... a thing.
