“Used to dread the month of June, cause it reminded me of you and always came around too soon, not anymore. A part of me I had to find, cause it was killing me inside, you were always like a bye I wasn’t ready for. I figured this was something I deal with my whole life” – Butterfly, Demi Lovato

***

Agatha was fascinated by the way time could twist and shift. For years, the hours had dragged painfully, trapping her in the suffocating gears of a broken clock. Now, however, time seemed to slip right through her fingers. Since arriving at the farm, the weeks had blurred together in a rush. And lately, ever since she promised herself to finally get her life back on track, the days vanished in the blink of an eye.

Darby had grown far beyond her expectations. Fueled by the Vidal family’s booming enterprises, the town was now bustling with new shops and eager entrepreneurs. Seizing the momentum, Agatha had already interviewed at two small companies with fledgling legal departments. While the roles were decidedly below her qualifications, she felt confident and optimistic — she just needed a place to start.

Finding work was only part of the battle. She spent countless hours on the phone with Alex, painstakingly organizing Nicky’s school and medical records — documents Agatha had secretly gathered behind her wife’s back. Soon, she hoped, Tessa would officially be her ex-wife. Agatha kept a few trump cards hidden away, praying she’d never actually have to play them. Chief among them was a flash drive. Despite her own dread, she had asked Alex to sneak into the apartment during Tessa’s work hours with a spare key to retrieve it.

Deep down, Agatha begged the universe that Alex wouldn’t peek at the drive’s contents. She had deliberately kept her instructions vague to avoid sparking her best friend’s curiosity, as there were secrets buried on that drive she wished could stay hidden forever. Meanwhile, the divorce was at a tense standstill; Alex reported that Tessa still flat-out refused to sign the papers. The memory of their last phone call suffocated Agatha, leaving her constantly on edge. Yet, despite the looming anxiety, she refused to let it break her focus. She had to take things one step at a time.

Thankfully, it wasn’t all stress and worry. Being at the farm brought her a profound sense of purpose and genuine joy. For the first time in years, she was surrounded by an unconditional support system and was building a life entirely for herself. She was happy — and more importantly, so was Nicky.

She had finally unlocked the doors to the house her godfather had given her as a wedding gift. After sitting empty for so long, the place was in desperate need of a renovation, but it was slowly coming back to life. With Benito generously pouring his time and resources into the project, the house was blossoming. Every careful update reflected her own personal touch. At long last, she was building a true home.

It was deeply ironic. After spending years running from this farm — a place she had once dismissed as the absolute middle of nowhere — Agatha now found herself smiling as she put down roots, rebuilding her life one pillar at a time. She couldn’t imagine calling anywhere else home.

The house was excessively grand, built with the same airy, ostentatious wooden foundation as the main manor, exactly to her godfather’s taste. But Agatha was making it her own. She and Kate spent countless hours poring over color palettes and arranging the steady stream of new furniture. It wasn’t a massive structural overhaul, but rather a slow, collaborative transformation where they shared every step.

As a result, Agatha rarely had a moment to spare. Her aunt had been right: amidst the whirlwind of getting their lives back on track, Nicky needed healthy distractions. Walking hand-in-hand with her son through the equestrian center, watching him practically skip with joy, Agatha couldn’t help but smile.

With his classes still a few days away, Nicky had become a permanent shadow on the farm — mostly to Rio. As reluctant as Agatha was to admit it, the two were growing inseparable. On late afternoons, Rio would wander onto Evanora’s porch, always armed with a sweet treat, just to hang out with Nicky. They would pass the time together, sometimes drawing, sometimes just sitting in a comfortable silence.

Nicholas completely adored her, and seeing Rio’s genuine attachment to him was a bittersweet blow to Agatha’s heart. She tried to brush it off, but it was impossible to ignore how sweet and attentive Rio was. She softened her voice for him, anticipated his needs, and listened closely not just to his words, but to his silences — as if she understood him better than anyone else.

Watching them, Agatha’s chest would tighten with a comforting ache. Nicky truly blossomed in Rio’s presence, sprinting toward the main house the second she arrived. And Rio, no matter how exhausted she was from a long day of farm work, always made time to take him to the stables, teaching him how to care for and feed the animals. Agatha often caught herself sighing at the sight of Rio’s meticulous affection, watching her son unfold petal by petal.

Unfortunately, Agatha simply didn’t have that kind of free time right now. Between the house renovations, navigating the divorce bureaucracy, building her custody case, and job hunting, her days were entirely consumed. Nicky needed a constructive routine to help him develop, rather than just trailing after his favorite people all day.

The day before, she had observed the classes at the equestrian center and loved what she saw. Rio poured her heart into everything she did, and Agatha knew Nicky would thrive there with her. With an initial consultation finally scheduled with Dr. Jennifer Kale to discuss Nicky’s case, Agatha decided the center was the perfect place for her son to safely spend the day.

To her son’s delight, the day was bright and sunny. Nicky could barely contain his excitement, his eyes wide as he silently pointed at the children practicing small vaults on horseback, while others simply played and petted the animals. A few years away, Rio was crouched beside a group of little ones, patiently giving instructions.

Agatha couldn’t help but admire her. This was a side of Rio she had never seen: a natural ease with children, complete with warm, engaging smile that easily captured their attention and drew out ripples of laughter. The sweetness of it made Agatha’s chest ache. Beneath Rio’s tough exterior, there were unmistakable cracks where her tender heart shone through.

Nicky practically skipped as they walked over. Spotting them, Rio’s face lit up with a smile. She quickly handed the lesson over to Yelena and walked over to greet them, rubbing the back of her neck in a sudden display of shyness.

“What a surprise!” she said.

Agatha pressed her lips together to hide her own smile. She found Rio’s nervous, restrained demeanor incredibly endearing. It showed she was trying, a vulnerability Agatha deeply appreciated — after all, she was trying, too.

“Cowboy!” Rio crouched down to hug him, and Nicky melted into her arms with a joyful laugh.

Agatha was endlessly fascinated by the way her son opened up to Rio, trusting her in a way he rarely did with anyone else.

“I couldn’t exactly say no to the invitation; he was too excited to come,” Agatha said politely. Nicky nodded enthusiastically, earning an affectionate look from Rio as she stood back up.

“I’m excited too. I’m glad you came, cowboy,” Rio replied warmly. Agatha stroked her son’s hair. Today, he was sporting a headband to keep his stubborn curls out of his eyes — a temporary truce in their ongoing battle for change over his steadfast refusal to get a haircut.

“I bet you’re going to love this. I have the perfect horse for you to ride today,” Rio told him. Nicky glanced back at his mother for permission. Agatha offered an encouraging nod, slipping his Toy Story backpack off his shoulders. Without a second thought, he reached out and took Rio’s hand.

Internally, Agatha was fighting a tight know of anxiety. Nicky was tiny and notoriously sensitive to sudden changes; the wrong trigger could spark a massive meltdown, turning the stables into absolute chaos. Crowds of more than three kids were usually too much for him, overwhelming him with loud voices and unpredictable movements. Yet, anchored by Rio’s hand, he walked tall, his chest puffed out with newfound bravery. Settling into the front row of the bleachers, Agatha had to suppress a proud smile.

When Rio gently introduced him to the rest of the kids, Nicky shrank against her side and offered a timid wave. Rio didn’t push him. Instead, she seamlessly guided him to a quieter spot away from the bustling group, leaving the others in Yelena’s capable hands. At a subtle signal from Rio, an assistant brought over an older, incredibly docile white mare.

Nicky practically bounced on his heels as Rio gestured toward the horse. From the bleachers, Agatha couldn’t hear what was being said, but she could see Rio’s undivided attention and the absolute awe written across her son’s face. Physically, Nicky was quite small for his age, and seeing him standing next to such a massive animal made Agatha’s heart skip a beat. Taking a deep, steadying breath, she watched their every move.

It was an entirely new experience for her to see him like this — so outgoing, smiling openly, and freely trusting the people around him. Nicholas had always been a reclusive, introverted child, prone to a hunched posture, fearful hesitation, and very few words. But here, Agatha saw him in a completely different light. He possessed a newfound thirst for adventure and a constant, vibrating excitement. It was a beautiful thing to watch him emerge from his shell so naturally.

She let out a soft sigh as she watched them out on the grass. The way Rio engaged with him was mesmerizing. She held him with such care, offering her devoted attention and a quiet patience that drew long, unrestrained laughter from the boy as he petted the mare and listened to her speak. He was talking a mile a minute, leaving Agatha in absolute awe.

Yet, beneath that comfort lay a sharp pang in her chest. Nicholas was a perfect mirror image of Rio, right down to the smallest details: the same large, expressive brown eyes, the shy smile, the cautious demeanor, and even the slight gap in his front teeth.

For years, Agatha had tried to bury the past in the deepest, most inaccessible corners of her mind, but she lived with Rio’s ghost every time she looked at her son. He was a daily reminder of a love that had once felt infinite — a love destiny refused to let her forget. Looking at Nicky, she saw a young Riandra. She remembered Rio as a little girl: smaller than the rest, shy, and distrustful. Back then, Rio rarely spoke, only truly opening up to Agatha. When they were alone, Rio would also chatter endlessly and laugh without hesitation, existing in their own private bubble — just as she and Nicholas were doing now.

Nicholas was living piece of her past. Agatha had once feared that living with that resemblance would eventually turn bitter, but the exact opposite had happened. As he grew and looked more like Rio, her tenderness for those memories only overflowed. Now, witnessing their bond firsthand made her chest tighten with emotion. It closed a perfect circle between the love of her past and the love of her life — her son. They were two puzzle pieces she had never thought to connect, yet seeing them together, they fit flawlessly.

Out in the arena, Nicholas looked like he was in his natural habitat, and Agatha couldn’t stop smiling. The mare was so gentle that Rio easily guided the animal to lower herself, allowing him to climb on. With endless patience, Rio taught him how to saddle up and hold the reins. She kept a firm, protective grip on his waist, adjusting his posture until he learned to balance at a slow trot.

Agatha was utterly enchanted. Whenever Nicky threw a hopeful glance toward the bleachers, seeking her approval, she made sure to respond with enthusiastic applause. She spent a long time just watching them, laughing softly to herself as she realized Rio had been right all along: Nicky was a natural. He had a genuine knack for riding, looking as though he had grown up in the saddle. It was yet another irony Agatha would have to accept, but it no longer left a bitter taste. Instead, it brought her deep comfort. It meant that building a new life here also meant building a home where her son finally belonged.

After a while, once Nicky was confidently guiding the mare at a calm trot all on his own, Agatha offered a faint smile as Rio’s gaze finally met hers. Riandra raised an eyebrow and gave a quick hand gesture, silently asking Agatha to wait. She called Yelena over to keep an eye on Nicholas, then started making her way toward the bleachers.

“You’re the only mom hovering out here. You know the other kids will tease him for being a mama’s boy,” Rio teased good-naturedly. She leaned back against the bleacher railing with a raised eyebrow, drawing a eye roll and an exasperated huff from Agatha.

“I’m just worried,” Agatha confessed, offering a helpless shrug beneath Rio’s unexpected tender gaze. “All of this is so new to him, and he usually struggles with change.”

“I think he’s doing amazing,” Rio countered, leaning sideways to keep an eye on Nicholas, who was currently following Yelena’s instructions. “I told you he was a natural. Just look at his posture.” She pointed toward the boy with a trace of pride that brought a smile to Agatha’s face. “Where have you been hiding him all this time, Agatha? It’s a waste keeping a kid like that locked up in the city.”

Agatha pressed her lips together to hide her smile, but her expression softened with deep affection. Hearing Rio speak of him so fondly — so thoroughly enchanted by everything he did — made Agatha swallow hard. She sounds exactly like a proud mother, she realized. She marveled at how effortlessly their lives had entangled once again, sneaking up on her before she even noticed.

She couldn’t tear her eyes away from Rio. It had been years since he had seen her this calm, the familiar, tense crease in her forehead completely smoothed away. Her sun-kissed, caramel skin practically glowed as she watched Nicholas with a quiet contented smile. A sudden ache gripped Agatha’s chest as she pictured what their life could have been — a life filled with these exact tender looks and effortless smiles. The sheer intensity of the affection washing over her left her feeling almost dizzy.

“He loves it here,” Agatha murmured softly, pulling Rio’s serene gaze back to her. They shared a brief, faint smile before looking away.

“You should really find him a place to ride when you go back to California. If he keeps this up, he could be quite the talent on a track,” Rio suggested casually.

Agatha took a slow, discreet breath. She had assumed it was already obvious that they were staying at the farm for good, but clearly, Rio hadn’t caught on.

“I don’t think he’s going to want to leave anytime soon”, Agatha replied with a dismissive shrug, ignoring Rio’s questioning eyebrow. “He’s loving every single minute of this.”

Rio broke into a genuine, bright smile before turning her attention back to the arena.

They settled into a comfortable silence, watching Nicky steadily gain confidence. Under Yelena’s steady stream of praise, he guided the mare with growing ease. Every so often, he would turn around and wave, beaming as both women smiled and cheered on him. The peaceful moment only shattered when Agatha felt her phone buzz — an alarm warning her that she needed to leave immediately to make her appointment.

“Rio, can I ask you a huge favor?” she asked hesitantly.

Rio looked at her with mild curiosity and nodded immediately.

“I have to run out of town to take care of a few things. If I don’t make it back in time, would you mind dropping Nicky off at my mom’s?”

Rio raised a curious eyebrow, but nodded without hesitation.

“Is everything alright? Do you need anything?” Rio asked, carefully masking her concern.

Agatha simply shook her head. “No, it’s just a few things I need to sort out, and I’m not sure how long it’s going to take.”

“Of course. I’ll watch him, no problem.”

A wave of relief washed over Agatha. It was funny how some things never changed. Even after all these years, that unshakable trust she had in Rio — that deep, comforting sense of security — remained completely intact. She knew Rio cared, and that was enough.

“Please, just take good care of him,” Agatha pleaded, her brow furrowing in a way that coaxed a faint smile form Rio. “I mean it, Riandra. He’s… he’s incredibly sensitive.”

“You have my word, Agatha,” Rio replied, her voice calm but resolute. “When you get back, he’ll be safe and sound at your mom’s house.”

“I’m trusting you.”

“You can trust me; I’m great with kids,” Rio murmured with a cocky little shrug, drawing a reluctant smile from Agatha. “Honestly, compared to the chaos of my godchildren, Nicky is a breeze. He’s no trouble at all.”

“That’s because Natasha and Wanda have two. I only have him,” Agatha shot back, earning a quiet laugh from Rio. “He’s all I have.”

“He’ll be perfectly fine, Agatha,” Rio assured her, flashing a lazy, confident smile. “Just look at him.”

She nodded toward Nicholas, who was currently riding with an ear-to-ear grin. Agatha let out a long, slow breath.

“Safe and sound. Without a single hair out of place,” Agatha warned.

Rio chuckled. “You can relax. He’s in very good hands.”

Agatha rolled her eyes, but as she watched them, she knew deep down that it was the absolute truth.

***

The drive took longer than Agatha anticipated; a sedan was hardly built for those rugged dirt roads. Still, she managed the trip in just over an hour, breathing a silent sigh of relief when she pulled into the neighboring town right on time. She definitely needed to buy a truck. The thought brought her a quiet laugh to her lips — she really was starting to put down roots here.

The drive gave her time to reflect on the subtle changes she’d undergone, unconsciously humming along to the country radio station. Since moving to the farm, she had abandoned her hair straightener, and honestly, she didn’t miss it. She loved her hair’s natural volume, letting the frizzy, heavy waves cascade freely down her back. Her wardrobe had shifted, too: she favored loose dresses, breezy fabrics, and comfortable pants, and had even bought a few pair of boots, easily adopting the local uniform of a tank top layered under an unbuttoned shirt.

She had barely noticed the transformation happening, but catching her reflection in the rearview mirror — big hair and sunglasses — she broke into a peaceful smile. Day by day, this new life was winning her over. She felt remarkably lighter without Tessa’s constant, nagging voice critiquing her clothes or demanding a frivolous air of sophistication. She was finally free, as if a massive, suffocating weight had been lifted from her shoulders.

Despite her unfamiliarity with the small town, Agatha navigated it with ease. It was a charming place, reminiscent of Darby a few years prior, though slightly more residential and bustling with local commerce and crops rather than stables. Dr. Jennifer’s office sat nestled between a quaint market and a two-story house with a lush, plant-draped porch. Agatha instantly liked it. It was ironic; she had spent so much of her life dazzled by towering skyscrapers and the chaotic energy of the city, yet here she was, finding profound comfort in the countryside’s natural simplicity. The deep tranquility of the place was seeping into her bones. Maybe Tessa had been right all along — deep down, she really was just a country bumpkin.

The doctor’s office blended seamlessly with the rest of the street, which felt more like a quaint, tree-lined village blanketed in fallen leaves. It looked just like an ordinary little house, set apart only by a discreet sign on its light-colored facade. Framed by low walls and overflowing with greenery, it even featured two small patio tables shaded by umbrellas in the front yard. It was incredibly inviting.

Agatha pushed though the low gate, walked up the grassy path and rang the bell beside the heavy wooden door. She was met by a woman a few years her junior, whose short hair, almond-shaped eyes, and warm expression immediately brought a smile to Agatha’s face.

“Good afternoon,” the woman greeted politely. “How can I help you?”

“My name is Agatha. Agatha Harkness. I have an appointment with Dr. Jennifer.”

“Oh, yes, please come in.” The woman stepped back, opening the door wider. “I’m Alice, the receptionist. I believe Dr. Jennifer is already available to see you, but let me just double-check.”

“Thank you,” Agatha replied. She settled into a plush armchair in the waiting room, taking a moment to appreciate the serene environment.

Painted in soothing shades of ivory and accented with beige, light-wood furniture, the office was a stark contrast to the clinics she had visited in Los Angeles. Those places had been a visual cacophony designed for kids, full of garish colors and scattered toys, their crowded waiting rooms overwhelmed by the constant, echoing chatter of parents and children. Even though they had seen excellent professionals there, Nicky had always completely shut down, overwhelmed by the tumultuous commotion. This space, however, was beautifully calm and quiet. Beyond the comfortable seating, large bookshelves and wall-mounted plants added life to the room. In one corner, a small play area was enclosed by a low fence, featuring tiny white chairs and toys methodically organized on low shelves. Agatha could easily picture Nicky here; for the first time in a long time, she felt certain he would be perfectly comfortable.

“Hello, Agatha. I’m Dr. Jennifer.”

The soft voice gently pulled Agatha from her thoughts. Standing before her was a striking, tall woman with a shaved head and a warm, welcoming smile, dressed in elegant blush-pink jumpsuit beneath her white lab coat. Agatha stood up immediately to greet her.

“Please, follow me,” the doctor said, leading the way to her office.

Agatha offered a faint smile as she stepped inside, relieved to find the consultation room just as peaceful as the reception area. It featured a plush leather sofa, a fluffy rug, and crisp white furniture. The only splashes of color came from a small children’s table, which was neatly arranged with paper, crayons, and a row of quiet toys.

“Thank you for your time,” Agatha said, taking the seat across the desk from Jennifer. “Wanda mentioned your schedule is fully booked, so I’m very grateful you could squeeze us in so last minute.”

“Thank you for trusting me,” Jennifer replied with an empathetic smile. “Based on what you shared about Nicky on the phone, I wanted our first meeting to be just the two of us. For children on the spectrum, predictability is everything. Before bringing him into a new space, I need to understand his sensory profile and how he communicates. If I know his history and interests beforehand, I can adapt this environment to help him feel safe, rather than triggering further withdrawal. The goal is to build a secure bond so he feels comfortable opening up on his on time.”

“I completely understand. We visited a few clinics a while back,” Agatha agreed. She pulled out the thick folder tucked under her arm, which held every piece of medical history she had managed to gather, alongside the extra files Alex had tracked down and emailed over. “He went through some initial evaluations, but we never followed through with the actual treatment.”

She slid the folder across the desk. Jennifer took it, nodding silently as she carefully leafed through the pages.

“I know how critical this is now,” Agatha added softly. “I want to get him the structured care he needs to truly thrive.”

“His school records show an accelerated learning profile for his age, but very low engagement with his peers,” Jennifer noted, her eyes scanning the reports before returning her focus to Agatha. “What does his interaction look like at home?”

Agatha gave a small, vulnerable shrug. “He’s always been a boy of few words. Nicky prefers observing over speaking. But a few years ago, he just… went mute. He started communicating only the bare minimum, mostly pointing or giving simple yes-or-no answers. He entirely stopped engaging in conversation. However, since we moved to the farm, I’ve seen a massive change and improvement. He’s so much more relaxed and far less withdrawn. He’s actually starting to talk and communicate again. He hasn’t had a meltdown in a while, and honestly, it’s been years since I’ve seen him this peaceful.”

“You were living in Los Angeles before, correct?” Jennifer asked, her expression warm but her gaze sharp and analytical. Agatha nodded. “How long ago did you move here?”

“A little over a month, I think.”

“And how did he handle that transition? Did the sudden change in routine cause any negative reactions?”

“Actually, it was quite the opposite,” Agatha replied, a faint, relieved smile touching her lips. “I was terrified that such a drastic move would overwhelm him, but he handled it naturally. He loves playing outside, he’s absolutely obsessed with the horses, and he’s embraced our new daily routine with real enthusiasm. Honestly, life is just so much more peaceful here in every possible way.”

Jennifer folded her hands neatly over the paperwork. “This sudden leap in his behavior and speech likely comes down to sensory accommodation,” she explained. “A neurodivergent brain is heavily impacted by its surroundings. Chaotic spaces with too much sensory input require so much processing power that it often leads to several mental exhaustion. For him, shutting down and isolating simply could be a defense mechanism against chronic overload. While it’s true that autistic children can struggle with change, transitioning to a calm, predictable environment actually acts a reset for the nervous system. His silence wasn’t a refusal to speak, it was a reaction to the overwhelming noise around him. Now, he finally feels safe enough to process the world at his own pace.”

***

Rio bit back a laugh as they rode. Tucked just in front of her, leaning back against her chest, Nicky was sporting a massive pout, letting out a dramatic huff every two minutes. When his equestrian classes had ended and Agatha was nowhere in sight, he’d been thrilled, eagerly asking what fun things they were going to do together. But the moment Rio told him she was taking him home, his excitement had vanished into a deep sulk.

“Why do you have to take me home?” he finally asked, breaking the stubborn silence he had maintained for the entire ride.

Rio glanced down at him, surprised he had actually spoken.

“Because your mom asked me to,” she explained gently, though her tone left little room for argument. “I can’t disobey her. Remember what we talked about? We always have to listen to your mom.”

“But I don’t wanna go home,” he grumbled as Rio brought the horse to a halt in front of Evanora’s house.

Rio dismounted first. She tried her best to keep a straight face, but her resolve melted the second she looked up and saw his furrowed little brow and those giant, pleading and adorable brown eyes. Letting out a soft laugh, she reached up and lifted him down from the saddle.

“Tell you what, let’s make a deal,” she proposed, catching his curious gaze. “We’ll go inside and ask your grandma. If she says it’s okay, you can come with me and help finish my chores around the farm. How does that sound?”

Nicky’s pout instantly transformed into a radiant smile. He nodded eagerly, and Rio couldn’t help but smile back, offering him her hand as they walked up to the front door together.

***

“You mentioned your wife’s reluctance to seek professional care for Nicholas,” Jennifer began. Agatha nodded, gnawing nervously on the inside of her cheek. “Where do things stand now? How did she accept this decision? Was there a specific catalyst with Nicky, or did you two simply reach a compromise?”

Agatha knew this was coming. Tessa was Nicky’s other mother; talking about her was unavoidable. Still, her stomach churned. It didn’t matter the context — her body instinctively tensed at the mere thought of her, and automatic physical reaction she hadn’t quite unlearned.

“We’re getting a divorce,” Agatha said, her voice tight. She fixed her gaze firmly on her lap to avoid the doctor’s attentive eyes as Jennifer glanced between her and the notepad. “I brought Nicky to the farm, and Tessa stayed in Los Angeles. She never entertained the possibility of him being neurodivergent. To her, a diagnosis meant he was somehow lesser, flawed. She flat-out refused to see it, let alone accept it.”

Despite Jennifer’s carefully neutral expression, Agatha caught a slight narrowing of the doctor’s eyes — the quiet look of someone slotting puzzles pieces together.

“Do you have sole custody of Nicky?”

“We’re still sorting that out,” Agatha murmured, shifting uncomfortably. “It wasn’t exactly an amicable split. I had to get out of that house. I needed the marriage to end, and fleeing to the farm was my escape route— it wasn’t some calculated plan. And my wife… my ex-wife,” she corrected, her eyebrows lifting at the unfamiliar weight of the word, “refuses to accept the separation. It’s a mess. We’re going to have to resolve it in court because she simply won’t agree to anything. That’s the reality.”

Jennifer nodded empathetically, allowing a heavy, quiet pause to settle over the room before pressing on.

“You called it an escape— a necessary, abrupt break. What exactly led to that point? What was the dynamic like between the two of you?”

Agatha took a deep, shaky breath, closing her eyes for a moment. When she opened them, Jennifer’s steady, judgment-free gaze coaxed her defenses down just a fraction. Staring down at her own tightly intertwined hands, she finally spoke.

“My marriage was unpredictable. In the most damaging way possible.” She let out a weary sigh, her lips curving into a bitter, humorless smile. “It took me years to realize how narcissistic she was, how methodically she was hollowing me out. Tessa is relentless, but she hides her iron will behind a careful voice of sweetness and concern. She made me feel like I was losing my mind. I’d be absolutely certain of a fact, and she would subtly twist things until I genuinely believed I was the one at fault.” Agatha let out a quiet, hollow laugh, her shoulders sagging under the weight of the memories. “We fought constantly. She yelled constantly. I spent my life on high alert, feeling cornered in my own home, until it became unbearable.”

“And these fights…” Jennifer began, weighing her words carefully. “Did they ever turn violent?”

Agatha drew a shaky breath, her brow furrowing with quiet anguish. “Sometimes,” she whispered, shrinking back into her chair.

“Did Nicky ever witness these conflicts? Where did he fit into this dynamic?”

“He wasn’t around for most of it, but unfortunately, he still saw things,” Agatha confessed, the weight of her own guilt heavy in her voice. “Tessa was obsessed with appearances, so our worst moments were usually kept strictly behind closed doors. But there were times he was home, and she saw and heard things no child ever should.

“Was she ever violent with him?”

Agatha pressed her lips into a tight line. She had to be honest, no matter how much it burned to admit it out loud.

“She never hit him. She wasn’t physically aggressive on a daily basis, but… she crossed the line.” Unable to watch the doctor take notes, Agatha turned her gaze to the window. “She yelled at him and…” She swallowed the lump in her throat. “She shook him once. She drank heavily at home, and when she did, she became completely unpredictable. I never knew what would set her off. She was only ever abusive toward him when she was drunk. Sober, she never let the mask slip; she played the role of the perfect, loving mother.”

“Aside from those episodes, what was her bond with him actually like? How did her relationship with him differ from yours?”

“Tessa was largely absent. During the pregnancy, she was incredibly attentive— she wanted a child so badly— and when he was a baby, she was very sweet. But the moment he started exhibiting behaviors that pointed toward autism, she grew cold. She was rarely home, and when she was, she barely engaged. It was always just the two of us.” Agatha let out a heavy sigh, resting her cheek against her hand. “I had a high-risk pregnancy and gave up my career to focus entirely on him. From the day he was born, I’ve been there for every single moment. I learned how to read his cues. I knew exactly when a meltdown was building and how to de-escalate it. Because I was his constant, he always turned to me.”

“So, he has a secure attachment bond with you. You are his emotional regulator,” Jennifer clarified, waiting for Agatha to nod before continuing. “And how does he react to Tessa?”

“Nicky is generally very withdrawn,” Agatha mused, her frown deepening. “He’s closed off, highly observant, and incredibly selective about who he trusts. Because Tessa was so absent, he naturally built a wall against her. He doesn’t actively reject her, but his reaction is… cold. Indifferent, I suppose.” She paused, reflection on her own words. “He rarely interacts with her and shows very little affection. In fact, since we moved here, he’s only mentioned her once— and that was only because I brought her up.”

“Agatha, while I certainly need to meet Nicky to fully understand his triggers, this history suggests we need to look beyond his sensory perception,” Jennifer explained gently. “His withdrawal and selective mutism might actually be a direct response to the chronic stress within your family environment.”

The words hit Agatha like a punch to the gut. The crushing realization that her desperate attempts to protect her son hadn’t been enough tore at her.

“Children are like sponges,” Jennifer continued. “They absorb the tension at home, especially the instability and loss of control of the adults around them long before they have the neurological maturity to process it. From what you’ve shared, Nicholas is highly sensitive to his surroundings. Living in a unpredictable home, witnessing explosive and even violent episodes directed at you, his absolute safe haven, forces his brain into a constant state of high alert. His mutism may simply be the shield he built to protect himself. It also perfectly explains the recent improvements you’ve seen. Now that the toxic tension is gone, he can finally breathe.”

Agatha nodded slowly, tears welling her eyes as the heavy truth of the doctor’s words settled over her.

“You mentioned he is quite selective about who he interacts with,” Jennifer said, carefully shifting the focus. “Besides you, how does he engage with the rest of his family and social circle?”

“He’s quiet, but incredibly observant. And despite being so withdrawn, he really is an affectionate boy,” Agatha explained, picturing her son. “He loves to be held. He’s perfectly happy just sitting in the presence of people he trusts, even in total silence. He adores his godparents, and a close friend who lives with us. And since coming to the farm, he connected almost instantly with…”

Agatha hesitated, struggling to find the right words to define Rio. Even now, she wasn’t entirely sure what they were to each other.

“… with Rio, my childhood best friend. She’s the daughter of my late godfather, who was essentially Nicky’s grandfather. Nicky grew up hearing stories about Rio and always admired her from afar, so he was thrilled to finally meet her. He still doesn’t speak much, but he’s definitely more verbal now, and his body language has completely shifted. He just seems so relaxed here. He’s also very fond of Tessa’s family, especially her mother.”

“And how is your relationship with your ex-in-laws?”

“It’s wonderful, actually,” she answered without hesitation. “They welcomed me with open arms from day one. Honestly, I have no idea where Tessa gets her temper, because her family is incredibly warm. Her father has always been a pillar of support for me, encouraging me both personally and professionally, and her mother is an absolute sweetheart.”

“That paints a very interesting picture,” Jennifer noted, jotting down a few quick lines before folding her hands over her notebook. “Based on what you’re telling me, Nicky doesn’t suffer from a social aversion at all. He just has a highly tuned radar for safety. You are his emotional anchor. If he spent years watching you withdraw, walk on eggshells, and shrink away from conflicts with your ex-wife, he likely internalized those same threats. Conversely, the people he opens up to are essentially extensions of your own support system. Neurodivergent children don’t need to see screaming matches to know an environment is hostile. They read your body language, the subtle shifts in your breathing, the tension in your face. If you feel safe here, in this new life, it makes perfect sense that he intuitively knows it’s safe to let his guard down, too.”

***

Normally, by this time of day, Rio would have already retreated to a quiet corner with a case of beer, sinking into her own thoughts. She relied on that late-afternoon solitude to clear her head and process the day. As much as she loved the farm and her work, the mental exhaustion often caught up with her. Because she wasn’t the type to talk about her feelings, she simply swallowed them down. As a result, drinking had quietly slipped back into her routine — a way to numb the noise and escape the heavy weight of her own mind. Honestly, it was taking every ounce of her willpower right now not to reach for a drink.

Yet, today was different. She felt strangely at ease with Nicholas trailing her like a little shadow. He skipped along beside her, hanging on her every word and movement. His boundless excitement was contagious as he leaned over the wooden corral fences, begging to pet the animals and asking a million questions about every creature they passed. Dusk was usually Rio’s sacred time for chores — a quiet, solitary ritual just for herself. But instead of intruding on her peace, the boy’s presence bought a comforting, warm new light to her evening routine.

They eventually made their way to the stables, which were undoubtedly his favorite part of the farm. Armed with those wide, adorable eyes, Nicky wanted to know everything. Rio could barely take a single step without him firing off another question: What were their names? What were their personalities like? How fast could they run?

His enchantment was written all over his face. Seeing the raw passion in his eyes filled Rio’s chest with a comforting warmth; he reminded her so much of herself at that age. Watching how naturally he rooted himself into the life of the farm, it was almost painful to imagine him cooped up in a city apartment all his life.

“Come here, I want to show you something,” Rio called out softly, raising an eyebrow with a conspiratorial smile as she unlatched the gate to one of the stalls.

At her excited tone, Nicky beamed. He stepped inside with careful, measured steps, his eyes widening at the sight of a mare resting heavily in the hay. The animal was breathing in slow, deep rhythms, her eyes closed and her belly visibly swollen.

“This is Daisy. She’s pregnant,” Rio explained. She sat down in the hay beside the mare and gave Nicky a gentle nod to do the same. He sat immediately, without a second thought.

“She’s pregnant,” he whispered in a hushed, reverent tone. Settling in just as carefully as Rio had shown him, he reached out. Rio had to press her lips together to keep from ginning at the sheer wonder shining in his brown eyes, watching the delicate, feather-light way he stroked the mare’s bulging stomach. “How many babies is she going to have?”

Rio let out a soft, genuine laugh at the pure sweetness of the question.

“Just one,” she answered softly, holding his undivided attention as he kept right on petting the mare. “Mares usually only have a single foal because they’re born pretty big. They come out of the belly already this size.” She gestured with her hands to show the scale, and his lips parted in pure amazement.

“Is it a boy or a girl?” he asked, never taking his eyes of Daisy. Rio let out a quiet breath, gently tucking a few stray curls back behind his ears as they slipped loose from his headband.

“It’s a little filly,” she said, joining him in stroking the mare’s coat. She smiled softly when Daisy let out a long, contented sigh, leaning into the affection. “Sometimes we sell them since we already have so many horses, but we’re keeping this one. Daisy is practically family, we’d never separate her from her babies.”

“Do you think she’ll be caramel-colored too?” Nicky asked, his voice bubbling with excitement. Rio gave a slight shake of her head.

“Hard to say… Her dad is white, so she’ll probably be light-colored, too.”

“When is she going to be born?” he pressed eagerly.

“Probably in a week or two, right around the change of the moon.”

“Can I see? Can I be here when she’s born?” he asked, flashing those irresistibly big, earnest eyes. Rio broke into a warm smile. He was so impossibly sweet it made her chest ache; a sudden, heavy pang hit her at the mere thought of how much she would miss him once he left the farm.

“Well, we’d have to ask your mom first. If you guys are still around and she says yes, then probably, yeah,” Rio said with a casual shrug.

Nicky immediately shook his head. “Why wouldn't we be here?”

Rio frowned, her brows knitting together as she looked up at him in confusion. “Aren’t you guys heading back home eventually?” she managed a faint laugh, desperately trying to mask the icy chill that spiked down her spine at the thought of saying goodbye to the little tyke who had captured her heart so quickly.

“No,” he replied with a careless shrug, sending a jolt of anxiety straight to Rio’s stomach. “Mom likes it here. She said we’re going to live here now.”

“Your mom said you’re going to live here?” Rio swallowed hard, fighting to keep her eyes from widening and ignoring the sudden sweat slicking her palms. Bitting the inside of her cheek, she was torn between a sharp wave of fear and a sudden, dizzying spark of hope as a whirlwind of emotions threatened to swallow her whole.

Nicholas just gave a simple nod, his sweet gaze drifting back to the mare.

“I like it here. Mom does too,” he said offhandedly, giving a small shake of his head. Rio watched him closely, her eyes narrowing slightly as he suddenly glanced back at her with a fleeting look of apprehension, his shoulders shrinking inward. “She doesn’t feel scared here.”

“Scared?” Rio echoed, her voice dropping as a tight knot formed in her chest.

Nicky, however, immediately looked away, pressing his lips into a firm line. She knew better than to push. She wasn’t about to interrogate him if he didn’t want to talk; she saw far too much of herself in the boy to make that mistake. Pressing too hard wouldn’t get her anywhere — it would only make him retreat into his shell. Even so, the sharp ache blooming in her chest was almost too heavy to ignore.

“Nicky…” she murmured gently, watching his brow furrow as he turned back to her. “Do you feel scared, too?”

Nicholas simply cast his gaze down. “I like it here,” he repeated in a quiet voice, and Rio nodded slowly.

Though she couldn’t fully put her finger on it, a sudden, fierce flared in her chest upon hearing those words — a quiet confession that they both carried a shared, hidden fear. It made something wild rise up inside Rio, igniting a raw, protective fury. Deep in her soul, she knew she would never let anything bad happen to them; she would guard them tooth and nail. Nicky was so small, yet blindingly sensitive and perceptive. Rio had already suspected Agatha might be staying for good, give she’s been at the farm for over a month now, but she had forced herself to ignore the thought to keep her hopes from getting the better of her. She hadn’t wanted to anchor her heart to the possibility of Agatha’s return, and she certainly hadn’t planned on getting attached to the boy. She had only wanted to dodge the crushing weight of another goodbye. But now, wondering what could have sparked that kind of fear in him, a solid, unshakeable certainty settled deep within her: she would do whatever it took to keep them safe, no matter the cost.

“Listen to me,” Rio said softly, catching one of Nicky’s small hands as he lifted his gaze to meet hers. “I don’t know what you’re afraid of, and you don’t ever have to tell me if you don’t want to, no matter what it is. But if you’re ever scared again, you can call me. Anytime. I’ll chase all your fears away until they’re gone.” She whispered the words like a sacred secret, before suddenly diving in to poke at his ribs with a playful tickle attack. The boy burst into a string of bright, bubbling giggles that melted straight through her heart.

***

“I don’t know how much research you’ve done or if you brought this up with other specialists, but autism has an 80 to 90 percent genetic factor,” Jennifer explained, folding her hands. “It’s not an absolute rule, of course, but having a mapped-out family history helps us understand a child’s profile and tailor their environment much more easily. Knowing the family’s behavioral phenotype makes managing the case straightforward. Do you or your ex-wife have any history of a diagnosis in the family?”

Agatha shook her head immediately.

“We tried several times during pregnancy process using Tessa’s eggs, but when I conceived Nicky, we used only mine. He has no genetic ties to her,” Agatha clarified, prompting an understanding nod from Jennifer. “Once I started spotting the first signs in him, I read up on the genetic predisposition and looked into my own family. Both my mother and I underwent neuropsychological evaluations, but nothing came up. We don’t know any cases.”

“What about the donor’s history?” Jennifer asked.

Agatha cleared her throat, pressing her lips together.

“I know Nicky’s donor,” she said. Jennifer simply nodded, entirely unfazed. “He’s someone I… know well.”

“Is he active in Nicky’s life?” Jennifer asked pointedly, pen poised over her notepad.

“Yes, he is,” Agatha nodded. “Though not as a father— that boundary we discussed and established very clearly, and he respects it completely. He’s entirely comfortable with the role he plays in Nicky’s life, and we’ve reached a healthy understanding.” Jennifer gave another affirming nod, leaving space for her to continue. “He underwent a neuropsychological evaluation as well, but showed no traits on the spectrum and has no knowledge of any cases in his family.”

“Our understanding of the spectrum has evolved quite a bit,” Jennifer noted, resting her hands over her notes. “Until a few years ago, there was a lot of ignorance surrounding it, and many neurodivergent individuals were neglected or labelled as difficult, problematic, or simply strong-willed. To the untrained eye, autism symptoms were routinely mistaken for mere personality quirks. It’s entirely possible there’s family history you aren’t aware of simply because nobody back then knew what signs to look for.”

“I don’t know, doctor,” Agatha said, shaking her head. “I picked up on Nicky’s signs right away, during his earliest developmental milestones. If there were anyone like that in the family, I’d like to think I would have noticed.”

“It’s different, Agatha,” Jennifer countered gently. “You’re his mother. You tracked every single stage of his development and gave him undivided attention from birth. Naturally, your radar is much sharper. But an adult in the family could easily have spent their entire life flying under the radar precisely because of that historical lack of awareness.”

“An undiagnosed adult? Wouldn’t that be obvious?” Agatha asked, genuinely puzzled.

“Autism presents differently at every stage of life. It’s a vast spectrum shaped by the environment, social and family dynamics, and how an individual processes their surroundings. As I mentioned, many traits get heavily masked. A child who is just written off as quiet, aloof, a bit averse to physical touch, resistant to changes in routine, and prone to emotional outbursts… all of that is frequently swept under the rug as just another difficult developmental phase.”

Agatha froze, her brow furrowing as she tilted her head. A child who was just considered quieter, more closed off, with a certain aversion to physical contact, who didn’t handle changes in routine very well, and had outbursts of emotional instability. The description hit her like a lightning bolt, widening her eyes as her thoughts raced.

“To survive everyday demands while those signs slip through the cracks, people learn to mask,” Jennifer continued. “I treat plenty of patients who aren’t diagnosed until adulthood, and most of them share the exact same exhaustion profile: muted sensory sensitivities, social hurdles, and a rigid mental inflexibility that often gets mistaken for selfishness.” Agatha’s eyes remained wide, her heart hammering against her ribs as she desperately tried to assemble a puzzle that had been sitting right in front of her face her entire life. “The later the diagnosis comes, the harder the obstacles. Individuals spend decades forcing themselves into compensatory behaviors just to fit in. Often, the sensory and emotional burnout is so overwhelming it drives them toward chemical coping mechanisms, like alcoholism, just to numb their minds and force a release. That spirals into all sorts of self-destructive patterns. Of course, because the spectrum is so wild, it often overlaps with co-occurring conditions like dyscalculia, ADHD, or untreated severe dyslexia. Fortunately, you’ve educated yourself well, and we’re looking at a very bright path for Nicholas. Because he’s still growing, we have a wonderful opportunity to build a solid foundation for his emotional regulation right now.”

Despite keeping up her posture and staring straight ahead, Agatha felt entirely paralyzed. Sirens were blaring deafeningly inside her head.

***

As twilight settled, Rio and Nicky still lingered side by side on the fluffy living room rug, completely at ease in each other’s company. By now, Lilia would normally be finishing up dinner, and Rio would have already slipped away to Pedra Purpura or gone looking for Bucky to bet on a race, maybe call Olivia. Instead, she had decided to stay in. Agatha hadn’t arrived yet, and Rio was genuinely enjoying the boy’s quiet presence.

Propped on their stomachs, each focused on their own sheet of paper, they shared Nicky’s colored pencils and sketchbooks. Inspired to create a comprehensive farm-animal manual detailing daily routines and care requirements, Nicky wanted to master the chores quickly so he could always help her out.

Amused by his ambition, Rio fell into a cozy silence with him. They rarely need to speak, trading occasional amused glances as they concentrated on their drawings.

“Look,” Nicky said, sliding his paper toward her.

Resting on her elbows, Rio raised her eyebrows and smiled softly at the simply sketch of a horse eating hay in its stall. Noticing some writing in the corner, she squinted slightly — battling her familiar jumbling of letters — and tilted her head, pointing to the sentence.

“What did you write here?” she asked, frowning.

Nicky crawled across the rug until he was right beside her, pressing his index finger to the words. “Horses eat hay in the morning and in the afternoon,” he read aloud.

Nodding in understanding, Rio flipped her own notebook around. “Look, I drew the little pigs.”

Nicky laughed, immediately reaching for a fresh sheet to start the next page.

Upstairs, leaning over the hallway railing with a clear view of the living room, Benito and Kate had been watching them for minutes, exchanging knowing looks. Lost in their own bubble, Rio and Nicholas were entirely unaware they were being observed.

“It’s almost disconcerting,” Kate murmured, shaking her head. “Even the way they hold their pencils is identical, the same expression of concentration, the way they move their feet. They look like each other’s shadows, the same person split into two bodies.”

“I always thought they looked alike,” Benito replied, blowing a quiet breath toward the pair. “I mean, she’s my sister and we look alike, so it makes sense. But this? They have the exact same mannerisms to a tee.”

Kate raised her eyebrows with a soft laugh. “Honestly, Agatha is the president of Pity City. Imagine having a kid who is the absolute spitting image of your ex. She really hasn’t had a single day of peace.”

“I’ve known Agatha my entire life, and I still don’t know how she deals with it,” Benito admitted, tilting his head thoughtfully. “You know her too… and I know it’s heavy to say, but I don’t think she’s entirely gotten over it. It’s still so intense and present, even across the distance.”

“I don’t know,” Kate pondered. “I don’t think it’s just about getting over it. I believe she’s moved on, but the roots go much deeper. Beyond their complicated relationship, there’s a lifetime of shared history that leaves a mark.”

They fell silent for a moment. Benito smiled as Nicky pointed to one of Rio’s drawings, both of them bursting into laughter. It was almost eerie how seamlessly they clicked, cocooned in a natural peace as if they had known each other forever.

He had never seen Nicholas so open, expressive, and relaxed — a total transformation from the withdrawn boy of a few months ago. Seeing this softer, attentive side of Rio filled him with a comforting warmth; he knew the sweet sister of his childhood was still in there, beneath the armor she had built over the years.

“How is it even possible?” Benito murmured, catching Kate’s eye. “It’s like they’ve known each other their whole lives.”

“I hardly recognize him when he’s this calm,” she agreed with a smile. “And your sister is completely different form where we first arrived.”

“It’s beautiful to watch everything fall into place. Something in me always knew we needed to end up together like this,” Benito said, learning further over the railing with an affectionate look. “They’re good for each other. But I can’t help wondering…” He took a deep breath. “How do you think she’s going to reach when she finds out?”

Kate sighed and shook her head.

“I don’t know, Benny…”

“What is going to be worse: Nicky or our marriage?” he asked with a suggestive grin.

Kate pressed her lips together to hold back a laugh and bumped him lightly with her shoulder. “Honestly, I’d rather not even think about it. But you’ll have to talk to her sooner or later, especially now that she’s wrapped up not just in your return, but in Nicky’s life, too. You and Agatha need to tell her yourselves; if she finds out on her own, it’s going to blow up. You know the kind of sister you have.”

“There’s no use running away from it, Kate. You’re going to be right in the middle of this conversation, too,” Benito pointed out.

She rolled her eyes and let out a soft groan. “When the bombs drop, I suppose we’ll all be here to hold down the fort,” she conceded. Then, softening, he added, “But at the end of the day, everything is going to be fine. I just know it… I can feel it.”

“Oh, here comes the psychic,” she murmured, laughing as he nudged her right back.

***

The drive back to Darby was shrouded in darkness. Agatha had spent the entire day at Dr. Jennifer’s office, and a profound sense of relief washed over her. After reviewing all of Nicholas’s medical records and evaluations, the neuropsychologist had offered an encouraging path forward, assuring her they had the right roadmap to meet his needs. For years, Agatha had felt paralyzed and helpless, constantly second-guessing herself as she watched her son struggle. Now, seeing a light at the end of the tunnel brought a rare, steady peace. Ever since he was a baby, she had witnessed the quiet agony he endured daily — from the smallest shifts in routine to a deep-seated social aversion and isolation.

Even with this newfound calm, knowing a long journey lay ahead in their new life, guilt gnawed at her. She had tried to desperately to shield Nicholas from the endless tension and fights, wanting him to know only the love of two moms — even if those mothers had grown cold and distant. Blinded by her own despair at rock-bottom, she had never imagined the toxic environment was pulling him inward, breaking him piece by piece.

She knew tormenting herself with past regrets was pointless; she couldn’t turn back the clock or walk away any sooner. Still, her chest tightened at the painful realization that she hadn’t been the only casualty. Nicholas had suffered right alongside her. Building a new life here wasn’t just about her own survival — it was about giving him the safe harbor and true home he deserved.

The impending legal batter with Tessa wouldn’t be easy. Agatha knew her ex-wife all too well; when Tessa was crossed and denied what she wanted, she became relentless. But Agatha was arming herself now, ready to fight tooth and nail for their future and their home. Tessa hadn’t just broken her; she had broken Nicholas, too. And while both of them, as his mothers, bore responsibility for the domestic chaos that trapped him, Agatha knew she hadn’t built that prison. She had been a prisoner right beside him, with Tessa turning the key.

Yet, the blaring sirens in Agatha’s mind weren’t just about Nicky — they were about Rio. Too many things had been happening right under her nose, entirely unnoticed until it was too late.

When Jennifer started talking about the genetic links of the spectrum, Agatha hadn’t considered any possibility of it applying to them. Despite her own evaluations and discussions with her mother and Benito, they simply didn’t have a roadmap for this. None of them had ever exhibited anything similar throughout their lives; it was completely uncharted history.

All Agatha had focused on was learning how to best support her son — helping him build confidence, emerge from his shell, and slowly feel comfortable sharing his feelings. She needed to learn from scratch how to navigate his meltdowns and difficult moments, and she was more than willing to do whatever it took. To her, Nicholas was entirely unique. But now, she realized she had missed a glaring part of her own family’s history, just as Benito had. Neither of them had recognized what was suddenly staring her in the face.

Nicholas had so much of Rio in him. It was something Agatha had grappled with since the day he was born — form his deep, dark eyes and dark hair to his long fingers and sweet smile. During her postpartum depression, she could barely look at her son. As she cared for him, she wept, feeling shackled to the past she had left behind and the choices that had dragged her into an unhappy life. In every developmental milestone, she saw Rio in him, from his expressive face to his few spoken words.

Over time, however, she had learned to cherish it. She came to feel blessed, finding in him not only the greatest love of her life, but the quiet comfort of someone she had loved forever. He was a piece of her, but in a way that defied explanation, he felt like a piece of Rio, too.

For years, guilt toward Tessa had lingered in the background, but the truth was that it had all been a strange twist of fate. She hadn’t known the donor when they chose it, she hadn’t hand-picked him. Yet beneath the guilt, she felt she had been handed a gift from the universe. Even though Nicholas was legally Tessa’s son as well, he was Agatha’s piece of the world — a living reflection of a life she had loved, even when she was still too young to understand how deeply.

Then, as Jennifer spoke, Agatha had begun to connect the dots.

Rio had always been so difficult. Growing up, the only people she spoke to were Agatha, her father, and her mother. It had taken her a long time to fit in at school, and even then, she had only ever made two friends — neither of whom were particularly outgoing. Rio was quiet, observant, and distant. For the longest time, Agatha had taken that as proof they were meant to be; she possessed a side of Rio that no one ever saw, anchored by the belief that Rio was her person, and she was Rio’s.

But there was so much more.

Rio’s fixed gaze, her tranquil silence, the way she struggled to comprehend why others saw the world so differently. The Rio who understood reality only through what was right in front of her eyes. The Rio who loathed school, constantly hiding behind excuses to dodge homework, yet sat with Agatha every day without ever opening a notebook.

The Rio who, every early on, had turned to alcohol just to quiet her nerves enough to fit in and talk to people. Rio, who bottled up her emotions until she imploded, who hated feeling vulnerable, who fled from confrontation and was never good with words. The Rio who felt everything so intensely yet couldn’t let a single drop it out, possessing zero knack for processing emotions — finding the only oxygen she had left, far away from everyone else, on the back of a horse.

The Rio who resisted any possibility of change so fiercely that she would withdraw and push away anyone who didn’t fit her rigid view of right and wrong. Who always gravitated toward the exact same things and never shifted. Rio and her silence, her animals, her unyielding routine from the moment she woke up until she went to sleep — doing the same things every day, wearing the same clothes, and dreading any distance from home, her only safe have. The Rio who viewed the world through a single, unbending lens and panicked whenever anyone tried to show her another way.

The Rio who loved her so deeply, yet could never manage to change, suffering immensely for it — spending years promising she wanted to be different, to act differently, but simply unable to bridge the gap.

Rio… The person everyone dismissed as difficult and selfish, a label Agatha herself had applied for years. But now, her chest tightened as a heartbreaking realization settled over her: all this time, Rio hadn’t been difficult. She had just been deeply, profoundly and completely misunderstood.

***

Two Years Ago

For a while now, Agatha had desperately needed to clear her head — to step outside and breath in a space that didn’t feel suffocating. Normally, her routine was a bitter monotony, amplified whenever her wife was home. Her world was anchored by Nicholas, her boy who was growing up too fast, filling her days with quiet laughter and countless silent discoveries that shone through his expressive eyes. She cherished those moments with him, even the grueling ones where she felt completely unequipped. Agatha was simply exhausted. That was why, on the days Tessa vanished without a word, she couldn’t help but feel a rush of relief.

No arguments. No forced smiles to preserve the illusion of a happy family. No cold, going-through-the-motion sex with Tessa reeking of alcohol.

Maybe it was wrong, but sometimes she welcomed her absence. As much as it hurt — knowing her wife was out there with other women — it was easier this way, a reality she had simply learned to accept. Of course she missed what they used to have: the feeling of being desired, the affection, the attention. She missed the woman she had once loved. But this was her life now, and there was nothing left to do. She had chosen this path; she had chosen Tessa.

It was already late, and heading home just in case her wife materialized seemed like the right thing to do. Yet, sprawled comfortably on the couch in Alex’s spacious living room while they worked through a second bottle of wine, Agatha felt an unusual lightness. In the corner, Nicholas was fast asleep in his rocking chair, dead to the world. It was precisely in these quiet, serene moments that she found herself truly observing him, tracing his features and feeling that familiar, bittersweet squeeze in her chest.

“Have you noticed how much he looks like her?” Agatha murmured softly, her gaze lingering on her son with a sweet, nostalgic ache. “The older he gets, the more undeniable it is. You just can’t unsee it.”

Alex let out a light laugh, peering over the rim of her wine glass with an amused smile. “Like who? Tessa? Are you blind? How on earth is that possible?”

Agatha merely turned to her with a pointed look, making her best friend sigh.

“I know,” Alex said, her expression turning serious and understanding. “It’s hard not to notice. Honestly, I have no idea how your hellish Barbie of a wife never caught on.”

“She saw Rio what, three times in her life?” Agatha retorted dismissively, rolling her eyes. “And it’s not like she doesn’t know the general traits we selected for the donor. It makes sense, I suppose.”

“Remember when Javier showed us that picture of Benito as a kid?” Alex called, causing Agatha to choke on her wine with a laugh. “Come on, Agatha, everyone noticed.”

“She just thought it was cute when people said Nicky had the exact same little dark berry eyes.”

“Yeah, the dark berry eyes of the entire Vidal family.”

“The brown eyes of the donor we chose, Alex,” Agatha pointed out with a warning look, though her friend could clearly see the humor behind it. “It’s basic genetics.”

“And how could it not be, considering you practically scoured that sperm bank looking for someone with your ex’s exact physical blueprint?”

“I did not!” Agatha countered instantly, pointing her wine glass at her friend. “At least… not consciously.”

Alex raised her eyebrows, prompting Agatha to let out a defeated sigh and take another sip of her drink.

“Oh, come on, Alex! It was our trillionth attempt. We tried every donor imaginable, and the first batches all had her exact traits: blonde hair, blue eyes, her brothers’ average height… We ran through every single type! It’s not my fault if, out of thousands of profiles in that bank, destiny decided to play this cosmic joke on me.”

“You definitely gravitated toward certain traits…”

“Alex!” Agatha reprimanded with an exasperated look.

“I know it was hard,” Alex said, dropping her laughter and looking at her with quiet understanding.

Agatha knit her eyebrows together and nodded. It had been hard — impossibly hard.

“Still, at least now we have this little masterpiece over there,” Alex added, nodding toward Nicholas, who was still fast asleep.

“Yeah, this perfect little masterpiece. My angel,” Agatha said softly, a tender smile touching her lips as she looked at her son. “My little boy… who happens to be the spitting image of Rio Vidal. Good grief, I am never going to escape her, am I?”

Alex chuckled, but her expression soon softened into deep, compassionate affection.

“Does it hurt you?” she asked gently, her brow furrowing. “The fact that he looks so much like her?”

Agatha shook her head, offering a faint, melancholic smile.

“Honestly? It brings me comfort,” she confessed, taking a deep breath. “He’s a piece of my, carrying a little piece of the things I love most in this world. He was made for me, from scratch. He is all mine.”

“You know, Agatha…” Alex began in a tone dripping with condescension. Agatha turned to her, her eyebrows already shooting up. “Divorce is just a piece of paper; you can print it, sign it, and have it stamped at the registry office.”

“I am not getting a divorce, Alex,” she replied with a heavy sigh, taking long sips from her glass under her best friend’s unimpressed gaze. “I am perfectly happy with my life.”

“Where is this perfectly happy woman, because I haven’t seen her in ages?” Alex rolled her head in sheer exasperation.

Agatha lowered her eyes, letting out a sorrowful breath. “Agatha, this was the first time in days I’ve seen you crack a genuine smile. Why do you refuse to admit it? Everyone who knows you can see it. You’ve been slowly dying in this marriage for years.”

“Alex…” Agatha murmured in a warning tone.

“I see how she treats you the moment her mask slips in front of us. I know she cuts you down and belittles you. And heaven knows what she does behind closed doors, because I know you don’t tell me everything. It breaks my heart to see you like this, Agatha. I just want you to wake up, because life is so much more than this. You deserve so much more.”

“We reap what we sow, Alex.”

“You are not responsible for this! Nobody chooses misery. Sometimes life takes turns we never wanted, and that’s okay— we move on. I just don’t understand why you stay trapped in this hole. I swear, I would do anything to pull you out. I’m right here by your side, always, but you won’t let me. You won’t let anyone save you."

“Alex, I love my wife,” Agatha declared firmly, watching her friend sigh. It was a mantra she repeated to herself every single day, because the truth is too awful.

“Agatha...” Alex murmured after a long, heavy exhale. “I don’t know what else to do. I don’t know how to help you if you won’t talk to me, if you won’t truly open up. Talk to me, Agatha. I’m right here.”

“I don’t want to talk about it,” Agatha cut her off, looking away and taking a deep breath.

“Fine. Have it your way,” Alex yielded, deflating in a defeat as she realized she had lost the battle yet again. She shook her head and reached back to refill her glass. “Let’s talk about your son instead, the one who, rather than looking like the Barbie you married, is the absolute spitting image of the ex-love your life.”

Agatha shook her head, letting a small, weary breath.

“They’re so alike…” she murmured, her gaze turning reflective. “Do you think… how do you think she’d react if she knew?”

Alex held back a nervous smile and took a slow sip of her wine. “You know how temperamental your country girl is… I honestly don’t know. But does she really need to know? Why would you even—” She interrupted herself, frowning in genuine confusion. “Tessa doesn’t know.”

“And for the sake of humanity and my own mental health, it’s best she never finds out,” Agatha retorted, widening her eyes theatrically.

Alex shook her head. “Then why would you ever tell Rio? What good would that possibly do after everything?”

“I don’t know…” Agatha admitted, her expression crumbling into sadness. “Sometimes I write to her, you know? I send letters like the old times… I actually never stopped writing.” She confesses the truth with a melancholic look.

At that, Alex’s expression softened entirely. She reached out, gently squeezing Agatha’s hand to comfort her. “Why, Agatha?”

“I don’t know…” she repeated with a helpless shrug. “She never answered me, not even when we were still…” She caught herself, letting out a shaky sigh. “I doubt she even reads them. But still… Sometimes I just want to talk to her. Tell her about things, about life, about Nicky… Things I think she’d want to know. I don’t ask for anything back; I know she won’t reply. I just… I just write.”

“Oh, Agatha…” Alex murmured, her voice thick with sorrow. She shook her head and scooted closer on the couch.

Agatha finally let her defenses crumble, melting into her best friend’s arms and letting out a long, shuddering sigh as she buried herself in the embrace.

“There will always be a space for you and me, right where you left and just maybe, enough time will pass we’ll look back and laugh” – Always, Daniel Caesar

***

It is hard to see life clearly when we spend years cloistered away. Languishing in the dark of a cocoon, we forget that existence stretches far beyond our immediate sight; we lose the perspective of its immensity and our own smallness. Yet, it is equally true that we sometimes shrink ourselves so drastically that the sheer vastness of the world feels terrifying rather than liberating.

Agatha had spent a long time lost in her own labyrinth, bound by a straitjacket of her own making. For years, she clung to such an abstract, idealized vision of the future that when she finally tried to live it, she found herself on a narrow, dead-end road. Believing that real life was always waiting at some unreachable point in the horizon, she obsessively chased tomorrow. In doing so, she pruned away her true self, shrinking her horizons to fit a path that existed only in her mind.

But life happens in the present. It is an ocean of unpredictable unimaginable waves that routinely defy our best-laid plans. Dreams that once meant everything can suddenly reveal themselves as insignificant. Agatha had spent so much time staring at a distant, fabricated ideal that she entirely missed the ground beneath her own feet.

As bitter as it is to admit, staying small is often easier than braving the world again — which is exactly why she had remained stagnant. Agatha felt so battered by her past choices and haunted by her old paths that the mere thought of breaking free paralyzed her. It was kind of Stockholm syndrome: imprisoned for so long, the crushing weight of potential freedom terrified her. She dreaded the possibility of taking a risk, only to find herself trapped in another dead end.

Deep down, she had long been aware of reality, but rationalizing is always easier than taking action. She hadn’t actually planned to drop everything, despite desiring it for years. The break came purely on impulse. The sudden news of her godfather’s death was a brutal wake-up call, a stab to the heart that proved time is fleeting, no matter how endless the days may feel. Losing Javier made her realize she didn’t have forever; she needed to start living while she still could. She simply couldn’t stay in that stagnant place any longer.

Grief washes over us in waves, and Agatha’s grief wasn’t just for Javier; she was mourning herself. It wasn’t until she packed her entire life into a car that the reality truly dawned on her: somewhere along the way, she had lost her own identity. She arrived at the farm completely shattered, honestly believing she might never heal.

But that is the poetry of freedom — it doesn’t strike all at once; it unfolds in verses. Like a poem read line by line, you slowly absorb the weight of each word until a masterpiece emerges. That was how her healing felt: a text of sorrowful lines gradually unraveling into something beautiful. She barely noticed the transformation happening; she simply let the waves wash over her until, one day, she finally felt right.

Day by day, the broken pieces settled into place, and she could finally breathe without a crushing weight on her chest. From the smallest moments to the grandest, the burden slipped away. She smiled easily now. She felt alive, realizing for the first time just how expansive life could be. If someone had told eighteen-year-old Agatha that a farm would become her true home, she would have laughed out loud. But growing up means recognizing that life is like the ocean: the waves may crest tall and fierce, but they eventually break into shallow, gentle foam at our feet. Her priorities had shifted. Flying had been a beautiful, idealistic dream, but putting down roots was exactly what she needed now.

For years, she had ruminated on the guilt of her past choices. Now, she understood that to move forward, the past had to stay exactly where it belonged. Yesterday is just as out of reach as tomorrow; neither is a place you can actually live. Remorse and guilty only serve to anchor us to a time we can no longer touch.

What remained was regret, but it no longer agonized her. Though is still carried a dull ache, it allowed her to reflect on her journey and appreciate the woman she had become. If she made mistakes now, they would be new ones — and that was exactly how it should be. Accepting the present meant embracing both the good and the bad. We cannot change the past or predict the future; all we can do is live. And for the first time in a long time, Agatha was truly living.

Her life with Tessa had been a mistake, but she was done torturing herself over it. It was time to accept that it was over, leaving her with a wide-open future of her own choosing. The same applied to her history with Rio. While it had recently haunted her with old scars, she could finally see past the wounds to the genuine good they shared. Those luminous moments were worth holding onto — proof that even within our worst choices, there is beauty worth watering until it blooms again.

Her life was finally catching a rhythm. She had heard back from her interviews and accepted a modest but promising position at a veterinary clinic. It was expanding, offered room to grow, and was conveniently close to the farm. She would start next week. Everything was falling into a comfortable routine: Nicky’s classes began on Monday, his appointments with Jennifer were set weekly and the equestrian lessons happened every day.

Best of all, her home was slowly taking shape. The renovations were demanding, but seeing the project come to life was increasingly beautiful. They were building a large, interactive outdoor area for Nicky to play in, and most of the furniture had already arrived. Her days living out of the basement were numbered, and there was a profound comfort in watching all the pieces of her life finally fit together.

“Where were you?” Lilia asked the moment she pulled open the front door.

Weighed down by an armful of shopping bags, Agatha could only let out a heavy sigh.

“I ran into town to grab Nicky’s school supplies, since I brought practically nothing for his classes from home,” she explained, unceremoniously dumping the bags onto the living room floor. “Jennifer also gave me a list of everyday essentials that would be useful for him.” Lilia offered a faint, remarkably proud smile. “By the way, where is he?” Agatha added. “I want to show him all this; I bought every horse-themed thing I could get my hands on.”

“He’s outside with Rio,” Lilia replied. “She brought a bunch of baby chicks over for him to see.”

Agatha rolled her eyes but couldn’t fight a faint smile — of course he was with Rio.

Navigating this new coexisting with Rio was… certainly something. It wasn’t that they were particularly close; they essentially only spoke about matters regarding Nicky, which inevitably meant crossing paths daily. Outside of that shared responsibility, they rarely talked and never simply hung out. Yet, no matter where Agatha looked, Rio was there. Now that a truce had been struck, ignoring her presence was impossible — especially as their lives grew more hopelessly intertwined with each passing day.

And with every passing day, it became exponentially harder not to notice her. Yes, Agatha noticed. She was a sexually frustrated woman who hadn’t been touched in a long time, and she still had functioning eyes; no one could really blame her. She knew it was entirely inappropriate, but god, maturity looked incredibly good on Rio. She was no longer that laid-back, unpretentious twenty-something girl floating through life. She had evolved into someone determined, wielding a steady gaze that Agatha felt could pierce straight through her soul — even if Rio almost always averted those deep brown eyes whenever they spoke. Rio was physically stronger now, radiating a quiet, confident air and a magnetic presence that simply demanded attention.

It was incredibly hard to look away when she showed up flushed and sweaty, actively seeking out chores around the farm, barking orders, and effortlessly displaying her physical strength. She would walk in using those toned arms to haul entire barrels of grapes for her mother; or casually spin Nicky through the air before hosting him into a horse’s saddle.
