Agatha absolutely hated that she occasionally caught herself sighing at the sight — watching this tough, ruggedly attractive woman melt into pure sweetness with her son, cater to every single whim of her mother’s, and suddenly turn bashful the second Agatha caught her eye.

She definitely needed to buy a vibrator. Not to use while fantasizing about Rio — absolutely not. That would cross every boundary of common sense and completely undermine the fragile, positive relationship they were finally building. But she definitely needed one. Entertaining those kinds of thoughts about Rio was something thar simply could not happen, which meant Agatha had to find a way to purge this mounting frustration before it drove her to think about things she had no business thinking about.

Day after day, she actively swept these lapses in judgment under the rug. She neither needed nor wanted this complication — especially not now, when it was finally time to look to the future rather than letting herself be seduced by the best, most tempting fragments of their past. Rio was being consistently cordial and friendly. For Nicky’s sake, they were constructing a brand-new healthy relationship of trust entirely from scratch. Agatha knew it was a highly peculiar, complex dynamic, but there was a genuine beauty in seeing Rio try so hard, because Agatha was trying just as hard. It was far from easy, though. No matter how thoroughly they had buried their shared history, lingering weirdness remained. Ultimately, it was just difficult to look at her and not remember… so many intensely intimate moments from their past.

Taking slow, cautious steps to ensure she wouldn’t be noticed, Agatha slipped into the kitchen and leaned quietly against the window frame. She tilted her head, a faint smile touching her lips as she held back a soft sigh at the scene unfolding outside. On the porch, Rio was sitting on the floor with Nicky right beside her, huddled around a large wooden box brimming with incessantly chirping baby chicks. Rio was pointing at the tiny birds, giving them names, while Nicky smiled in rapt attention. He had both hands gently inside the box, playing with the chicks and letting out soft musical giggles whenever they tried to peck at his fingers. It was such a comforting, intimately domestic scene that Agatha could actually feel her heart warming inside her chest.

“This one is the smallest, which is why his name is Pip,” Rio said, gently scooping up the little bird. Nicky’s eyes went wide with sheer adoration, holding out his cupped hand so she could pass it over.

Cradling the chick, Nicky brought his face close to the yellow fluff to nuzzle it, and the tiny creature curled itself into a perfect ball. As he stroked it, Rio leaned back on her hands, stretching out her legs and watching him with a tender smile. She looked beautiful like this — radiating a quiet peacefulness, her dark leather hat tipped slightly askew.

“What are you two up to this time?” Agatha finally interrupted.

They both snapped their heads toward her in perfect, synchronized innocence; she had to swallow a sigh.

“Mom, come see the chicks!” Nicky exclaimed brightly.

Agatha’s eyes widened a fraction, momentarily caught off guard by his absolute spontaneity. Smiling, she pushed open the porch door and dropped down onto the floor right next to her son. When she glanced over at Rio, a faint smile tugged at her lips — those deep brown eyes were already anchored on hers, Rio’s mouth curving into a shy, silent greeting.

“They are so small,” Agatha murmured. She reached into the box, laughing as the agitated chicks offered weak little pecks against her skin, their chirping growing frantic at the new arrival. “How old are they?” she asked Rio, who blinked, raising an eyebrow as she realized she was being addressed.

“Three days,” Rio answered with a lazy, easy grin. “I brought the whole brood so Nicky could pick one.”

“What do you mean, pick one?” Agatha asked, her gaze snapping back and forth between Rio and her son.

“To keep,” Rio stated, as if it were the most obvious thing in the world.

Agatha arched a sharp eyebrow at Nicky. He just shrugged, offering a terribly sly smile while clutching his new feathery friend.

“To keep out here on the farm, right?” Agatha clarified.

“In the house, Agatha,” Rio corrected, thoroughly amused.

Agatha shook her head instantly. “Do you honestly think I’m going to raise a chicken in my living room?”

“He said he wanted one!” Rio defended herself, shooting a look at Nicky, whose face was now the picture of mischief. Both women narrowed their eyes at him, but Nicholas simply pressed the chick against his cheek and knitted his brows together in a devastatingly pathetic plea. “Didn’t you ask your mom?” Rio asked him. “I thought you asked.”

“Mom, please,” he begged, his lower lip jutting out.

Agatha sighed, shaking her head at her own crumbling resolve. “He’s small. He’s teeny-tiny.”

“But he is not going to stay teeny-tiny for long.”

“Chickens are small,” Rio unhelpfully pointed out with a shrug. Nicky beamed at her, nodding in fervent agreement. “What?” Rio laughed, catching Agatha’s deadpan glare. “It’s smaller than a dog.”

“You’re not helping,” Agatha noted, which only made Rio laugh harder.

“I can build a chicken coop out here; there’s plenty of space,” Rio offered, gesturing toward the vast brush that stretched across her mother’s backyard. “That way, he gets a little spot outside and doesn’t have to live in your house.”

“Riandra!” Agatha scolded — largely because she could see Nichola’s face completely light up at the idea.

“Mom, please!” he repeated. He weaponized those massive brown eyes, holding his hands and the chick out toward her.

Agatha laughed softly, carefully taking the tiny creature from him. Her strict expression entirely melted at the touch of the impossibly soft fluff. He really was the smallest and quietest of the bunch.

“It seems like Pip likes you, too. There’s no going back now,” Rio pointed out, deeply amused.

Agatha just stared at her. Rio merely shrugged, pressing her lips together to contain her grin. Agatha sighed, rolling her eyes. Great, now she had two pairs of adorable brown eyes to resist. But honestly, it wouldn’t be so bad. They lived on a farm now. Fostering this bond with the animals was incredibly good for Nicky; it made him calm, happy, engaged, and so much more outgoing. Besides, Jennifer had mentioned that a daily routine with animals would be good for developing his sense of responsibility and care.

“On two conditions,” Agatha finally yielded, leveling them with a pointed look.

The two conspirators instantly grinned, exchanging a triumphant glance before turning their full attention back to her.

“You are going to take care of him, entirely by yourself,” Agatha warned, holding back the chick gently against her chest as she pointed directly at Nicky. He nodded with fervent speed. “And you,” she said, shifting her accusing finger to Rio, “are going to build him a chicken coop.”

Rio broke into a brilliant smile and offered a crisp, mock salute, making Agatha roll her eyes all over again.

“Thanks, mommy!” Nicholas cheered. His voice was overwhelmingly sweet and excited as he threw her arms around her neck.

“You two are nothing but trouble,” Agatha murmured affectionately, hugging him back.

Rio parted her lips to add something, but a harsh buzz from her pants pocked cut her off. Without bothering to check the screen, she reached down, clicked the phone off, and let out a long, relaxed sigh.

“I’ve got to go,” she announced, pushing herself up from the porch floor. She furrowed her brow affectionately when she caught Nicky’s immediately disappointed pout. “I have to work, cowboy, and I’m already late.”

“Mom, can Rio stay and have lunch with us before she goes?” Nicky asked instantly, jumping to his feet.

Agatha carefully transferred the chick back into his waiting hands before standing up herself. “If she wants too…” she offered with an easy shrug, turning a welcoming smile toward Rio.

“My bad, cowboy, but I really can’t today,” Rio apologized. She ruffled his curls, which only made him pout harder. “But how about I leave the chicks here for now, and come pick the rest of them up later? Then I’ll stop by this evening, and you can help me with the horses.”

Nicholas looked immediately to Agatha, silently begging for permission. She gave a faint smile and nodded.

“It’s a deal, then,” Rio declared, pulling him in for a quick side hug.

When they passed through the kitchen, Lilia enthusiastically insisted that Rio stay. Rio politely declined, promising she would join them for lunch another day and reminding them she’d be back that evening. Lilia still managed to make Rio laugh by sternly ordering her to eat something during the day, quoting that an empty sack can’t stand upright. Agatha couldn’t help but smile at the easy familiarity of the exchange. Everything just seemed to fit perfectly into place; they were all so incredibly comfortable in each other’s lives again.

Almost without realizing it, Agatha naturally fell into step beside Rio, walking her out to the pickup truck parked in the drive.

“I honestly thought he had asked you,” Rio confessed about the chick, turning to lean casually against the truck with her arms crossed.

Agatha just shook her head. “He knew perfectly well I was going to say no,” she murmured, giving a knowing look that made Rio laugh out loud.

“Are you going to be mad if I admit I suspected that, but brought them anyway?” Rio murmured, leaning in like she was sharing a scandalous secret.

It was Agatha’s turn to laugh, shaking her head in defeat. “You two are in cahoots over the exact same things.”

“It’s not my fault,” Rio justified, offering a genuinely bashful shrug. “I physically cannot say no to him. Have you seen those big eyes?” she asked, her brow furrowed in defeat.

Agatha let out a soft, amused breath. “Oh, yes. I know those eyes very well… They literally never fail.”

“You did a really good job with him, Agatha. He’s a wonderful kid,” Rio said, her voice dropping into a tone heavy with sincere affection. The quiet praise made Agatha’s chest bloom with a comforting warmth.

“You’re great with him, too,” Agatha confessed softly. She shrugged, earning a slightly awkward, entirely pleased smile from Rio. “I don’t even know how you do it, honestly. He’s just so open with you.”

“It’s my irresistible charm,” Rio joked, rolling her eyes with mock smugness, which drew a soft chuckle from Agatha.

“Probably,” Agatha agreed easily. Rio bit the inside of her cheek, suddenly looking incredibly shy.

“I really have to go,” Rio finally announced. Agatha took a deep breath and nodded. “But I did bring something for you,” Rio added, stepping back to pull open the rear door of the truck.

“For me?” Agatha asked, blinking in surprise as she watched Rio wrestle a massive bowl out of the backseat. “Rio, I swear to god, if that is another animal…”

“It’s corn,” Rio revealed with a bright laugh, holding the heavy bowl out to her. Agatha broke into a massive, delighted smile. “We started planting recently, and these are the very first ears we’ve harvested,” Rio explained. “I remembered you liked it, so I decided to bring some over.”

“My god, I don’t even remember the last time I had proper boiled corn.” Agatha beamed, offering a huge smile and Rio scratched the back of her neck, shrugging off. “Thank you, Rio! Honestly, I might boil it all right now and even bake a cake.”

“Does Nicky like it?”

“Actually, I have no idea,” Agatha admitted, looking thoughtfully down at the bowl in her arms. “I don’t think he’s ever even tried it.”

“He’s never had corn?” Rio asked, her incredulity rapidly morphing into an offended frown. “What on earth were you feeding him in California? Caviar?”

“Yes, of course. For every single meal,” Agatha deadpanned and Rio rolled her eyes.

Slamming the back door shut, Rio pulled open the driver’s side and hoisted herself up behind the wheel.

“Have a good day at work, Rio,” Agatha offered softly.

Rio just nodded, turning the key to bring the engine to life.

Clutching the heavy bowl of fresh corn against her chest, Agatha stood in the drive, her eyes tracking the truck down the dirt road until it completely disappeared from sight. Only then did she let out a long, lingering sigh and finally turn back toward the house.

***

Rio sat in her parked truck on the dirt road leading into the vineyard for several minutes. She knew she was inexcusable late and Natasha would likely subject her to an endless lecture about it, but she just didn’t feel like herself. A tangled mess of thoughts weighed heavily on her mind, slowly dragging her down. Pushing her seat back and stretching her feet up onto the dashboard, Rio let out a heavy sigh as she drained the last of her second beet.

Knowing you aren’t doing well is entirely different from actually being able to get better. She objectively knew she was doing far better than she had ever imagined she would be at this stage. She genuinely felt she was slowly making peace with her father’s loss and finally starting to belong somewhere again, feeling like she had a real family. But the progress didn’t stop the sudden, sharp pangs in her chest that occasionally made the air feel thin. She was just functioning. She was working, she was more present in the lives of the people she loved, yet, a large part of it felt like her body was simply operating on autopilot, while the truth was she remained backed into a corner inside her own mind.

She was experiencing so many conflicting emotions simultaneously that she could no longer decipher what she was actually feeling, and that complete lack of control terrified her. She was paralyzed. She couldn’t stop thinking about Nicky. She couldn’t stop thinking about Agatha. It felt as though her current reality was a cruel distortion of the exact past she had spent her entire youth desperately chasing, and the subsequent years fighting relentlessly to forget and let go.

With a final, resigned sigh, she gave both her cheeks a light slap, climbed out of the truck, and headed down the vineyard trail, aggressively whistling a tune to keep her spiraling thoughts at bay. She desperately wanted a break from her own mind — to simply blink out of existence for a while and breathe without feeling trapped inside herself. She just had absolutely no idea how to accomplish that. God, she missed her father. He would have known the exact right thing to say at a moment like this.

The second she stepped into the winery’s main office, she found Natasha quite literally buried under a mountain of paperwork. Rio had to bite her lip to keep from laughing when her best friend immediately narrowed her eyes, looking perfectly ready to strangle her.

“Did your sundial break today,” Natasha muttered dryly.

Rio let out a quiet breath, ignoring her friend’s scathing glare as she plucked a bottle of wine from a nearby display shelf. She sat down at her desk, rummaging in a drawer for a corkscrew.

“I had some things I needed to sort out this morning,” Rio offered dismissively, watching Natasha take a deep breath as she attempted to organize her precarious stacks of paper.

“Really?” Natasha muttered, suddenly just looking tired. “I told you I needed to discuss some things with you. I could barely get anything done this morning because I need your final approval to process these new hires.”

“Natasha, I trust you blindly. Whatever you decide, I’ll sign off on. Just hand me the pen and point to where I need to initial,” Rio said. She took a few long gulps straight from the wine bottle, watching Natasha shake her head in deep judgment. “You could have just talked to Benny, the business is half his, after all.”

“Rio, your brother has an appallingly minimal grasp on actual negotiations; he’s only good for the bureaucracy. You are the face of this business. Benito lacks the tact required for our high-level partners; they expect to negotiate with you,” Natasha explained with the exhausted patience of a mother speaking to a toddler. “Besides, he manages to be even worse than you are. He didn’t even bother showing up today.”

“Give him a break, the kid’s getting married,” Rio replied with a faint smile, taking another swig of wine. “I’ll talk to him about it. I know you’ve been completely overwhelmed lately, and the entire advantage of having him here is for him to run things alongside you.”

“We need to talk about that, too” Natasha warned, making Rio raise an eyebrow. “But first, we have to talk about the new Casa Vidal franchises. We have three pending projects, and I need you to finalize the rollout schedule.” Rio nodded, finally adjusting her posture in her chair to pay proper attention. “We have three franchises currently underway: Madrid, Paris, and New York. I was discussing it with the advertising team, and if we launch all three simultaneously, we’ll get massive global visibility. But I know you won’t want to travel to three different countries in the same week to open them.”

“No way,” Rio stated resolutely, shaking her head. Natasha sighed. She loved her job, but the Vidal siblings were perpetually one minor inconvenience away from giving her a stroke. “I won’t spend more than three consecutive days away from home. The openings have to be spaced out by at least two weeks,” Rio dictated. Natasha nodded, quickly jotting down noted. “And another thing: do I really have to go to all three? Why don’t we send Benny to a couple? Honestly, that would be so much better for me.”

“Rio, there are a lot of big names involved in these projects, and you were the one who courted them and brought them into the process. They trust you; the investment capital is tied to you. I fully support Benito going with you, but he needs to observe you, learn the ropes, and earn our partners’ trust on his own merit. You have to be there. That is entirely non-negotiable.”

“Then I don’t see what we’re even discussing,” Rio muttered, offering a lazy shrug.

“If we have to stagger the openings, I need you to decide which location we are prioritizing,” Natasha explained. “Compared to the others, New York is the closest and the project is highly modern and urban, guaranteeing a lot of immediate visibility. Madrid, on the other hand, is leaning into our traditional format and features significantly more artisanal lines than New York…”

“Paris,” Rio interrupted before Natasha could even finish the thought. Natasha looked up, silently waiting for the justification. “Paris will be the franchise carrying the most artisanal lines, which makes it perfect for promoting the other two. We launch Paris to showcase the new catalog and then use the development and integration of those artisanal lines as the official excuse for the delay in Madrid and New York.” Natasha nodded slowly, clearly agreeing with the sharp business logic. “New York can go last. It’s closer to home and it’s our boldest project. Wrapping up the rollout with our most modern aesthetic will generate a really interesting, forward-looking vibe for future expansions.”

“Done,” Natasha agreed. She stood up, gathered the necessary contracts, and dropped them onto Rio’s desk. Rio didn’t even bother to skin the front pages, immediately scribbling her signature wherever a sticky note pointed. “Are you honestly not even going to read them? These are your million-dollar projects, Rio.”

“Which is exactly why I know exactly what’s in them,” Rio replied casually. Natasha just sighed, shrugging in defeat as she returned to her desk to file the signed contracts and grab yet another towering stack of paperwork. “And I trust you,” Rio added softly. Natasha offered a faint, appreciative smile. “What else do you need from me? I need to head down to the cellar. I have to brainstorm the next vintage lines, and I have a tasting meeting with the signature wines team to finalize the last barrels for this month.”

Rio frowned as she watched a look of deeply contained exasperation wash over Natasha’s face. The COO let out a long, heavy sigh and shook her head, seemingly weighing her next words carefully.

“What is it, Natasha?” Rio asked, her casual demeanor instantly shifting into a mix of genuine concern and curiosity.

“Rio, I am really, truly overwhelmed,” Natasha confessed, her gaze pointed and unwavering. Rio nodded slowly, giving her the floor. “There is simply no way for me to keep managing all of this alone. This is a multinational corporation.”

“But what about our partner firms—” Rio started, but was immediately cut off.

“Our partner firms scattered across every time zone in this country?” Natasha countered, raising her eyebrows to hammer home her point.

Rio took a deep breath. She knew the logistical nightmare they were facing. They had tried everything to lure top-tier corporate talent to Darby, but convincing elite professionals to relocate to a tiny, rural farming town was a nearly impossible challenge, regardless of the exorbitant salaries they offered.

“We have the best partners available, I know that,” Natasha continued. “The best law firms, the best accountants, and the best analysts in the country. But it is completely unfeasible to continue operating without centralizing at least one executive-level professional from each of those fields right here in this office to spearhead their respective departments. We have to control the loose ends in-house. All this constant back-and-forth communication with external agencies isn’t just counterproductive and time-consuming; it generates a literal sea of rework.”

“Nat, what do you want me to do?” Rio asked, her tone bleeding exasperation as she folded her hands on her desk. “I gave you a blank check and total freedom to hire whoever you deemed necessary. Honestly, I don’t know what else I can possibly do. Tell me what you need. Just name it, and I will make it happen.”

“I need someone here to share the executive load. Benito and I simply cannot keep pace with this level of rapid expansion.”

“He’s taking care of that,” Rio stated, prompting Natasha to raise a skeptical eyebrow. “There’s a kid from New York— William, I think. Benito says he’s a total prodigy. He’s twenty-two and already finishing his PhD.”

“You want to hire a child for an executive role?” Natasha retorted, her expression souring.

“Benito is essentially a child, too,” Rio shrugged, earning a sharp exhale from Natasha. “The kid is highly competent; Benito personally vouched for him. Plus, there are a half-dozen massive corporations currently engaged in a bidding war over him, which is usually a pretty good sign, right? Benny is supposed to forward his resume to you today. As far as I’m concerned, if you like it, we can make an immediate offer.”

“If he’s in such high demand, what’s the guarantee he’d even want to move to Darby?”

“The boy has a rough background,” Rio murmured, shaking her head slightly and catching her friend’s attention. “He was kicked out of his house for being gay when he was just a pre-teen. He has no one. If it weren’t for scholarships, he couldn’t afford his education; he’s living under immense pressure. Benito talked to him, and the kid loved the idea of putting down roots and having a place where he’d be welcomed, seen, and valued for more than just his degree. I liked that. Beneath all that ambition, the kid has a lot of heart.” Rio paused, leaning back in her chair. “I told Benito to double any offer he gets, and we’ll fully fund the rest of his studies if he joins us so he can keep specializing. He’ll have a place to live and everything he could possibly need. I think he and Yelena will hit it off, considering their similar backgrounds. It’ll be good to have fresh, young energy around here.”

A fond smile broke through Natasha’s professional veneer. “You put on this tough-girl act, but deep down, you can never hear a sad story without it melting your heart,” she teased, earning an eye roll from Rio.

“He’s good. It’ll be mutually beneficial,” Rio deflected gently. “Besides, it’s like my dad always said: this farm is like a mother’s heart, there’s always room for one more. He’ll be welcomed here. We’ve always operated as a big family, and Benito already looks at the kid like a little brother. It’s practically keeping it in the family.”

“Alright, I’ll review his resume,” Natasha yielded, prompting a satisfied nod from Rio. “That’s one problem solved. But we still have another.”

“Fantastic,” Rio muttered, her sarcasm dripping.

More than anything, Rio just wanted to wash her hands of all these bureaucratic headaches. If it were up to her, she’d hire twenty people just so she wouldn’t have to make these kinds of decisions. She simply wasn’t in the right headspace for it, practically thanking god when her brother stepped up to help ease her best friend’s crushing workload. She desperately needed to clear her mind; she was in no condition to talk business. But deep down, she knew her father would want her leading from the front, exactly as he always had.

“We need a lawyer,” Natasha stated firmly, causing Rio to furrow her brow in confusion.

“Another one?” she laughed nervously. “I couldn’t even tell you how many we already have on retainer.’

“Here in Darby. We need an in-house lawyer here,” Natasha clarified.

Rio could see the sheer desperation etched into her friend’s features. Natasha was drowning in work, and Rio felt a pang of guilt for being so lost in her own complicated mess that she couldn’t support her the way she should. Even though she loathed bureaucracy and famously never read the contracts herself, when she was in a clear state of mind, she always made these strategic decisions alongside her COO. They were normally perfectly in sync, tackling problems with ruthless efficiency whenever they operated as a team.

“Every single day, more contracts pile up. With how fragmented everything is, it’s becoming impossible to manage, especially with us expanding on so many different fronts,” Natasha vented. “It’s an absolute nightmare having to review the same documents a million times. I send a contract out, wait days, and when it finally comes back, it’s still lacking. Then I send it back, again and again, trapped in an endless cycle of revisions because we aren’t in the room guiding the process with them. Obviously, a lot of the legal work still needs to be outsourced, and maintaining our external firms is essential, but we need someone in-house to spearhead the operation.”

“I thought you were already handling that. It’s definitely not the first time you’ve brought it up.”

“Rio, we need a top-tier lawyer. Someone highly qualified, with the chops to tackle everything head-on and stay up to speed firsthand. Absolutely no one with those kinds of qualifications wants to relocate here, not even for all the money in the world, because they’re already making top dollar at their current firms.”

“I’ll ask again: what can I do to fix this? You name it, I’ll do it, and I’ll pay for it,” Rio insisted casually. But her easy demeanor faltered into a frown when she noticed a sudden, heavy uncertainty clouding her friend’s face. “What is it?”

“Wanda came to talk to me,” Natasha began, choosing her words so deliberately that Rio immediately arched an eyebrow. “She told me Agatha is planning to stay on the farm. She’s not going back to California.”

Rio nodded slowly, feeling an uncomfortable knot in her stomach. It wasn’t a bad feeling, but it was certainly far from comfortable. Agatha is going to stay on the farm. Rio wondered for how long. And she hated that, hated that bitter expectation that made her feel like a teenager again, at the mercy of feelings she couldn’t control.

“I know,” Rio murmured, bitting the inside of her cheek, and Natasha raised her eyebrows, surprised by the confession.

“Do you want to talk about it?” she asked in an empathetic tone, but Rio let out a heavy breath.

“I don’t, but you certainly do.” The words came out more sour than she intended, but Natasha just nodded.

“You know I’m not her biggest fan,” Natasha said with a shake of her head.

Rio nodded apathetically, her gaze impenetrable. She knew that very well and felt guilty too, because she was fully aware that Natasha’s aversion was the fault of her own pitiful state that had dragged on for years until she finally got her life back on track.

“She’s looking for a job,” Natasha said with a guarded expression. “She’s even doing interviews. Wanda didn’t tell me much, apparently they are back to being joined at the hip, but she came to talk to me because she knows we are in need of a heavy hitter here. As much as I have my reservations about her as a person, it’s impossible to deny she is good at what she does. Her resume, her experience, the cases she’s worked on… It’s enough to put many big firms to shame. She was the head of contracts department at one of the biggest firms in the country, Rio.”

“I didn’t know she was looking for a job.” It was the only thing Rio managed to say, her mind still reeling with her own thoughts.

"It would be a hell of a hire," Natasha admitted reluctantly.

"And why didn't you talk to Benito? He knows her better than I do; I think he's much more capable of making that decision. Does she want to work here? Does she want to work with us, in our business?"

"I wanted to talk to you first. I know you gave me carte blanche for hiring, but I wouldn't do this without talking to you beforehand," Natasha explained, now in a softer tone, and Rio nodded, trying to force the anxiety down her throat, feeling the knot tighten. "I don't know if she wants to work with us, but honestly, it's the best offer for her, and it's not like it's a small thing; we are a multinational, Rio, a million-dollar business. It would be great for her career too."

Rio agreed in silence. It was true. She had no idea what the hell had happened in Agatha's life for her to decide to return to the farm, of all places in the world. It bordered on ironic, and somewhat bitter, that after everything, she wanted to put down roots right there, in the place she had always wanted to escape from.

Rio didn't want to feel that uncomfortable twinge, much less go back to thinking about the turbulence of the past and how that farm had been the breaking point between them. But rationally, she knew it was a deal she couldn't refuse. Agatha was much more than competent, she was brilliant, and Rio knew it more than she would have liked, since her own father had made a point of bragging about her career over the years. In the end, Agatha had become what she always wanted and much more.

It would be a stellar hire for the company, far superior to what they hoped to get for Darby. Furthermore, if Agatha was really settling there, it would be good for her to have a stable job, something financially up to her standards, that would be more than enough for her and Nicky to live the life they deserved. Agatha deserved that opportunity — she deserved the world.

As Rio tried to silence her own mind, she felt Natasha's nervous gaze on her.

"You can run this by my brother." That was what Rio said after long minutes in silence. Natasha narrowed her eyes as if expecting a different reaction, but nodded.

"If she wants the position, the job is hers," Rio shrugged, getting up from her chair. "She is more than qualified, she has spearheaded huge international negotiations and is perfect for this. If she accepts, you can double the offer; I want her to make what she would make taking on a multinational directorship in California. I don't want to spare any resources, I know she'll do a great job, I have no doubts about that." She spoke in her best professional tone, trying to mask the tension that was, little by little, making her entire body stiffen.

"Are you really okay with this?" Natasha asked, and now it wasn't her COO speaking, but her best friend. "Are you okay knowing that she's staying?"

"I have a lot to do today," Rio deflected, looking away and heading toward the door. "I need to go to the cellar, I'm late enough as it is."

"Rio..." her friend called, but Rio had already walked out the door.

Rio could barely register the walk to the cellar. Her legs felt like they weighed a ton, but her entire body was wobbly, overcome by a nauseating vertigo. She didn't want to have sounded so bitter, didn't even know where all that acidity had come from. She didn't hate Agatha, had no aversion to her, quite the opposite, but there was so much feeling choked up inside her, so much she had never really been able to process and digest, and over the years, all she had managed to do was sweep it under the rug. But now, all that accumulated dust was rising up like a tornado, leaving her blind and disoriented.

She had loved Agatha her whole life, had never been able to stop loving her and honestly, knew she would love her for the rest of her life. It was no longer a painful or desperate infatuation as it used to be, but a certainty rooted in her heart — a certainty from which she had never managed to break free, even when she had tried her hardest. The truth is she had never truly let Agatha go; she had merely accepted reality because she had tried with all her might to make it different, but it hadn't been enough. She tried to convince herself that it was all in the past, but throughout all those years, there she was, searching for news from California, wanting to know if she was okay, if she was happy. She wanted her to be happy, even if it was far away from her — she would never have been able to move on or get back on her feet if she didn't know Agatha was happy, that all of it, in the end, had been worth it, that even if it hurt, it had been the right choice.

But the truth was she missed her, not just romantically; she missed her presence, having her in her life, and mourned every moment she never had the chance to share with her. It hurt to think that, after everything they had been through, Agatha never got the chance to know her best version. And now she was back, right at the moment when Rio had turned into a disaster again. It was a cycle that seemed endless, a curse upon herself, the confirmation that she would never be enough. She would never be the right choice for Agatha.

Rio leaned against the cellar counter to keep from falling, grabbing the first bottle she saw, taking long, desperate gulps all at once. The wine ran down her chin, staining her shirt, but she didn't stop drinking. She wanted the alcohol to burn her throat, to numb her, but ironically, it was sweet.

She had never been able to hold a grudge against the person she had loved most in her entire life. The grudge eating away at her inside, that dense and bitter resentment, was toward herself, for being a failure, for spending her whole life hiding behind a wall she had built so no one would see how broken she was. She had always been like this, broken.

She had never imagined she would have Agatha in her life again, never even dared to dream of it, and now that this was reality, she was panicking. She didn't want her for herself — or at least she thought she didn't — but the sheer terror of losing her once more paralyzed her completely. She was terrified of accepting that she was there, only to have to deal with the void of yet another goodbye a short while later. She hated catching herself seeking her out with her eyes, looking for her just to make sure she was there.

Agatha was a piece of herself she had lost, and now that she was back, Rio had no idea where she fit in. She didn't know what they were, didn't know what they could become, didn't know how to act. She wanted to be close, but felt the urge to run away. At the same time she yearned to be close to her again, she was terrified of that proximity. It was suffocating, and she started to feel short of breath.

Rio's hands began to break out in a cold sweat and her whole body trembled; her chest tightened as if it were being crushed. Tears spilled down her face and she hadn't even realized she had started crying. What if she let her guard down again, let Agatha into her life, and then she left once more? Rio no longer knew who she was, didn't know her anymore, and the truth was Agatha didn't know her anymore either. From everything, they had turned into nothing.

How do you cope when someone's presence hurts just as much as their absence?

Rio hated change, hated not understanding why things needed to change, hated running into a detour in her routine. Her entire being shrank back and she didn't know what to do; she felt minuscule. What did Agatha being there mean? Why did she want to stay? What did she expect from Rio now? Did she expect anything at all? Not knowing was the thing Rio feared most in the world. Unpredictability destroyed her, because it stopped her from preparing for the pain. She knew she loved Agatha, knew she wanted her there, but the simple fact that nothing was like before was terrifying.

The air seemed to have vanished, and Rio gasped, struggling to breathe, but her lungs felt locked. Her whole body trembled, shaking in involuntary spasms. The world was spinning too fast and, little by little, everything was going dark.

"Rio?" She felt Natasha's hand on her shoulder, but her voice sounded muffled, distant. "Rio, look at me."

Rio tried to lift her head, but the vertigo pulled her down. She was hyperventilating and felt her legs give way until her knees hit the floor. She could barely move.

She felt Natasha's hands grip her shoulders, trying to hold her in place, but her vision was blurry and everything seemed to spin. She was paralyzed, catatonic, and terrified, scared to death.

"Rio, look at me, breathe with me," Natasha pleaded.

In an act of pure reflex, her hands groped the counter searching for the bottle; she needed to numb herself, but Natasha grabbed her arm, pulling her close.

"No, you are not going to drink; you are going to breathe."

"I can't... breathe," Rio choked out. Her voice was thick, and the knot in her throat hurt.

Natasha nodded, kneeling to be at her eye level, holding her by the shoulders.

"Look at me, focus on me," Natasha insisted, holding Rio's face between her hands. "I need you to hold onto me, and we're going to get out of here, okay?"

"I can't... I can't," Rio sobbed, her voice thick and her face drenched in tears.

"You can, we'll go together. You don't need to think about anything right now, just come with me," Natasha said, draping Rio's arm over her own shoulder to help her up. "We're going to the stables, we're going for a ride and we're going to breathe together, alright? You are going to breathe."

***

As there was little time left before starting her new job, Agatha used her free time to admire the house that was slowly taking shape. It was a drastic change of scenery compared to the penthouse in California. Far from the cold black-and-white minimalism, her kitchen was now covered in pastel-yellow tiles adorned with tiny flowers; her furniture was light but full of color; the windowsills were brimming with plants, and the windows were huge on all sides, flooding everything with light, carrying that smell of the farm’s brush and earth — that smell that made her relax completely. Every room seemed to pulse with life, and she was in love with every detail, with every colorful corner of her rooms, and with the coziness of her new home.

The back of the house opened onto a large pond filled with ducks, and the porch was actually a pier with a gentle view stretching across the entire farm, where one could spot, in the distance, the stables and the fields where the horses roamed free all day; Nicky was enchanted, and so was she. Around it rose several orange trees and immense almond trees, and Benito was already planning to build a treehouse in one of them for Nicky. She was enchanted by it all. It was much more than a house; it was truly a home.

It was already late afternoon, and Agatha had a calm, satisfied smile on her face. She was sitting in a light leather armchair on the pier, watching the sky turn orange alongside Kate and Benito, who were in armchairs identical to hers. The three of them formed a kind of circle around the round wooden table that had been made by Javier years ago. She had never felt such peace. It was as if the world spun slower there, and honestly, this was everything she needed to feel: that she was finally managing to live lightly, truly rooted in the present.

But despite all that tranquility, her mind would sometimes cloud over with a few concerns: the divorce, Tessa, Nicky, and, inevitably, Rio. Since the first appointment with Jennifer, Agatha couldn't stop making connections, noticing details she had always let slip by. Now, even without meaning to, she had started seeing Rio with different eyes, in an infinitely more tender way.

Agatha had always believed it was impossible to love her more than she already had in the past, but now she felt herself overflowing with intense, protective affection. She saw not only the woman Riandra had become, but also little Rio — the girl who had gone through so much inside herself without ever truly being seen.

The more she reflected on it, the deeper her tenderness grew, alongside an aching desire to reconnect. But she knew it was incredibly complicated. Rio had always built impenetrable fortresses around herself, and now that they were practically strangers again, Agatha couldn't even fathom how to take the first step. They were on amicable terms, but Agatha craved more than that. She wanted to truly bridge the gap, to relearn who Rio was through this new, empathetic lens, and to unravel the layers she was only just beginning to understand. Still, she could sense Rio’s hesitation. Agatha constantly debated internally whether it was even fair to try, especially given the emotions that surfaced every time they shared a space.

"You're miles away," Kate murmured, breaking into her reverie. Agatha blinked, turning her gaze toward her with a gentle shake of her head. "Is everything okay?"

"Yes, I think so," Agatha sighed softly, relaxing deeper into her armchair. "But you're right. I really was deep in thought."

"About what?" Benito asked. He leaned forward, resting his elbows on his knees and cradling his face in his hands.

Agatha hesitated under their concerned, curious gazes. She hadn't shared much about her appointment with either of them, and she certainly hadn't brought up Rio. She had been turning it over in her mind relentlessly, wondering if she should intervene or simply step back. She didn't want to meddle where she wasn't welcome or overstep carefully drawn boundaries. If she was going to get closer to Rio, she needed to do it the right way — gradually, and with profound respect for her space. She didn't know exactly how to act. But at the same time, Benito was Rio's brother. They were family. If she couldn't confide in them, she couldn't talk to anyone else.

"It's about Rio," she began cautiously.

Instantly, Benito's eyebrows arched in a suggestive swoop.

"Grow up, Benito. It's not like that."

"I didn't even say anything!" he defended, masking his face in feigned innocence, though Agatha merely narrowed her eyes in disapproval.

"You can't take a single thing seriously, can you?" Kate muttered, fighting a smile.

Benito just shrugged and rolled his eyes, prompting a long, heavy sigh from Agatha.

Dropping the act, Benito's expression softened into something more earnest. "What are you thinking about?"

"Do you remember when I first started noticing the signs with Nicky? When we started researching the autism spectrum?" Agatha asked. She bit the inside of her cheek, trying to mask her sudden nerves.

Benito nodded. "I remember. Your mom helped out, too."

"We did all the evaluations, and we ruled out all the obvious links," Agatha pointed out with a shrug. She paused, bracing herself. "But we never considered Rio."

Benito frowned, letting out a dismissive laugh as he shook his head. "My sister? Why would we? She's not autistic, Agatha. You know her."

"Exactly. I do know her," Agatha murmured, her gaze pointed. She watched the amusement instantly evaporate from his face, melting into genuine confusion. "But I think it’s precisely because we know her so well that we let it slide. We just got used to her being the way she is. We never actually stopped to look deeper."

"Do you really think..." he started, but the words died in his throat. His brown eyes sharpened. Agatha could practically see the gears turning as he slowly began connecting the very same dots she had pieced together in Jennifer's office.

"During the first appointment, when Jennifer asked about Nicky's family genetic profile, I told her there was no history. That's when she started explaining the profile of undiagnosed adults," Agatha explained.

Benito knitted his brows, sitting up straighter in his chair.

"She told me that our current awareness of the spectrum is incredibly recent," Agatha continued softly. "Not that long ago, the only people receiving diagnoses were those with much more severe presentations or notable comorbidities. The stigma was huge. Because of that, a lot of children, especially girls, grew up entirely under the radar. They were forced to adapt on their own, mimicking the people around them just to fit in, masking their constant discomfort just to survive."

"My god..." Benito whispered. He dragged his hands down his face, the realization hitting him in real-time as the pieces finally clicked into place.

"The signs... She was always difficult, marked by this enormous rigidity," Agatha murmured, holding his gaze. "That's exactly what everyone used to say about her."

"My mom always called Rio headstrong... stubborn as a mule," Benito murmured, his expression turning thoughtful.

"That is exactly what Jennifer described to me," Agatha sighed heavily. "Rio was so quiet. She hated being swallowed by crowds; she basically only talked to us, and sometimes, only to me. She was always so closed off, she hated being touched, and the way she reacted to even the slightest change..."

"My god, Agatha..." Benito shook his head, the weight of it all sinking in. "How did we never see it?"

"How were we supposed to?" she countered with a gentle shrug. "We had absolutely no idea."

"Do you really think Rio could be autistic?" Kate asked, her gaze darting between the two of them.

"It would explain so much," Benito whispered. His eyes widened for a moment before he sank back into his armchair. "You have no idea, Kate. If even the tiniest thing was out of place, she would completely freak out. She stopped speaking to me for years just because I moved away. She never accepted it; she couldn't comprehend why things had to change. I always wrote it off as her being selfish, but... what if her entire world was falling apart and she simply didn't know how to process it?"

"Obviously, she needs to see a professional. It isn't right to assume a diagnosis without a proper evaluation, it's not something to trivialize," Agatha cautioned carefully, prompting an agreeing nod from Kate. "But yes, it makes a lot of sense. When Jennifer talked about patients who were only diagnosed in adulthood, it felt like she was describing Rio verbatim. She explained the emotional overload of spending your entire life swallowing everything just to seem normal, never quite managing to stabilize. It’s such an exhausting performance that it breaks a person from the inside out, often leading to drug or alcohol dependency just to silence the noise in their mind. It's as if they finally explode after spending a lifetime imploding."

"She stopped just short of actually saying my sister's name," Benito murmured, letting out a dry, hollow laugh.

"It gave me a lot to think about," Agatha confessed, her tone dropping into complete vulnerability. When her eyes met Benito's, he nodded, clearly sharing the exact same thought.

"Are you thinking the same thing I am?" he asked, his brows knitted in a look of almost physical pain. "That maybe, after all this time, we never actually saw her the right way."

Hearing the choked thickness in his voice, Agatha shook her head empathetically and reached out to grasp his hand. She could see the bitter conflict and guilt warring on his face — feelings she understood perfectly because she had been drowning in them, too. But the passage of time, and the journey that had brought her back here, had taught her that torturing herself over the past was entirely useless. Guilt was subjective, often existing only as a phantom in their own minds. Things just happen, and despite the daily choices we make, so much of life remains wildly out of our control.

"I thought the same thing," she confessed. Benito looked at her as if she held all the answers in the universe — an expression he used to wear when he was just a little boy, which coaxed a faint, bittersweet smile from her. Nicky shared that exact same look. "But how could we possibly have known, Benny? It does no good to dwell on it. Yes, maybe we never understood her the way she needed to be understood, but what truly matters is what we do moving forward. It's about how we see her now."

"As someone who just needs to be seen and understood," he said, his tone thick with self-deprecating mockery. "And not as some selfish motherfucker who refuses to put herself in anyone else's shoes."

Agatha laughed softly.

"She was hard on me," he justified quietly, "which is why I was hard on her."

"And that is okay," Agatha assured him calmly. "You two are getting along now, aren't you? You're both trying." Benito nodded. "I think that's the only way forward."

"So, are you planning to talk to her about this?" Kate interjected, raising her eyebrows.

Agatha shook her head instantly. "That falls on you," she said, pointing firmly at Benito before leaning back into her armchair.

"On me?" he gaped, pointing at his own chest. "Why me? Why not you?"

"Me?!" Agatha let out a loud, incredulous laugh.

"You’ve always had a way with her. Nobody in this world even came close to understanding her the way you did. You were the only person she ever actually listened to."

"Yeah, over a decade ago!" Agatha countered in exasperated, nervous laughter. "We don't even know each other anymore, Benny. Things just aren't that simple. God knows I wish they were, but they aren't."

"I thought the two of you were getting closer," Kate noted, arching an eyebrow.

Benito nodded vehemently as he lit a cigarette, pointing the burning tip at his fiancée as if declaring she had just spoken the absolute gospel truth. "I see the two of you together practically every single day," he mumbled, coughing through his first drag.

Agatha hated it when he smoked, just as she had always despised the way Rio drank. But apparently, the entire Vidal family was pathologically incapable of processing stress or intense emotion without a chemical escape hatch. They all desperately needed good therapy. She felt a profound wave of relief that Nicky was starting so young, and she had already booked her own appointment. One step at a time. Who knew? Maybe, eventually, the Vidal siblings would cave to the idea, too.

"We only interact because of Nicky," Agatha insisted. "That's it."

"You wish it were more," Benito challenged softly. He looked her dead in the eye, stripping away all his usual teasing and malice. It was just the raw truth; he knew her far too well.

"I do," she finally admitted. He nodded in quiet understanding, his gaze aching with sweetness. "I miss her."

Agatha let out a long, shuddering breath. Simply saying the words aloud felt like lifting a one-ton weight straight off her chest. "She has always been a part of my life. She’s woven into almost all of my core memories. We went through so much together and I mean that far beyond just the romantic history we had, you know?" God, it felt euphoric to finally let that out without the crushing weight of guilt or fear, finding nothing but warm acceptance in the eyes of two people who loved her. "I know we had the most chaotic, volatile relationship on the planet, but it was also so much more than that." She offered a soft, reminiscent smile. "I don't think I have ever loved anyone quite like that, and I don't just mean romantically. She was my person."

"She was," Benito agreed, a fond smile gracing his features. "And you were hers. I’ve honestly never seen anything like it; it was a frequency only the two of you operated on."

"During all those years bouncing between here and California, we fought so much. Every single time. But even through all of that, we understood each other. In fact, that was exactly why we fought so much: we understood each other perfectly, we just refused to accept each other," Agatha explained, laughing softly at the bittersweet memories. "But even after our most explosive arguments, whenever we finally sat down to talk, she really listened. She truly saw me. I honestly think Rio is the only person who has ever seen me for who I really am. She knows me better than anyone else in the entire world."

"She certainly knows you biblically," Kate murmured, pressing her lips tightly together to stifle a laugh.

Benito barked out a loud laugh, and Agatha just rolled her eyes. It didn't even bother her anymore; she actually found it funny. It was incredibly comforting to just feel light about it all for once.

"My bad," Kate grinned. "Benito got in my head."

"You two are absolute children."

"I know I'm a massive pain in the ass about this, but it’s only because I love both of you," Benito said, his tone sobering. "I remember exactly how you two were together. I remember how you brought out the best in one another, and how you understood each other in a way no one else on earth could touch. You had this impenetrable bubble... Look, I joke around, but I know this isn't just about the romance you used to share. It's different now; it has to be. But I know you miss her, and I would bet my life that she misses you, too."

"Probably," Agatha murmured, shaking her head slowly. "There’s no erasing our history, and no erasing what we used to be. And that’s a good thing, because beneath all the chaos, there was so much good. She was a beautiful chapter of my life. I miss that bubble. I miss understanding someone without having to try, just existing and being understood as if it were the most effortless thing in the world. She made me believe I could do anything, be anyone. Now, I watch her doing that exact same thing with Nicky, and it is so incredibly beautiful... but it just makes me miss her even more."

"If you miss her so much, why don't you just talk to her?" Kate asked simply.

Agatha practically wanted to laugh at the innocent suggestion. "It just isn't that simple, Kate," she replied, a faint, breathless chuckle escaping her. "We walked down completely different paths and entirely exited each other's lives. Just because I'm physically back here now doesn't magically undo everything that happened. We survived a lot, but there is an entire lifetime of distance standing between us now."

"It's not exactly a whole lifetime..." Benito muttered quietly, but Agatha just shook her head, dismissing the thought.

"We aren't on bad terms. We've talked about it," Agatha explained, laughing nervously as Benito and Kate nodded. "We’re okay with the past, which is great. But that doesn't mean... I don't know. I don't really know what our coexistence means right now. Yes, we talk, she's perfectly nice, and I’m open to it, but I can't shake the feeling that she still has one foot out the door. I can't blame her, honestly; it isn't easy for me, either. She’s absolutely amazing with Nicky, but when it comes to me... sometimes I think she hesitates."

"We were just talking about this, Rio isn't very good with change," Benito pointed out, offering a small shrug. Agatha knitted her brows, waiting for him to elaborate. "And since we got here, her entire world has turned upside down. My dad is gone. But I’m here, and now you’re here, too. For the past few years, her whole life revolved around my dad and whatever they were doing together. I only came around every now and then, we barely spoke, and I always left. And you hadn't set foot here in over a decade. Now we're both back, and we're staying. It’s a massive change."

"I think she's terrified," Kate added gently. Agatha turned to her in surprise. "It's not just one big change; it’s that everything keeps changing all the time. Her anchor, the only person who was consistently by her side, is gone. Meanwhile, the people who were never here have suddenly decided to stay. Nothing is the way it used to be. Every single day brings something new, and she has absolutely no control over any of it." Kate shrugged timidly, looking profoundly sympathetic, and Agatha slowly nodded.

Kate then shifted her gaze to Benito. "Yes, you came back, but your dynamic isn't the same. You're taking steps forward every day. Plus, I’m a new variable, I'm just as much a part of your life now as I am of hers." She turned back to Agatha. "You came back, too, and you brought Nicky. She didn't even know him, but now he's a huge part of her daily routine. With everything shifting constantly, how can she be certain of anything? Based on how you both say she processes the world, she must be paralyzed by it all."

"I think you're right," Benito agreed. He lit another cigarette, letting a brief, contemplative silence settle over the three of them. "I think that's exactly why she reacted so poorly those first few days. It wasn't just the grief of losing him; it was the fact that she was completely disoriented by everything else."

"Rio always had a tendency to do that," Agatha lamented, sighing softly. "Whenever she feels cornered or pressured, she goes on the offensive to defend herself. She explodes, and then she runs."

"She’s gotten a little better about that, actually," Benito observed, and Agatha nodded. "We've been talking more. Even though she doesn't open up much, she really listens. I know she's trying, and seeing that makes me want to try even harder."

"I know the feeling," Agatha confessed, a faint smile touching her lips. "At first, I had no idea how to act around her. Not just because I was bracing for a bad reaction, but because I truly didn't know how she was doing or how she was processing the situation. I think I still walk on eggshells a bit, trying to read her mood before I speak or act, kind of like how I do with Nicky."

"I've never been able to read Rio," Benito admitted with a soft laugh. "Sometimes, I just want to give her a hug, but I always back out, convinced she'll punch me in the face if I try." The two women laughed. "Seriously, it's impossible to tell. She never shows what she's actually feeling."

"She let me hug her."

Instantly, two pairs of wide, stunned eyes locked onto Agatha. She laughed softly, shaking her head as she felt the heat rise in her cheeks.

"I hugged her, actually. At Pedra Purpura, the day we talked."

"Wait... what?" Benito asked, laughing nervously.

"I told you guys we talked that day," Agatha said, shrugging in a futile attempt to downplay how intimately special that moment had been to her. "It was the closure we never got. Our breakup was so harsh, so abrupt, and so painful. For years, that was the final, bleeding impression we left each other with; it was a wound we never bothered to treat. It felt so good to finally lay it all out, to make it clear that it’s firmly in the past, that we’re okay now, and that the pain doesn't matter anymore. I desperately needed that moment. And right then, I just... I hugged her."

"And she hugged you back?" Kate asked slowly, an eyebrow raised in pure disbelief. Agatha simply nodded, pressing her lips tightly together to fight off a smile. "My god. We've been here for almost two months, and the only person I've seen her hug so far is Nicky."

"She probably doesn't even hug Natasha," Benito muttered, letting out a breath of sheer disbelief. His thoughtful brown eyes studied Agatha so intently that it made her shrink back slightly into her armchair. "Clearly, it was an important moment for her, too."

"She said it was," Agatha admitted, suddenly feeling a bit bashful. "I think it was a truce."

A comfortable silence fell over them for a few seconds, until Agatha raised an inquiring eyebrow at Benito, whose gaze was still fixed on her.

"What?" she muttered, feigning boredom.

"We spend a lot of time talking about how Rio swallows her feelings, but I think you've spent the last few years doing the exact same thing," he pointed out gently. Agatha frowned. "You spent years of your life swallowing everything you felt, keeping your head down, and staying quiet."

She looked down, swallowing hard. She knew exactly what he meant.

"Coming here wasn't just an escape, Agatha. It's a fresh start," Benito continued, his brows drawing together in deep understanding. "It's a chance to do things differently, to finally let yourself feel, to voice those feelings, to just allow yourself to exist. You deserve that. I don't want to pressure you or dictate what you should do, but if you miss her, I really think you should talk to her." Despite the sudden knot forming in her throat, Agatha felt profoundly supported. "Why keep holding it all inside?" he asked softly. "You don't have to do that anymore. You can be whoever you want to be here. I think you owe it to yourself to be honest. You deserve to be free. If you feel this is important, then act on it."

"I hate it when he's right," Kate muttered, offering Agatha a sympathetic grimace. Agatha rolled her eyes, though her heart squeezed tightly in her chest. "Like you said yourself, there's a whole lifetime of distance between you two. You are not the same person you were back then, and neither is she. But now you can be whoever you choose to be. If this new Agatha wants Rio to be part of her life, it’s worth giving it a shot. Rio is a different person now, too. Maybe it would be good for both of you to get to know each other again, to recognize each other as the people you are today, without carrying all that dead weight from the past."

Agatha let out a heavy breath, but beneath the nerves, a profound sense of relief washed over her. She had been thinking about it endlessly; the idea had been planted in her mind the very first time she saw Rio upon arriving at the farm. She remembered looking at her and realizing that, while she recognized the woman standing before her, she no longer knew who she was. It was a paradox — knowing someone down to their bones, yet having no idea who they had become. Agatha wanted to recognize Rio again, and more than anything, she wanted Rio to recognize her. It wasn't about reopening or healing old wounds; it was about discovering each other in the present, meeting as the women they were now, rather than clinging to the ghosts of a time that would never return.

"I think I prefer it when you two act like idiotic children," Agatha muttered with a fond eye roll, making them both laugh.

"Do whatever your heart tells you," Benito advised, blowing a long stream of cigarette smoke into the evening air. "If you feel it's the right move, don't hold back. You don't have to pretend here anymore. You can just be."

"I really love it here," Agatha confessed on a long, contented sigh. "It feels like a butterfly finally emerging from its cocoon, you know? That's how I've been feeling lately." She paused, her gaze drifting toward the warm glow of the stable lights in the distance. "I was terrified when I first arrived. Those first few days were brutal. But as time went on, it felt like my cocoon slowly began to unravel. Seeing how happy Nicky is here, so engaged, so interested in everything, the way he looks at me now... I could see he was thriving. Seeing that made all the pieces inside me start falling into place. I started to open up and truly accept this place. I started writing again. I started doing little things just for myself. I really feel like I can be whoever I want to be here."

"I gotta say, I love country Agatha," Benito teased, nodding down at her boots, pulling a bright laugh from her lips.

"I rode into town on horseback the other day, can you believe it?" she said, prompting them both to laugh and shake their heads. "I never thought I'd take to this life, but I do. I really, really like it."

"I'm liking it too," Benito admitted, making a futile attempt to swallow the smile spreading across his face. "It feels like time actually slows down here."

"That's exactly it, it feels like the world is infinite," Agatha said, her smile broadening. "I've been swamped these last few days, hunting for a job, setting up Nicky's routine, managing the renovations. Yet, not once did I feel stressed or overwhelmed. I still had all the time in the world in the mornings to brew my coffee, read with him, play, and take him down to the equestrian center. I had time to sit and write, soak up the sun in the hammock, go for a ride... I even booked my very first therapy appointment."

Kate beamed, breaking into a wide smile. "You're starting therapy? That's amazing, Agatha. I think it'll do you so much good."

Agatha arched an eyebrow, pointing directly at the two of them. "You guys should start, too. Especially you," she added, locking her gaze onto Kate, whose jaw dropped open in a stunned, silent gasp.

"Agatha..." she whimpered, shrinking back into her armchair like someone begging for mercy.

Agatha only shook her head, catching Benito out of the corner of her eye as he hurriedly lit another cigarette, suddenly acting as though he had turned invisible.

"I'm not trying to be harsh, but seriously, do you expect me to act like nothing is happening?” Agatha asked, her voice tight with an exasperation that almost pushed her into nervous laughter. She flicked her gaze between them, but they just stared back in heavy silence. She let out a breathless, disbelieving laugh. "Are you serious right now?"

"Agatha..." Benito started, but she held up a sharp finger to cut him off.

"How many packs have you smoked today?" she challenged, raising a skeptical brow. Benito slumped into a heavy sigh, proving her point without a word. "Ever since we arrived, you've been burning through them faster and faster. You reek of smoke, Benito. How long do you think it's going to take your sister to figure it out?"

"And if she does?" he snapped back defensively, his brows pulling low. Agatha just shook her head. Ah, the Vidals — petulance ran deep in that bloodline. "She smells like alcohol half the time, and I don't give her a hard time about it."

"Oh, really?" Agatha fired back instantly, her tone shifting into something firm and fiercely maternal. Benito immediately dropped his gaze. "Don't be a hypocrite, Benito. It doesn't suit you, and it makes you look like a jerk," she scolded, entirely ignoring how tightly his jaw locked.

When Agatha turned back to Kate, the younger woman looked entirely defeated, pulled into herself with her knees drawn tight against her chest, hugging them like a shield. Agatha's expression softened into immediate, profound pity.

"Kate, I know how hard this is for you. But you can't keep living a lie, you know the truth. You aren't alone; we are right here with you. I am right here. You guys don't need to go through with this. You don't have to do this, and deep down, you don't want to do this."

"I do want to, Agatha," Kate insisted, though her voice trembled so violently that even Benito shot her a look of pained sympathy. "I have to do this. I need to."

"For the love of god, Kate, what century do you think we're living in? You don't have to do anything!" Agatha threw her hands up in a flash of frustration before letting them drop limply onto her lap as Kate shrank away again. "This town is microscopic. You know it's only a matter of time before everyone finds out, don't you? Honestly, I'm amazed nobody's put it together yet, because you—"

"Agatha, please," Benito interrupted. His posture had shifted entirely, forming an immediate, protective barrier around his fiancée. Agatha opened her mouth to argue, but ultimately let it go with a heavy sigh.

Those two kids had stood by her through thick and thin; Benito had been in her corner longer than almost anyone else. They had sheltered her during her absolute darkest hours, and she refused to play the villain here. But they were being catastrophically stupid. Agatha suddenly realized she was standing in the exact same shoes they had once worn during her own trainwreck of a marriage — pleading with someone who flat-out refused to listen to reason.

"I am in your corner for whatever you need, you know that. If you truly decide to go through with this, I won't say a single word or do anything to stop you," she promised, earning a grateful nod from Benito. Her gaze softened as she looked back at Kate. "But you don't have to do this, darling. You already have a family here. You don't have to prove a damn thing to anyone. All I want is for you to be happy. We'll figure out the rest, I swear."

"We haven't set a date yet," Kate whispered, a tiny concession that made Agatha let out a quiet breath of relief.

"Just... think about it a little more," Agatha pleaded gently. She turned to Benito, offering a faint, melancholic smile as she saw him nodding at Kate with matching tenderness. A sharp ache hit her chest; she knew he would blindly follow whatever Kate decided, even if it shattered him in the process. "I swear to you, there are a million and one ways out of this, and I will be standing right by your side through every single one of them. I know it feels impossible, Kate, but you aren't alone. Please, just take a step back and think. You deserve a real, genuine happiness. Don't do something just because you think it's the right thing to do."

Kate kept her eyes glued to the floor. Agatha sighed, turning her attention back to Benito with a look of fierce affection.

"I know you'd lay down your life for her, Benny. But you deserve to be happy, too. Both of you do, just the right way."

***

Six years ago

The first thing Agatha registered upon waking was a raw, searing burn in her throat. She had likely thrown up until she passed out again — a miserable routine marking the fifth time it had happened just this week. Keeping her eyes firmly shut, she drew a slow, trembling breath. Her head felt impossibly heavy, spinning with a sickening vertigo, yet her very first instinct was to press a protective hand against her belly. Feeling the solid, reassuring swell beneath her palm allowed her muscles to finally relax. She felt entirely wretched, but she knew that, ultimately, it would all be worth the agony, provided he continued to grow safely inside her.

Her entire body ached with a leaden weight, drenched in a layer of cold sweat. Agatha let out a frustrated grunt, her face twisting in confusion as she tangled with the thick blankets swaddling her. Instinctively, she tried to roll onto her side to bury her face in Tessa's pillow, but the moment her cheek brushed against unfamiliar upholstery, her eyes snapped open. She blinked through the disorientation, realizing she was stretched out on the living room sofa, not in their bed. Fighting a fresh wave of nausea, she managed a monumental effort just to prop herself up on her elbows, needing to see if sitting was even a possibility before she dared to stand.

"No, no, my love! Don't get up. I'm right here, you don't need to move," Tessa's voice rang out, laced with frantic urgency.

Agatha instantly let out a long breath, a wave of relief washing over her as she watched her wife hurry across the room and drop to her knees beside the sofa.

Sinking back into the cushions, Agatha squeezed her eyes shut and forced herself to breathe, exhaling in a heavy, deliberate rhythm — one, two, three times. She just needed to hold on for two more months. Only two more months, and he would finally be in their arms. Two months until they were a complete family. Just two more months. She needed to be okay — but god, she didn't feel even remotely okay.

"Are you feeling any better?" Tessa asked softly.

Agatha opened her eyes, her brow knitting with deep tenderness as she met her wife's sweet, anxious gaze. She desperately wanted to be well for her. Tessa had been wonderful lately; she had promised to fix their fractured dynamic, to change for the better, and she genuinely had. Agatha constantly reminded herself that it was all just a matter of time and that they were in a good place now. The storm had passed. They were fine, and that was all that mattered.

However, the dizziness was so overwhelming that Agatha couldn't even process the words; she merely watched Tessa's mouth moving and offered a sluggish, unconvincing nod. Apparently, her mask was slipping, because Tessa’s brow immediately furrowed, her expression melting right back into pure, unadulterated worry. Shaking her head fondly, Tessa reached out to stroke Agatha's cheek, pressing a lingering, affectionate kiss to her lips that coaxed a faint smile.

"You didn't catch a single word of what I just said, did you?" Tessa asked affectionately. This time, Agatha actually tuned in and nodded in defeat.

"Why am I on the sofa?" Agatha croaked, frowning at the raw scrape in her throat as she spoke.

Tessa was quick to act, snagging a bottled water fitted with a straw from the coffee table and holding it to Agatha's lips. Agatha nearly groaned in sheer bliss as she drank, taking long, uninterrupted gulps to soothe the burn.

"Don't you remember?" Tessa asked, her worry spiking anew as Agatha shook her head. "You got sick last night and started having intense contractions, but you were so out of it... You just kept mumbling and shivering. I was so desperate, Agatha. I was terrified." Tessa spoke with a tight, pained expression, her bright blue eyes welling with unshed tears. The sight stirred a wave of tenderness in Agatha, prompting her to lift a hand to her wife's cheek. She smiled faintly as Tessa leaned into the touch, resting the full weight of her face against her palm. "I called the doctors, and they had to stretcher you down to the hospital. We were there for hours, and you were so sick you could barely keep your eyes open. When we finally got back, you begged the EMTs to leave you down here on the couch. I practically begged you to come to bed, but you insisted my perfume was making you sick and that our bedroom was completely contaminated."

Tessa finished the recounting with a light, teasing smile, and Agatha exhaled a quiet breath.

"I'm so sorry, baby," Agatha murmured, laughing softly, but Tessa merely shook her head.

"I threw every single bottle away and had the entire room professionally disinfected this morning."

"Tessa!" Agatha scolded the dramatic overreaction, though her wife just offered an unrepentant shrug.

"Agatha, I'm just worried about you, about our little prince," Tessa whispered, resting a gentle hand over her wife's swollen belly. Agatha instantly placed her own hand right on top of it. "If there is anything in this world I can do to make you feel better, I'll do it. Anything for the two of you," she added, leaning down to press a soft kiss directly against the bump.

Agatha let out a miserable groan, rolling her eyes. "Can we please cancel the baby shower?"

"It's just this weekend, my love," Tessa replied instantly, tilting her head to stroke her face once more.

Agatha let out a frustrated huff. She could barely sit upright without the room violently spinning; the mere thought of enduring a massive baby shower packed with a hundred guests made her want to weep. "You'll feel so much better by then. These are just a few bad days, and the doctor said everything is completely under control."

Agatha wanted to tell that doctor to go straight to hell. After all, she was the one carrying a literal human being inside her body, and she could state with absolute certainty that no, absolutely nothing was under control.

When she and Tessa had first started trying to conceive, Agatha naively assumed the hardest part was the punishing, cyclical loop of hope and heartbreak they endured for nearly two full years. A crushing wave of guilt would consume her every time a test came back negative, as though her long-standing, innate aversion to motherhood were manifesting physically, entirely out of her control. The worst part had been the sheer frustration — the mental exhaustion of having to paste on a smile and march through daily life as if nothing had happened, silently mourning a life she hadn't even gotten the chance to meet yet.

Tessa had flatly refused to give up, and seeing that relentless devotion slowly pulled Agatha back toward the dream of building a family. Of course, it wasn't all sunshine and roses, but Tessa genuinely seemed to be trying her best to grow every single day. At least, that was what Agatha desperately needed to believe, and it was what kept her holding on. When they finally beat the odds and conceived, Agatha foolishly thought the worst was behind them. Unfortunately, she couldn't have been more wrong.

They had been practically living at the hospital, eventually reaching a point where private doctors and nurses were kept on standby right inside their apartment. Every single aspect of the pregnancy remained dangerously unstable, and Agatha could barely string two conscious days together without fainting from sheer exhaustion. Instead of gaining weight, she was actively wasting away. It was only now, halfway through her seventh month, that she had finally stabilized enough to put on some mass. She could feel her body truly embracing the child within as her belly surged outward to make up for lost time. She felt massive now, finally building a proper nest for her son. Even so, her cheekbones remained sharply prominent and she weighed far less than she should have — even if this was the healthiest she had felt the entire term.

Tessa bent over backward to keep her comfortable, and honestly, Agatha knew she never could have survived this ordeal without her wife by her side. It felt as though Tessa had finally grown into the steadfast woman she had promised to be at the altar. She had transitioned to working remotely full-time, spending every waking hour right by Agatha's side — attentive, eager, and fiercely protective. Even in the darkest moments, when they both feared the worst, Tessa's presence offered a sanctuary of absolute safety. She felt truly loved.

Yet, for all her good intentions, Tessa was hopelessly clumsy, and while Agatha usually found it endearing, it occasionally drove her insane. Her wife had a chronic flair for the dramatic, and all Agatha wanted right now was profound, uninterrupted rest; she saw zero logic in having an army of people constantly shuffling through their home. Tessa had outsourced literally every facet of their lives, hiring a dedicated crew for every conceivable need: deep cleaning, private chefs, medical attendants, early-contraction doulas to help navigate the pain, and clinical nutritionists who worked desperately around the clock to strike an impossible compromise between the baby's nutritional demands and Agatha's violent physical rejection of almost everything she tried to consume.

Agatha knew her wife meant no malice. Even trapped at home, Tessa was buried alive under work, and this overwhelming army of help was just her chaotic way of ensuring Agatha had maximum support. But the cold truth was that Agatha just wanted some peace and quiet.
