She had always adored the noisy, high-octane pulse of Los Angeles, but now she yearned for nothing more than absolute silence and stillness. She didn't dare voice it aloud, but for months, her deepest, most desperate wish had been to spend the remainder of her pregnancy back at the farm. Her mouth practically watered at the thought of fresh fruit, her mother's home-cooked meals, and Lilia's pastries. She just wanted to stretch out in the backyard hammock, listen to her godfather softly strum his guitar, and hear Rio sing.

She didn't even allow herself to linger on those thoughts, paralyzed by the irrational fear that Tessa might somehow pluck them right out of her mind. She knew she had rambled deliriously in her semi-conscious states whenever the sickness peaked, pushed past the point of knowing whether she was awake or asleep. She was acutely aware that her wife would never, in a million years, agree to pack up and spend months at the farm — that was a dead issue buried deep in the past since the very start of their marriage. But deep down, home was the only place Agatha wanted to be.

The entire apartment currently nauseated her. The food failed to appeal, tasting either far too refined or entirely like nothing at all. Every sensory input repulsed her, smells most of all. She genuinely loved her wife and felt profoundly grateful for the relentless care, but the moment Tessa walked into a room wearing any perfume whatsoever, Agatha felt her stomach violently heave.

All she wanted was that single scent — brushwood tangled with damp earth. Just that. She was utterly convinced that if she could only breathe it in, the sickness would finally vanish.

Naturally, her wife could never know about it. But at least Agatha had an ace up her sleeve, and frankly, she didn't care who judged her; she was only trying to do what was best for the baby. She figured Tessa would swallow whatever flimsy excuse she managed to invent if anything seemed amiss, though Agatha was far too bone-tired to stress over it. All she wanted was to send that damn baby shower straight to hell. She just wanted to rest in peace.

Agatha only snapped back to awareness when a sudden, violent wave of nausea surged from the pit of her stomach. Taking a deep breath, it triggered her gag reflex, nearly making her throw up right then and there.

"Babe, are you okay?" Tessa asked, panic lacing her voice.

It was the first time in what felt like hours that Agatha truly heard her wife’s voice; she had likely slipped out of reality yet again. Wrinkling her nose as the nausea surged, she clung to the bucket Tessa thrust into her hands, meeting her wife’s wide, terrified blue eyes.

"What is that smell?" Agatha rasped, pressing a forearm desperately over her nose.

"What smell, my love? I don't smell a thing."

"But I do," Agatha gagged, spitting into the bucket. "Is that fish? Are they cooking fish? For the love of god, Tessa, get that out of the kitchen right now," she pleaded, doubling over for another dry heave.

Tessa didn’t hesitate for a single second. She spun on her heel and marched toward the archway leading to the formal dining hall and kitchen.

Taking a shaky breath, Agatha sipped a little water, fighting to keep her stomach settled. Even from the far end of the sprawling penthouse, she could hear the sharp, muffled edge of her wife’s shouting, followed by the frantic clatter of cookware being hastily cleared away. Agatha rolled her eyes with a pang of guilt; Tessa lost her temper over the smallest things, and Agatha couldn't help but pity the kitchen staff caught in the crossfire.

It took barely any time for Tessa to reappear, wearing a sickeningly sweet smile as if she hadn't just terrorized half a dozen employees. She carried a silver tray holding a steaming bowl and a tall glass filled with a thick, opaque pink liquid. The rich aroma drifting from the bowl made Agatha’s mouth flood with saliva instantly, and that glass... it looked exactly like authentic, full-bodied guava juice. God, I must be hallucinating.

"I don't mean to undermine anyone's professional expertise, but I fired the nutritionists this morning," Tessa announced, raising her brows in feigned remorse. Agatha narrowed her eyes, but she couldn't pull her focus from the heavenly scent right under her nose as Tessa knelt beside the sofa. "I called your mother and asked what you loved to eat when you were sick," Tessa explained. "She gave me the recipe for this sweet corn cream soup with bacon and potatoes and everything you love. I swear I only let them sneak a few vegetables in for our baby's sake, okay?"

Agatha nodded frantically, practically drooling. Tessa laughed as a groan of pure bliss escaped Agatha after the very first spoonful.

"I also had them source fresh guavas. Your mom said you're obsessed with guava juice."

"My god, I think I'm going to have an orgasm," Agatha mumbled around a mouthful, shoveling the soup down so fast she was a breath away from just tipping the bowl back and swallowing it whole. Tessa chuckled softly, gently stroking her hair.

"I asked her to come stay with us until Nicky is born. I thought it would do you good."

"My mom is coming?" Agatha froze, her spoon hovering as her chest bloomed with warmth. Her eyes welled up the instant Tessa nodded. "Babe, thank you... I miss her so much." She choked out the words through sudden tears, but Tessa just shook her head dismissively.

"She was already flying out for the baby shower, but I paid to move her flight up so she can stay through the birth. I figure she'll know how to take care of you better than anyone else in this house right now."

Fuck the baby shower. Agatha wanted the entire event and every pompous guest on the list to go straight to hell. The absolute last thing she wanted was to force herself through the motions, pretending she wasn't passing out from sheer misery in front of a crowd she couldn't care less about. But with her mother there? She’d make the sacrifice.

"Thank you, baby, thank you," Agatha chanted, setting the bowl down on the tray to grab her wife's face and smother her in grateful kisses.

"Babysitters to the rescue!" Benito's cheerful voice punctured the moment.

Agatha craned her neck, her face breaking into a bright smile as he strode into the living room hauling a massive box, closely followed by Kate. Her eyes practically sparkled — he had actually pulled it off. God bless that boy.

"What on earth is in that box?" Tessa asked, her curiosity piqued.

Instantly, Agatha felt a sickening plunge in her stomach, a spike of cold panic threatening to make her lose the soup.

"Alex left some junk at the beach house and asked Benito to haul it up here so she could swing by and grab it later," Agatha blurted out with uncharacteristic haste, fighting to keep her body rigid. She ignored the tight, knowing line of Benito's mouth as he offered Tessa a polite nod to back up the improvised lie. "Wait, what are you two even doing here?" she quickly pivoted, narrowing her eyes between them. "Shouldn't you be at class?"

"It's two in the afternoon, Agatha," Kate replied with a fond, pitying look.

Agatha shot a wide-eyed, helpless glance at her wife. Tessa just offered a sympathetic shrug, pressing a kiss to Agatha's forehead — a silent apology for how thoroughly she had been dead to the world all day.

"I told them they could come over, and Benito mentioned he was heading this way anyway," Tessa explained. Agatha offered a long, weary yawn, nudging the tray aside so Tessa could set it on the coffee table. "I have to run down to the venue and finalize some logistics for the shower, okay? My mom called, too she wants to help prep some things, so I might be a while. But if you need anything at all, just call me and I'll come straight home."

"You guys are seriously still going through with the baby shower?" Benito demanded, arching a skeptical brow as he took in Agatha's thoroughly deplorable state.

"Canceling isn't an option," Tessa replied smoothly, pressing a parting kiss to the crown of Agatha's head. Agatha forced a tight, unconvincing smile in return. "Call me if you need anything, okay? Literally anything."

"Don't worry, I will."

"Take good care of her, please," Tessa instructed the two of them before heading toward the private elevator doors.

The second the doors slid shut, Benito practically vibrated with indignation. "You're actually not canceling it? Are you out of your mind?"

Agatha let out a long, heavy sigh, squeezing her eyes shut for a moment as she pressed a hand to her belly and laboriously tried to sit up. Kate was there in a flash, sliding a hand under her lower back while using the other to help bear the immense weight of the pregnancy. Agatha hissed out a breath of pure relief once she was finally propped into a somewhat bearable position.

"It's important, Benny," she answered, her voice dragging with bone-deep exhaustion. She grunted appreciatively as Kate claimed the opposite end of the sofa, hoisting Agatha's swollen feet into her lap to start a slow, soothing massage. "Most of Tessa's family flew in from Italy, and this is their first time celebrating something like this with us."

"Celebrating?" Benito scoffed incredulously.

Agatha caught the sharp, warning glare Kate shot his way, but Benito ignored it. He dropped the cardboard box next to his best friend and claimed the opposite side of the sectional, sitting directly across from Agatha with the coffee table between them.

"Agatha, have you ever seen that Twilight movie? Breaking Dawn? Because you are looking terrifyingly like Bella Swan right now."

"Thank you so very much," Agatha muttered acidly, watching him give a slow shake of his head. "Did you bring what I asked for?"

"You mean Alex's junk?" he teased, arching a brow. Agatha scraped together her remaining strength to raise a hand and flip him off. "Everything you requested, Your Majesty. Though I sincerely hope my sister doesn't notice she's suddenly missing six shirts and a sweater."

"You actually made him steal Rio's clothes for you?" Kate asked, letting out a disbelieving laugh.

Even with her cheeks burning a bright, mortified red, Agatha ignored the jab and simply held her arms out for the box. Kate slid it over immediately, and Agatha carefully rested the heavy cardboard across her lap before flipping the flaps open.

"What kind of unholy cravings are these?" Kate pressed.

"I had to, alright? How was she supposed to explain to Tessa that the baby came out looking exactly like my sister? Everyone knows if a pregnant woman gets hit with a specific craving, the kid takes on that person's face."

"I am desperate, okay?" Agatha snapped, cutting off the jokes. She ignored Benito's suppressed snicker while Kate playfully pressed her fingers over her lips like a zipper. "I just need to smell something that won't make me vomit."

Agatha plunged her hand into the box, her fingers wrapping around the first piece of fabric. Her brows knitted into a soft, tender expression as she pulled out an olive-green fleece sweater Rio had owned since she was a teenager. The fabric was practically threadbare and covered in pills, but she loved it all the same.

A heavy pang of guilt twisted in her chest for missing her so intensely — an aching, oversized longing that threatened to burst out when she least expected it. It was a persistent ache she had never managed to banish from her heart, and as much as she hated to admit it, hated doing it behind her wife's back, Riandra's scent had always been her absolute favorite thing in the world. No one had the right to judge her right now. She truly was desperate.

Agatha clutched the fabric tightly, bunching it into her fists before burying her face into the worn material and inhaling deeply. Her entire body went slack in an instant, washed over by the crisp, clean scent of brushwood, damp earth, and a subtle undertone of campfire smoke. God. For the first time in months, actual peace settled over her nervous system.

"That has got to be the single most homoerotic thing I have ever witnessed in my life," Kate declared, her voice hushed with awe.

Agatha cracked her eyes open, her face instantly catching fire with embarrassment under Kate's stunned, wide-eyed stare, while Benito cackled outright.

"You have absolutely no idea how desperate I am," Agatha mumbled, her face drawn with bone-deep exhaustion as she hugged the worn sweater tightly against her chest, gently stroking her swollen belly with her other hand. "I am constantly sick. I pass out from sheer exhaustion, yet I always wake up feeling like I haven't slept a wink. I just want to relax. I want to sleep. To actually, really sleep."

"Just look at the state of you. Going through with this baby shower is a psychotic idea."

"Benny, please," Agatha pleaded in a ragged whisper, but he merely shook his head, looking entirely unimpressed.

"I know this isn't your doing, so you don't need to justify it to me," he grumbled, visibly sulking. "But it pisses me off regardless. You are completely wrecked, Agatha."

"I am," she conceded on a long, heavy sigh. "But now that you've delivered my package, I think I might actually stand a chance at sleeping." She stifled a massive yawn, carefully folding one of Rio's shirts. She pressed her face into the fabric one last time to breathe in the scent before wedging it firmly between the sofa cushion and her head. She felt her tense muscles begin to melt into the cushions almost immediately.

"Seriously," Kate murmured, still sounding entirely baffled. "This is so... I'm at a complete loss for words."

"Please, no comments from the peanut gallery," Agatha requested, letting her eyes drift shut.

"So, what actually happened last night?" Benito shifted gears. Agatha forced her eyes open just in time to watch him slide off the sofa and drop cross-legged onto the plush living room rug, resting his back comfortably against the upholstery. "Tessa mentioned you ended up at the hospital. I thought you guys already had a small army of medical professionals hovering around the apartment."

"I honestly don't remember much of it, but apparently, I started having very severe contractions."

"Oh, Agatha, I'm so sorry," Kate murmured with sweet sincerity, and Agatha offered a slow, grateful nod.

"What is all this?" Benito asked, suddenly distracted. Agatha followed his gaze, watching him stare in morbid fascination at the absurd, towering mountain of paperwork stacked precariously on the coffee table.

"My record."

"Is this your actual medical chart?" he asked in horror, startled by the sheer thickness of the scattered stacks. Agatha let out a dry, exhausted laugh, shaking her head.

"It's my treatment history, asshole. It logs every single fertility round, the procedure descriptions, medical evaluations... every miserable detail up to this point."

"How many times did you guys even try?" Kate asked, her eyebrows shooting toward her hairline in disbelief at the sheer volume of paper.

"Far more times than I care to count."

"Holy shit, your donor list is right here!" Benito gasped excitedly, yanking a thick, stapled packet out from the middle of the pile.

"It's anonymous, Benny," Agatha mumbled without an ounce of enthusiasm.

"I know, but you know my friends and I have that group chat, and we pool money to make donations every month. Imagine if it's one of my friends?" he asked, finding the concept immensely funny, though Agatha merely shot him a withering death glare.

"I would rather die than know that the donor who helped conceive my child is one of your weird friends," she stared him down pointedly. Benito just shrugged, an amused, unrepentant smirk on his face. "Thank god the list is anonymous."

"Yes, but we have that group chat; I have all their registration numbers memorized."

"Benito, turn on the TV. Put on a movie. Go play a video game... do literally anything. I don't want to know. Just let me rest in peace."

"The chances of it being someone we know are astronomically low, but statistically, they still exist!" he insisted. Agatha rolled her eyes as he excitedly held the papers out to Kate, who merely shrugged and played along. "I won't say any names out loud, I swear! Kate reads the numbers, and I'll just say yes or no if I recognize them. It’s just to calculate the raw probability of finding an acquaintance in a massive database like this! We can use my friend group as a limited test sample to calculate against the total and—"

"You two nerds have fun, you have my express permission," Agatha muttered dismissively, yawning hugely as she pulled another of Rio's shirts from the box and threw it directly over her own face. "Do whatever you want, just stop talking to me. I just want to rest."

She heard their squeals of celebration and rolled her eyes beneath the safety of the fabric. Probability calculations. Since when do young people consider math a fun leisure activity?

For a few blissful minutes, eyes closed and Rio's comforting scent blanketing her face, Agatha finally managed to feel entirely relaxed. She only vaguely registered Kate's voice dictating a series of random numbers, followed by Benito answering with a rapid-fire sequence of nos. From what she could mentally track, there had been only one yes so far. She couldn't believe they were actually entertaining themselves with this nonsense, but deep down, she found it somewhat amusing. She almost wanted to see the final result of their absurd calculation when they compared their tiny list to the database's total volume.

Then, Kate dictated another number. Only this time, Benito said nothing. The dead, suffocating silence that suddenly swallowed the living room sent a strange, cold tension rippling across the very tip of Agatha's belly.

"What is it?" Kate's voice sounded uncertain, suddenly tight with tension.

Slowly, Agatha dragged the shirt off her face and turned her head toward Benito. The boy was utterly livid — white as a sheet, the hands gripping his cell phone trembling violently.

"What is it, Benny? Do you recognize him or not? Why do you look like you just shit your pants?" Kate insisted, her words tripping over themselves in her haste.

"What number... What number did you just say?" Benito asked, his voice barely a hollow whisper. The expression of sheer, unadulterated terror frozen on his face was enough to make Agatha's entire body stiffen on the sofa.

"Please, if my child's donor was a psychopath, I really don't want to know." Agatha tried to inject some levity into the room, but her own laugh came out tight and strained when she saw him merely swallow hard, actively refusing to meet her eyes.

"561917," Kate read the numbers again.

"For god's sake, Benito, what is it?" Agatha demanded, her patience snapping, the nervous edge in her voice spiking at his continued, horrifying silence.

Benito finally looked up. His eyes were bulging, unseeing:

"That's my number," he whispered.

Agatha gasped for breath, instantly dragging the bucket into her lap as her stomach plummeted and hot nausea surged like acid up her throat.

"And that..." Kate stuttered, her face draining entirely of color as she flicked her terrified gaze from the paper down to Agatha's massive belly. "That's the very last number on the list."

"What do you mean, the last number on the list?" Agatha choked out, a sudden, brutal wave of vertigo spinning the room violently around her.

"Your final try," Kate answered softly, her wide eyes locked back onto Agatha's stomach.

Agatha's body reacted long before her brain could even begin to process the sheer, impossible absurdity of the situation. She pitched violently forward, vomiting into the bucket with a force that nearly sent her tumbling right off the sofa. Benito scrambled desperately across the rug, throwing his arms around her to brace her back with one hand while gathering her hair with the other. Kate practically launched herself off the couch, hitting the floor to help anchor Agatha's weight and keep her securely propped up.

How? What? What is that supposed to mean? What on earth is happening? This has to be a joke. It has to be. A sick, twisted prank. No. Impossible. It can't be. No. Absolutely not.

"I am pregnant, and I am not well at all!" Agatha screamed, her voice raw and hoarse from stomach acid and pure panic as she shoved herself backward, desperately trying to retreat from the bucket. With the frantic, stunned help of her friends, she managed to lean back heavily against the cushions. "If this is some kind of sick joke you two cooked up, I swear to god it isn't funny!"

The next few minutes dissolved into a blur of frantic chaos and shouting. Agatha railed against the sheer madness of it, feeling completely dissociated from her own body, while Benito babbled a mile a minute. He desperately tried to defend himself, swearing he had no way of knowing and that the statistical probability of this happening was practically zero. Caught directly in the crossfire, Kate scrambled between them, fanning Agatha's face and trying desperately to manage the mounting crisis.

Agatha broke down, crying from sheer, unadulterated nerves. Her mind spun so fast it triggered a dizzying vertigo, bombarding her with a million catastrophic scenarios all at once. This had to be some cruel cosmic joke — a sadistic force swooping in to rob her of her peace the exact second her life finally seemed to be falling into place. What were the actual statistical odds of this happening? Reality felt like it was warping around the edges of the room, and no matter how desperately Benito tried to explain the math, she simply refused to accept that it was real. Her mind kept violently looping back to Tessa. How on earth was she supposed to explain this? It was impossible. It couldn't possibly be real.

"How am I supposed to explain this to Tessa?" Agatha gasped for air, while Kate patiently fanned her, whispering frantic reassurances that she needed to breathe and everything would be alright.

"You don't need to explain anything," Benito pleaded urgently, dropping to his knees right in front of her. As much as Agatha wanted to scream and tear her hair out, her heart squeezed at the raw, disoriented terror mirrored in his eyes. "You don't have to explain a damn thing. Nobody else ever has to know about this, Agatha. It makes no difference whatsoever; it changes absolutely nothing."

"How does it not change anything, Benito? How am I supposed to look people in the eye and tell them you are the..." Agatha froze, her eyes blowing wide with absolute dread. "That my child is your child? Fuck, my child is your child!" she shrieked in a high-pitched panic, her hands trembling violently.

Benito shook his head furiously, his hands clamping down hard over hers to anchor her.

"He is not my son," Benito stressed with absolute, unyielding resolution, holding her gaze steady. Agatha took deep, ragged breaths, forcing herself to anchor to his certainty. "He is not my son, Agatha. I am not his father; I don't want to be a father. He is your son, all yours. He belongs to you and Tessa. You don't owe an explanation to a single soul because this doesn't alter the facts. I love your baby because he's yours, and I would have loved him regardless. I am just a doting uncle. One of your best friends. I am going to be a part of his life because I am a part of yours, and nothing more. That is all I am, and that is all I will ever be to him. He is not my son."

"It's just like that little seed story!" Kate suddenly chimed in with frantic, overly cheerful optimism, trying desperately to help. Agatha blinked, staring at her wide-eyed. What the actual fuck was this nonsense about a seed story? "When two mommies love each other and want to have a baby, they get a very pretty pot together, fill it with rich dirt, and plant the seed. They do everything together, and then the watering can comes along to water the dirt so the little plant can grow," Kate explained as though she were recounting a harmless nursery rhyme. "Benny is just the watering can! It could have been any other watering can; the little plant would have grown up just the same."

"What?" Agatha and Benito blurted out in perfect unison, making Kate shrink back sheepishly into her shoulders.

"It's just a helpful metaphor to explain that nothing fundamentally changes," Kate insisted stubbornly, reaching out to gently stroke Agatha's swollen belly. "The baby is yours, Agatha; he's already right in there. He was always going to be yours, no matter who helped him grow."

Agatha went completely silent. Kate's words hung in the air, but the frantic gears inside Agatha's mind had suddenly shifted in a wholly unexpected direction.

"My son..." Agatha whispered, her eyes fixed in a wide, glassy stare on empty space. "My son is a Vidal."

Confronted with her sudden catatonic state, Kate and Benito exchanged a grim, knowing look, silently agreeing on their next move.

"Yep. We broke her," Kate declared solemnly, pulling out her phone. "I'm calling Alex."

***

Present day

That day had been unbearably intense for Rio. It had been years since she last unraveled like that — not since the earliest, most grueling days of her sobriety. That total loss of control, the suffocating sensation of being trapped between her own soul and body, was a terror that had haunted her for a lifetime. She remembered the first time it happened, right after losing her mother, and the countless times she was forced to navigate subsequent losses and her own overwhelming emotions. Whenever she felt too deeply, Rio lost her grip. That was exactly why quitting drinking had been so agonizing: alcohol had been her anchor, chaining her safely to her physical form and keeping the blinding fog of her mind at bay.

What she found hardest to admit was that talking actually helped. Watching her father waste away had driven her back into her shell — the same impenetrable armor she had worn her entire life. She knew that sanctuary was a double-edged sword, acting as both a safe haven and a prison. Only when she finally stepped outside of it and began to speak did she find a sliver of peace, even while still haunted by hidden fragments of herself. Those fragments now filled her with dread; she could feel herself losing control over them, over herself.

She didn't know how she had reached this breaking point today, but she knew she had been shrinking back, day by day. Only this time, her retreat wasn't driven by her usual self-deprecation. Rio was pulling away because she was terrified.

She harbored no bitterness toward Agatha — quite the opposite. She knew with absolute certainty that Agatha was the person she had loved most in her life. Through every dizzying high and devastating low of their volatile relationship, Rio had never felt anything but pure love for her. Even during the times she had unjustly blamed Agatha for her wounds, desperately trying to numb her own tearing pain. That blame had been nothing but a web of lies spun to make herself feel better. Agatha was never the architect of their ruin. Rio was angry, yes, but at herself. For years, she had shifted the blame onto Agatha's shoulders simply because she couldn't bear to carry her own crushing weight alone.

Everything was different now, and Rio was paralyzed by it. Just months ago, her life had been perfectly predictable, her days running on a comfortable, unending loop. Since childhood, she had found safety in routine, rising and resting with the sun. But now, no two days were alike. She was slowly relearning her brother, stumbling through the process of merging their lives, facing a brand-new scenario every single day. While she was thrilled to have him back, the constant shift left her restless and cornered. All she wanted was to saddle a horse and ride off into the horizon, never to return.

That was why her afternoon ride with Natasha had been a lifeline. They had ridden aimlessly for hours, finally allowing Rio to catch her breath.

Natasha possessed a sly, elusive charm that Rio loved. She knew exactly when to listen, when to speak, and when to sit in comfortable silence. Sometimes, it felt like her best friend could read her mind — a profound comfort that also stung with a quiet vulnerability, born from the paralyzing fear of disappointing her.

Rio often felt like the physical embodiment of fear — a gray, shapeless creature shifting forms just to hide how hollow she was underneath. She feared feeling, talking, and listening. She feared the passage of time, the future, getting attached only to lose people, and watching the world change around her. Deep down, the only absolute truth she knew was that she was profoundly afraid.

Natasha always said fear was nothing but an accumulation of unshared secrets. Rio never argued, knowing she was a vault of secrets she fully intended to take to her grave.

But today, she had spoken. And listened. And thought. Despite the raw terror of opening up and exposing her edges, she knew Natasha was the one person she could truly trust. And whether anyone believed it or not, Rio really was trying to heal.

After all that introspection, Rio realized her deepest anguish wasn't just the world changing around her, but the terrifying realization that she was changing, too.

She didn't know how or why the transformation had begun, but she was changing. Not necessarily for better or worse — she was coming undone, reforming along entirely new contours. Having spent a lifetime meticulously sculpting herself to fit one exact mold, this expansion left her entirely unmoored. If her own footing wasn't solid, what was certain? She felt small and insecure.

Initially, she had blamed her grief, assuming the sudden absence of her father had knocked her off course. But now she recognized the exact opposite was true: her terror was rooted in the arrivals — Benito, Kate, Agatha, and Nicky — and the imminent goodbyes that shadowed them.

She felt catapulted back to her youth, drifting with the wind while frantically trying to force the rest of the world to stand still. All these sudden arrivals forced Rio to mold and remold herself daily, desperately trying to ensure they never mutated into departures, even though she knew she had zero control over the outcome.

Rio wasn't angry that Agatha was here; she was terrified of the prospect of having to lose her all over again. And that fear was precisely why she could feel herself locking all her doors once more.

What Natasha had made her realize — just as she had years ago — was that when you barricade your doors, you don't merely keep the outside world at bay; you trap yourself on the inside, entirely alone with nowhere to run. And it was within the hollow echo of that emptiness that her fears inevitably reared their heads again.

So there she sat late into the night, sinking into her father's favorite armchair, trying to force her chaotic thoughts to match the tranquil rhythm of the darkness — the steady hum of crickets, the freezing wind tugging at her hair, and the comforting crackle of the campfire. She was desperately searching for a way to make peace with the person she was becoming, though the unspoken truth remained: she was terrified. She was bone-tired of carrying that terror and simply wanted to exist without locked doors, she just had no idea how. Lacking answers, she sought solace in the void her father had left behind, wrapped thickly in a faux-leather coat while taking slow sips of a beer.

Rio had been pleading so desperately with the universe for a sign that she nearly let out a nervous laugh when a familiar silhouette — one she knew more intimately than anyone else on earth — emerged from the dark and stepped onto her porch. Seconds later, bathed in the warm, amber glow of the fire, Rio saw her clearly. Agatha. Her voluminous hair catching the wind, arms wrapped tightly around a thick white sweater, wearing a cautious yet achingly tender expression, as though silently asking for permission to exist in that space.

Rio sighed, shaking her head at herself. The universe possessed a deeply twisted sense of humor. But having just resolved to stop locking her doors, she swallowed the frantic hammer of her heart and forced her lips into a welcoming smile.

"Hey, neighbor," Agatha greeted softly, a contained smile touching her lips.

"Neighbor," Rio echoed, tasting the word on her tongue, struck by a flicker of playful amusement she hadn't seen on Agatha's face in over a decade. "So I've heard."

This time, Rio didn't dart her eyes away. Instead, she let herself dive straight into those familiar blue eyes, watching them crinkle with an answering smile. Rio smiled back. She had once heard someone claim that blue was a color of pure calm; she had never put much stock in the metaphor, but standing there, she could swear to god she finally understood it. For the first time in an eternity, she allowed herself to simply look at Agatha — truly look at her — and nearly let out a sigh. God, it had genuinely been so long.

Agatha was still Agatha, yet entirely a different woman. The flighty girlishness had vanished, replaced by a grounded maturity that suited her remarkably well. Fine expression lines now traced her face, softening the skin around her eyes. She seemed firm, stable.

Though Rio recognized her, she couldn't honestly claim to know her anymore. Yet that realization didn't feel unsettling. For the first time in her life, she saw Agatha standing with her feet planted firmly on the ground.

"May I?" Agatha asked, nodding toward the cooler of beer. Rio gave her assent.

She settled right beside her in what used to be Rio's favorite armchair, popping open a can with a casual familiarity that caught Rio off guard. Agatha hadn't been a beer drinker. But this was a new woman, and Rio was in no position to judge, especially after coming to terms with the fact that she herself was no longer who she thought she was.

"So you mean to tell me you've heard?" Agatha broke the silence with an easy, casual cadence. Rio pressed her lips into a half-smile and offered a calm nod.

"You know how it is in a small town," Rio played along, keeping the banter light as Agatha took a slow sip. "I saw the commotion at the lake house recently, all those moving trucks going back and forth."

"If you think about it, that house was always mine," Agatha countered with a playful glint in her eye.

"That's true," Rio conceded, opening her mouth to keep the thread going, only to freeze when she caught sight of Agatha's left hand on the can. The white-gold ring was entirely gone, replaced only by a faint band of pale skin left behind by time. Rio arched an eyebrow. When she looked back up, Agatha was watching her, silently daring her to finish her thought. "You aren't wearing your wedding ring."

Agatha blinked in brief surprise, glancing down at her own hand before raising her gaze back to Rio's. Instead of the sharp reprimand she half-expected, Agatha simply shrugged.

"I'm getting divorced, Rio," she said smoothly.

Rio’s brows knitted together, and she swallowed so hard she had to knock back three quick gulps of beer just to clear her throat.

"What on earth did Miss Sunshine do to break the spell?" Rio asked, forcing a light, breezy tone.

"Why automatically assume she did something?" Agatha shot back. Though it sounded playful, Rio could spot the sudden defensive edge.

"Because I always figured she was a bit dull," Rio teased with a crooked smile.

Agatha laughed — an uninhibited sound that caught Rio entirely off guard. A wave of unexpected tenderness washed over her as she realized just how long it had been since she last heard that laugh.

"Fair point. Actually, I was the one who asked for it," Agatha admitted, offering a sheepish little shrug. Rio nodded vaguely, desperately trying to ignore the frantic hammering of her heart against her ribs.

"Good for you, I suppose," Rio murmured, attempting to play it cool. "If you must know, I never really liked her much anyway."

Agatha threw her head back and laughed aloud, a full, bright sound that made it impossible for Rio not to join in.

"You're joking? I never would have guessed," Agatha murmured through her amusement, while Rio offered a mask of feigned innocence.

"Are you alright with it? The divorce, I mean?" Rio asked once the laughter subsided, her voice softening into something cautious and gentle. She felt a profound wave of relief when Agatha nodded.

"It was simply the right thing to do," Agatha replied. Rio felt a quiet fascination stirring inside her; even if she didn't know this version of Agatha, she knew her well enough to see that far more was hiding beneath the surface. "It hasn't been easy, but looking back now, I can even find some dark humor in it."

"Humor?" Rio echoed, her eyebrows lifting in surprise.

"You know... when we were younger, we were so arrogantly certain of everything. I was so certain of everything," Agatha reflected, her tone carrying a hint of self-deprecation. "The reality is, we knew absolutely nothing." She locked her blue eyes straight onto Rio's, and Rio nodded, feeling the heavy truth of those words settle deep in her chest. "I was drowning in convictions in a world where nothing is ever guaranteed, having no clue that, ultimately, nothing turns out the way you plan. Time passes, yes, but we change right along with it."

"Speak for yourself, I haven't changed a bit," Rio countered with a theatrical display of arrogance, hoping to deflect the sudden gravity of the conversation.

"Of course you haven't," Agatha agreed, her dry humor coaxing a soft laugh out of Rio before she even finished the thought. "Look how many years have vanished, and the very moment I arrive, I find you drunk and snapping at anyone who dares look your way."

Rio opened and closed her mouth in utter disbelief, watching Agatha narrow her eyes in quiet evaluation, testing to see if she had crossed a line. But all Rio did was break into a sudden laugh, and Agatha quickly joined her.

"Low blow," Rio pointed an accusing finger. Agatha just rolled her eyes.

"You've changed, Rio," Agatha murmured, her voice dropping into a register so tender Rio could practically feel it against her skin.

"I know," Rio agreed quietly. "You've changed, too."

"You have no idea," Agatha whispered, unable to suppress a shaky, tremulous laugh. "I feel like a completely different person now."

"I can see that," Rio replied immediately, rewarded by a soft, half-formed smile from Agatha.

"I know we haven't really spoken since Pedra Purpura, but I genuinely wanted to talk to you. Just... talk," Agatha confessed in a gentle, cautious tone, offering a bashful shrug. Rio nodded, biting the inside of her cheek to manage a sudden wave of anxiety, because deep down, that was all she wanted, too. "I'm staying this time. For good."

Rio already knew; Nicky had let it slip, and Natasha had confirmed it. She had watched the house undergo frantic renovations with her own eyes. She knew. Yet, despite all of that, nothing could have prepared her for the sheer impact of those words — the heavy, echoing weight of hearing everything she had ever dreamed of, even if it no longer carried the exact same meaning it once had. Not like before.

"I have to admit, I was a little surprised," Rio said, swirling the beer can in her hand to mask the sudden spike of nerves. "Out of everywhere in the world, you chose the absolute edge of nowhere." She kept her tone light, tossing it out as a joke to avoid throwing open the doors she had kept firmly bolted for a decade.

Agatha offered a faint smile, though a shadow of melancholy lingered in her blue eyes.

"I've traveled a lot," she replied, her voice matching Rio's cautious ease. They were both walking on eggshells, though the fragility didn't feel dangerous. "I've seen a lot of different skies." She paused, and Rio's brow furrowed, a sudden warmth unfurling in her chest as Agatha held her gaze. It was a look stripped of the guardedness they had worn for years. "But I finally figured out that this little piece right here"—she lifted her can toward the stars—"is the one I love most."

The words hit Rio like a crashing wave — not the terrifying kind that pulls you under, but the kind you dive through, coming up laughing on the other side. She felt a sudden, bracing freshness, like the mist of a waterfall hitting her face when she was twelve years old. Something soft and long-dormant bloomed in her chest.

"I'm glad you're here," Rio confessed. As the words left her mouth, a ton of invisible weight slipped from her shoulders.

Agatha smiled. "Me too. I honestly didn't realize how much I missed this place."

"I missed you, Agatha," Rio whispered, her voice thick.

Agatha let out a shaky sigh, her blue eyes shimmering with unshed tears as she offered a tender nod. "I missed you too, Rio. More than you know."

Silence settled between them, heavy and profound. They just stared at each other, both feeling the slow, inevitable collapse of the walls that had separated them for so long. The quiet stretched out, speaking volumes they still lacked the courage to say aloud.

"I never stopped writing to you," Agatha confessed softly, her brows pulling together.

Rio nodded, a pang of heavy regret in her chest. "I know."

"Did you ever read them?"

"No," Rio answered truthfully, her heart squeezing at the flash of sadness in Agatha's eyes. "But I know a lot more than you think."

"How?" Agatha asked, her skepticism clear, but Rio only smiled faintly.

"My dad was a talker. Every time he flew back from California, he'd spend hours filling me in on everything," Rio explained with a casual shrug. Agatha nodded, taking a slow sip of her beer. "I traveled a fair amount, too."

"So I've heard," Agatha murmured, an impressed smile touching her lips.

"It's not exactly my scene, but it comes with the job," Rio deflected under Agatha's intense gaze. "I went to California a few times. Managed to see you from a distance."

"You talked to Alex, didn't you?" Agatha asked, her tone entirely unimpressed, prompting Rio to wince in a guilty grimace. "I knew it!"

"I always cared about you, Agatha. I couldn't just pretend you didn't exist anymore."

"I know the feeling," Agatha agreed softly. "I actually went to a few of your launches, the artisanal ones."

"Did you like them?" Rio asked, instantly curious.

Agatha laughed. "I collect them," she said, raising a triumphant brow. Rio couldn't stop the proud, helpless grin that spread across her face.
